P1 · Probability Basics and Counting


                  
                  Why this matters for the TF 
                  
                

No past term final asks “define a sample space”, but every probability question is built on this note.
Combinations are used every time you pick balls, pens or cars at random (2021-22 Q6(c), 2023-24 Q2(b)).
The addition and complement rules appear inside almost every Bayes and distribution question.
Treat this note as a warm-up: solve every problem below until counting feels automatic.


Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize: the only formulas you need here 
                  
                

Classical probability
Use when all outcomes are equally likely.
P(A)=\frac{n(A)}{n(S)}
Complement
Use for “at least one” and “neither”.
P(A^c)=1-P(A)
Addition rule (two events)
Use for “A or B”.
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)
Addition rule (three events)
P(A\cup B\cup C)=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)-P(A\cap B)-P(A\cap C)-P(B\cap C)+P(A\cap B\cap C)
De Morgan
Use for “neither”.
(A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c
P(\text{neither})=1-P(A\cup B)
Combination
Order does not matter. Use for “drawn at random”, committees, samples.
{}^nC_r=\binom{n}{r}=\frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}
Permutation
Order matters. Use for arrangements and posts like president/secretary.
{}^nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}
Odds in favour of A are a:b
P(A)=\frac{a}{a+b}
Odds against A are a:b
P(A)=\frac{b}{a+b}


Two short definitions are enough for this course.
Events are mutually exclusive if they cannot happen together, so P(A\cap B)=0.
Events are exhaustive if together they cover the whole sample space.
A set of events that is both mutually exclusive and exhaustive is a partition. That is exactly what you need for the total probability rule and Bayes’ theorem in P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes.


                  
                  Do not mix these up 
                  
                

Mutually exclusive (“cannot happen together”) is not the same as independent (“one does not change the chance of the other”).
2023-24 Q1(a) asked about this; the exam answer is in P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes.



Problem types you will face
Type 1 — Drawing items at random (combinations)
How to recognise it: “a bag contains … balls, … are drawn at random”, “a committee is chosen”, “a lot contains defective items”.
Recipe:

Count the total number of samples with \binom{N}{n}.
Count the favourable samples by choosing each colour separately and multiplying.
Divide.

General formula (three types of item):
P(\text{exactly } x \text{ of type 1 and } y \text{ of type 2})=\frac{\binom{N_1}{x}\binom{N_2}{y}\binom{N_3}{n-x-y}}{\binom{N}{n}}


                  
                  Example 1.1 (lecture) — black balls 
                  
                

Given. A bag has 10 balls, 4 black and 6 white. Three are drawn without replacement. Find P(\text{exactly 2 black}).
Step 1 — Total samples.
\binom{10}{3}=120
Step 2 — Favourable samples. Choose 2 of the 4 black and 1 of the 6 white.
\binom42\binom61=6\times6=36
Answer.
P(\text{exactly 2 black})=\frac{36}{120}=\mathbf{0.3}




                  
                  Practice 1.2 (TF style) — three colours 
                  
                

Given. A bag contains 5 red, 4 white and 3 blue balls. Three balls are drawn at random. Find the probability that (i) all are red, (ii) one of each colour is drawn, (iii) at least one is blue.
Step 1 — Total samples. There are 12 balls.
\binom{12}{3}=220
Step 2 — (i) All red. There are \binom53=10 ways.
P=\frac{10}{220}=\frac1{22}\approx0.0455
Step 3 — (ii) One of each colour. There are \binom51\binom41\binom31=60 ways.
P=\frac{60}{220}=\frac3{11}\approx0.2727
Step 4 — (iii) At least one blue. This has many cases, so use the complement “no blue”. With no blue, all 3 balls come from the 9 non-blue balls: \binom93=84 ways.
P(\text{at least one blue})=1-\frac{84}{220}=\frac{34}{55}\approx0.6182
Answer. (i) 0.0455, (ii) 0.2727, (iii) 0.6182.




                  
                  Practice 1.3 (TF style) — committee 
                  
                

Given. A committee of 4 is chosen at random from 6 men and 4 women. Find the probability that it contains (i) exactly 2 women, (ii) at least one woman.
Step 1 — Total committees.
\binom{10}{4}=210
Step 2 — (i) Exactly 2 women. Choose 2 of the 4 women and 2 of the 6 men.
\binom42\binom62=6\times15=90
P=\frac{90}{210}=\frac37\approx0.4286
Step 3 — (ii) At least one woman. The complement is “no woman”, i.e. all 4 are men: \binom64=15 ways.
P(\text{at least one woman})=1-\frac{15}{210}=\frac{13}{14}\approx0.9286
Answer. (i) 0.4286, (ii) 0.9286.




                  
                  Practice 1.4 — cards 
                  
                

Given. Two cards are drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52. Find the probability that (i) one is a king and the other a queen, (ii) both are of the same suit.
Step 1 — Total.
\binom{52}{2}=1326
Step 2 — (i) King and queen. One king from 4 and one queen from 4 gives 4\times4=16 ways.
P=\frac{16}{1326}=\frac{8}{663}\approx0.0121
Step 3 — (ii) Same suit. Choose the suit (4 ways), then 2 cards of that suit, \binom{13}{2}=78. Total 4\times78=312.
P=\frac{312}{1326}=\frac4{17}\approx0.2353
Answer. (i) 0.0121, (ii) 0.2353.




                  
                  Permutation or combination? 
                  
                

Ask: “If I swap two chosen objects, is it a different result?”
Choosing a team of 3 from 5 is a combination: {}^5C_3=10.
Electing a president, vice-president and secretary from 5 is a permutation: {}^5P_3=60.
In TF bag problems it is almost always combinations.



Type 2 — Overlapping events (addition rule and “neither”)
How to recognise it: percentages of people who do A, do B, and do both.
Recipe:

Write P(A), P(B) and P(A\cap B).
Use the addition rule for “at least one”.
Use 1-P(A\cup B) for “neither”.
Use P(A)-P(A\cap B) for “A only”.



                  
                  Example 2.1 (lecture) — newspapers 
                  
                

Given. In an office of 100 employees, 75 read an English daily, 50 read a Bangla daily and 40 read both. Find the probability that a randomly chosen employee reads at least one paper, and neither.
P(E)=0.75, P(B)=0.50, P(E\cap B)=0.40.
Step 1 — At least one.
P(E\cup B)=0.75+0.50-0.40=0.85
Step 2 — Neither.
P(\text{neither})=1-0.85=0.15
Answer. At least one: 0.85. Neither: 0.15.




                  
                  Practice 2.2 — rings and necklaces (lecture style) 
                  
                

Given. At a college, 60% of students wear neither a ring nor a necklace, 20% wear a ring and 30% wear a necklace. Find the probability that a student wears both.
Step 1 — At least one. “Neither” is 0.60, so
P(R\cup N)=1-0.60=0.40
Step 2 — Rearrange the addition rule.
\begin{aligned}
P(R\cap N)&=P(R)+P(N)-P(R\cup N)\\
&=0.20+0.30-0.40\\
&=0.10
\end{aligned}
Answer. P(\text{both})=\mathbf{0.10}.




                  
                  Practice 2.3 — subjects 
                  
                

Given. In a class, 60% passed Mathematics, 50% passed Physics and 30% passed both. Find the probability that a student passed (i) at least one subject, (ii) neither, (iii) Mathematics only.
Step 1 — (i) At least one.
P(M\cup P)=0.6+0.5-0.3=0.8
Step 2 — (ii) Neither.
P(\text{neither})=1-0.8=0.2
Step 3 — (iii) Mathematics only.
P(M \text{ only})=P(M)-P(M\cap P)=0.6-0.3=0.3
Answer. (i) 0.8, (ii) 0.2, (iii) 0.3.




                  
                  Example 2.4 (lecture) — men or brown eyes 
                  
                

Given. A class has 10 men and 20 women; half of each group has brown eyes. Find P(\text{man or brown eyes}).
Step 1 — Count. Of 30 people, 10 are men, 15 have brown eyes and 5 are brown-eyed men.
Step 2 — Addition rule.
P(M\cup Br)=\frac{10}{30}+\frac{15}{30}-\frac{5}{30}=\frac{20}{30}
Answer. P=\mathbf{2/3}.



Type 3 — Odds
How to recognise it: “odds in favour” or “odds against”.
Recipe:

Convert the odds to probabilities first.
Then solve as a normal (usually independent) probability problem.

Odds in favour a:b:
P=\frac{a}{a+b}
Odds against a:b:
P=\frac{b}{a+b}


                  
                  Example 3.1 (lecture) — two students 
                  
                

Given. The odds against X solving a problem are 8:6 and the odds in favour of Y solving it are 14:16. They work independently. Find the probability that (a) both solve, (b) at least one solves, (c) exactly one solves.
Step 1 — Convert odds to probabilities.
P(X)=\frac{6}{14}=\frac37,\qquad P(\bar X)=\frac47
P(Y)=\frac{14}{30}=\frac7{15},\qquad P(\bar Y)=\frac8{15}
Step 2 — (a) Both solve.
P(X\cap Y)=\frac37\cdot\frac7{15}=\frac15
Step 3 — (b) At least one solves.
\begin{aligned}
P(\text{at least one})&=1-P(\bar X)P(\bar Y)\\
&=1-\frac47\cdot\frac8{15}\\
&=1-\frac{32}{105}=\frac{73}{105}\approx0.695
\end{aligned}
Step 4 — (c) Exactly one solves. Remove the “both” case from “at least one”.
P(\text{exactly one})=\frac{73}{105}-\frac{21}{105}=\frac{52}{105}\approx0.495
Answer. (a) 1/5, (b) 0.695, (c) 0.495.




                  
                  Practice 3.2 
                  
                

Given. The odds against A hitting a target are 3:2 and the odds in favour of B hitting it are 4:5. They shoot independently. Find the probability that (i) both hit, (ii) exactly one hits, (iii) the target is hit.
Step 1 — Convert odds.
P(A)=\frac{2}{5},\qquad P(B)=\frac{4}{9}
Step 2 — (i) Both hit.
\frac25\cdot\frac49=\frac{8}{45}\approx0.178
Step 3 — (ii) Exactly one hits.
\begin{aligned}
P(A)P(\bar B)+P(\bar A)P(B)&=\frac25\cdot\frac59+\frac35\cdot\frac49\\
&=\frac{10+12}{45}=\frac{22}{45}\approx0.489
\end{aligned}
Step 4 — (iii) Target is hit (at least one hits).
1-P(\bar A)P(\bar B)=1-\frac35\cdot\frac59=1-\frac13=\frac23
Answer. (i) 0.178, (ii) 0.489, (iii) 2/3.



Type 4 — “At least one” with independent events
How to recognise it: several independent parts, trials or people; “at least one fails”, “the problem is solved”.
Recipe:
P(\text{at least one})=1-P(\text{none})
and P(\text{none}) is a product of complements.


                  
                  Practice 4.1 — machine components 
                  
                

Given. A machine has three independent components that fail with probabilities 0.10, 0.20 and 0.05. Find the probability that (i) at least one fails, (ii) exactly one fails.
Step 1 — (i) None fails.
P(\text{none fails})=0.9\times0.8\times0.95=0.684
P(\text{at least one fails})=1-0.684=0.316
Step 2 — (ii) Exactly one fails. Add the three “only this one fails” cases.
\begin{aligned}
P&=0.1(0.8)(0.95)+0.9(0.2)(0.95)+0.9(0.8)(0.05)\\
&=0.076+0.171+0.036\\
&=0.283
\end{aligned}
Answer. (i) 0.316, (ii) 0.283.




                  
                  Practice 4.2 — how many trials? 
                  
                

Given. How many times must a fair die be rolled so that the probability of getting at least one six is at least 0.9?
Step 1 — Set up the inequality.
P(\text{at least one six in } n \text{ rolls})=1-\left(\frac56\right)^n\ge0.9
\left(\frac56\right)^n\le0.1
Step 2 — Take logs.
n\ge\frac{\ln 0.1}{\ln(5/6)}=12.6
Step 3 — Check. 1-(5/6)^{13}=0.9065, while 12 rolls give only 0.8878.
Answer. n=\mathbf{13} rolls.



Extra practice


                  
                  Answers (try first) 
                  
                

1. From 8 red and 4 green pens, 3 are chosen. P(exactly 1 green)?
Answer: \binom41\binom82/\binom{12}3=112/220=28/55\approx0.509.
2. P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4, P(A\cup B)=0.7. Find P(A\cap B) and P(\text{neither}).
Answer: 0.2 and 0.3.
3. Odds in favour of an event are 5:3. Find its probability.
Answer: 5/8.
4. Three coins are tossed. P(at least one head)?
Answer: 1-1/8=7/8.
5. In how many ways can a president, secretary and treasurer be chosen from 7 members?
Answer: {}^7P_3=210.
6. Two dice are thrown. P(sum = 8)?
Answer: 5/36.

P2 · Conditional Probability, Independence and Bayes’ Rule


                  
                  Why this matters for the TF 
                  
                

This is the most reliable topic in Section A.
It appeared in 2019-20 Q7(a) (truth serum), 2022-23 Q1(a) (ball transfer) and Q1(b) (three machines), and 2023-24 Q1(a), (b) and (c) (a whole 35-mark question). Expect one full question from this note.
The 2022-23 and 2023-24 versions are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions; every problem shape they use is practised below.


Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize 
                  
                

Conditional probability
Use when something is “given” or “known”.
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}
Multiplication law
Use for events happening one after another.
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B\mid A)
Independence test
A and B are independent if and only if
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)
Total probability
Use when the final event can happen through several routes B_1,\dots,B_k.
P(A)=\sum_{i} P(B_i)\,P(A\mid B_i)
Bayes’ rule
Use when the result is given and you want the probability of a route.
P(B_r\mid A)=\frac{P(B_r)\,P(A\mid B_r)}{\sum_i P(B_i)\,P(A\mid B_i)}



Theory the TF actually asks
Define the multiplication law (2023-24 Q1(b))


                  
                  Exam answer: multiplication law of probability 
                  
                

For two events A and B, the probability of their simultaneous occurrence is equal to the unconditional probability of one of them multiplied by the conditional probability of the other, given that the first has occurred.
Symbolically,
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B\mid A)=P(B)\,P(A\mid B)
For three events,
P(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3)=P(A_1)\,P(A_2\mid A_1)\,P(A_3\mid A_1\cap A_2)
and so on for k events.
If A and B are independent, then P(B\mid A)=P(B) and the law becomes
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)
Example. Drawing two cards without replacement,
P(\text{both aces})=\frac{4}{52}\cdot\frac{3}{51}=\frac{1}{221}


Can two events be mutually exclusive and independent at the same time? (2023-24 Q1(a))


                  
                  Exam answer 
                  
                

If A and B are mutually exclusive, then A\cap B=\varnothing, so
P(A\cap B)=0
If they are also independent, then
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)
Together these give P(A)P(B)=0, which is possible only if P(A)=0 or P(B)=0.
Therefore two events with non-zero probabilities can never be both mutually exclusive and independent.
In fact mutually exclusive events are strongly dependent: if A occurs, B certainly does not, so P(B\mid A)=0\ne P(B). The only exception is the trivial case where one event has probability zero.
Example. One roll of a die, A=\{1\}, B=\{2\}. They are mutually exclusive, but
P(A\cap B)=0\ne\frac16\cdot\frac16
so they are not independent.



Problem types you will face
Type 1 — Two-stage problems: ball transfer and “choose a bag” (total probability)
How to recognise it: “one ball is transferred unseen from bag I to bag II, then a ball is drawn from bag II”, or “a bag is selected at random, then a ball is drawn”.
Recipe:

Define the first-stage events (they form a partition).
After a transfer, recount bag II, which now has one more ball.
Multiply along each branch and add.



                  
                  Practice 1.1 (same shape as 2022-23 Q1(a) and 2023-24 Q1(b)) 
                  
                

Given. Bag I has 6 red and 4 green balls. Bag II has 3 red and 7 green balls. One ball is moved from bag I to bag II unseen, then a ball is drawn from bag II. Find P(red).
Step 1 — Name the first-stage events. Let R_1 = “transferred ball is red” and G_1 = “transferred ball is green”.
P(R_1)=\frac{6}{10},\qquad P(G_1)=\frac4{10}
Let R_2 = “ball drawn from bag II is red”.
Step 2 — Recount bag II for each branch. If red was moved, bag II has 4 red out of 11. If green was moved, bag II has 3 red out of 11.
P(R_2\mid R_1)=\frac4{11}
P(R_2\mid G_1)=\frac3{11}
Step 3 — Total probability.
\begin{aligned}
P(R_2)&=\frac{6}{10}\cdot\frac{4}{11}+\frac{4}{10}\cdot\frac{3}{11}\\
&=\frac{24+12}{110}\\
&=\frac{18}{55}\approx0.3273
\end{aligned}
Answer. P(\text{red})=\mathbf{18/55\approx0.3273}.


The tree for this problem looks like this. Multiply along each branch and add the branches that end in the event you want.
flowchart LR
    S((Start)) -- "6/10" --> R1["Red transferred<br/>Bag II: 4R, 7G"]
    S -- "4/10" --> G1["Green transferred<br/>Bag II: 3R, 8G"]
    R1 -- "4/11" --> A1["Red drawn: 24/110"]
    R1 -- "7/11" --> A2["Green drawn"]
    G1 -- "3/11" --> A3["Red drawn: 12/110"]
    G1 -- "8/11" --> A4["Green drawn"]



                  
                  Practice 1.2 — two balls transferred 
                  
                

Given. Bag I has 3 white and 2 black balls; bag II has 2 white and 4 black balls. Two balls are transferred at random from bag I to bag II, then one ball is drawn from bag II. Find P(white).
Step 1 — What can be transferred. The two transferred balls can be WW, WB or BB, out of \binom52=10 ways.
P(WW)=\frac{\binom32}{10}=\frac{3}{10}
P(WB)=\frac{3\cdot2}{10}=\frac{6}{10}
P(BB)=\frac{1}{10}
Step 2 — Recount bag II. After the transfer, bag II has 8 balls, with 4, 3 or 2 white respectively.
Step 3 — Total probability.
\begin{aligned}
P(W)&=\frac{3}{10}\cdot\frac48+\frac{6}{10}\cdot\frac38+\frac{1}{10}\cdot\frac28\\
&=\frac{12+18+2}{80}\\
&=\frac{32}{80}=0.4
\end{aligned}
Answer. P(\text{white})=\mathbf{0.4}.




                  
                  Practice 1.3 — choose a bag, then reverse it with Bayes 
                  
                

Given. Urn 1 has 2 white and 3 red balls; urn 2 has 4 white and 1 red. A fair coin decides the urn, then one ball is drawn. (i) Find P(white). (ii) If the ball is white, find the probability it came from urn 1.
Step 1 — (i) Total probability.
P(W)=\frac12\cdot\frac25+\frac12\cdot\frac45=\frac15+\frac25=\frac35=0.6
Step 2 — (ii) Bayes.
P(U_1\mid W)=\frac{\frac12\cdot\frac25}{\frac35}=\frac{1/5}{3/5}=\frac13
Answer. (i) 0.6, (ii) 1/3.




                  
                  Common mistake in transfer problems 
                  
                

After moving one ball, bag II has one more ball in total.
Students often keep the old total (11 instead of 12, or 10 instead of 11) in the denominator.



Type 2 — Bayes’ rule with 2 to 4 causes
How to recognise it: an observed result (defective, positive test, did not vote, late, judged guilty) and the question asks for the probability of one cause.
Recipe (5 steps):

Define the causes B_i and write their priors (they add to 1).
Define the observed event A and write P(A\mid B_i). If the data describe the opposite event, take 1- the given value.
Multiply each prior by its likelihood.
Add the products to get P(A).
Divide each product by P(A), and check the answers add to 1.



                  
                  Past TF 2019-20 Q7(a) (17 marks) — the truth serum 
                  
                

Given. Let G = guilty and I = innocent. Let J = the serum judges the suspect guilty.
Step 1 — Priors.
P(G)=0.05,\qquad P(I)=0.95
Step 2 — Likelihoods. 90% of the guilty are judged guilty, and innocent suspects are misjudged 1% of the time.
P(J\mid G)=0.90
P(J\mid I)=0.01
Step 3 — Total probability.
\begin{aligned}
P(J)&=0.05(0.90)+0.95(0.01)\\
&=0.045+0.0095\\
&=0.0545
\end{aligned}
Step 4 — Bayes.
P(I\mid J)=\frac{0.95(0.01)}{0.0545}=\frac{0.0095}{0.0545}=0.1743
Answer. P(\text{innocent}\mid\text{judged guilty})=\mathbf{0.1743}.
Comment. About 17.4% of the suspects the serum calls guilty are actually innocent. Innocent people are so common (95%) that even a 1% error rate produces many false “guilty” verdicts.




                  
                  Practice 2.1 (same shape as 2022-23 Q1(b)) — three suppliers 
                  
                

Given. Suppliers S_1,S_2,S_3 provide 50%, 30%, 20% of a component; their defect rates are 1%, 4%, 5%. A component is found defective. Find the probability it came from each supplier.
Step 1 — Branch products.
P(S_1)P(D\mid S_1)=0.5(0.01)=0.005
P(S_2)P(D\mid S_2)=0.3(0.04)=0.012
P(S_3)P(D\mid S_3)=0.2(0.05)=0.010
Step 2 — Total.
P(D)=0.005+0.012+0.010=0.027
Step 3 — Bayes for each supplier.
P(S_1\mid D)=\frac{0.005}{0.027}=0.1852
P(S_2\mid D)=\frac{0.012}{0.027}=0.4444
P(S_3\mid D)=\frac{0.010}{0.027}=0.3704
Answer. 0.1852, 0.4444, 0.3704 (they add to 1).




                  
                  Practice 2.2 (same shape as 2023-24 Q1(c)) — the "did NOT" twist with four groups 
                  
                

Given. In a town, 40% support party A, 30% party B, 20% party C and 10% party D. In the last election 70% of A, 60% of B, 80% of C and 50% of D supporters voted. A person chosen at random did not vote. Find the probability that the person supports each party.
Step 1 — Use the observed event. The observed event is N = “did not vote”, so the likelihoods are 0.30, 0.40, 0.20, 0.50.
Step 2 — Branch products.
0.4(0.3)=0.12
0.3(0.4)=0.12
0.2(0.2)=0.04
0.1(0.5)=0.05
Step 3 — Total.
P(N)=0.12+0.12+0.04+0.05=0.33
Step 4 — Bayes for each party.
P(A\mid N)=\frac{0.12}{0.33}=0.3636
P(B\mid N)=\frac{0.12}{0.33}=0.3636
P(C\mid N)=\frac{0.04}{0.33}=0.1212
P(D\mid N)=\frac{0.05}{0.33}=0.1515
Answer. A 0.3636, B 0.3636, C 0.1212, D 0.1515.




                  
                  Practice 2.3 — medical test 
                  
                

Given. A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects it in 90% of people who have it, but also gives a positive result for 2% of healthy people. (i) Find P(positive). (ii) A person tests positive; find the probability they have the disease. (iii) A person tests negative; find the probability they still have the disease.
Step 1 — (i) Total probability.
\begin{aligned}
P(+)&=0.01(0.90)+0.99(0.02)\\
&=0.009+0.0198\\
&=0.0288
\end{aligned}
Step 2 — (ii) Bayes for a positive result.
P(D\mid +)=\frac{0.009}{0.0288}=0.3125
Step 3 — (iii) Bayes for a negative result.
P(D\mid -)=\frac{0.01(0.10)}{1-0.0288}=\frac{0.001}{0.9712}=0.00103
Answer. (i) 0.0288, (ii) 0.3125, (iii) 0.00103.
Comment. Only about 31% of positive results are real, because the disease is rare.




                  
                  Practice 2.4 — getting to work 
                  
                

Given. A person goes to work by car 30% of the time, walks 30% of the time and takes the bus 40% of the time. The probability of being late is 0.05 by car, 0.10 walking and 0.20 by bus. Given that the person was late, which mode is most likely?
Step 1 — Branch products.
0.3(0.05)=0.015
0.3(0.10)=0.03
0.4(0.20)=0.08
Step 2 — Total.
P(L)=0.015+0.03+0.08=0.125
Step 3 — Bayes.
P(\text{car}\mid L)=\frac{0.015}{0.125}=0.12
P(\text{walk}\mid L)=\frac{0.03}{0.125}=0.24
P(\text{bus}\mid L)=\frac{0.08}{0.125}=0.64
Answer. The bus is the most likely mode (0.64).




                  
                  The most common Bayes mistake 
                  
                

When the data say “65% of A supporters voted” but the chosen person did not vote, you must use 0.35, not 0.65.
Always use the probability of the event that was actually observed.



Type 3 — Dependent draws (multiplication law)
How to recognise it: items drawn one after another without replacement, and a specific sequence is asked.
Recipe: multiply the probabilities step by step, updating the counts after each draw.


                  
                  Practice 3.1 — sequence of draws 
                  
                

Given. A box has 20 items, 5 defective. Three are drawn one by one without replacement. Find P(first two good and third defective).
Step 1 — Multiply, updating counts after each draw.
P(G_1\cap G_2\cap D_3)=\frac{15}{20}\cdot\frac{14}{19}\cdot\frac{5}{18}=\frac{35}{228}
Answer. \mathbf{35/228\approx0.1535}.




                  
                  Example 3.2 (lecture) — TV show 
                  
                

Given. P(H)=0.4 (husband watches), P(W)=0.5 (wife watches), P(H\mid W)=0.7. Find (a) P(both watch), (b) P(W\mid H), (c) P(at least one watches).
Step 1 — (a) Both watch (multiplication law).
P(W\cap H)=P(W)\,P(H\mid W)=0.5\times0.7=0.35
Step 2 — (b) Conditional probability.
P(W\mid H)=\frac{0.35}{0.4}=0.875
Step 3 — (c) Addition rule.
P(W\cup H)=0.5+0.4-0.35=0.55
Answer. (a) 0.35, (b) 0.875, (c) 0.55.




                  
                  Example 3.3 (lecture) — dice 
                  
                

Given. Two dice are thrown. Find P(sum \ge10 given the first die shows 5).
Step 1 — Count. B = “first die is 5” has 6 outcomes. Of these, (5,5) and (5,6) give sum \ge 10.
Step 2 — Conditional probability.
P(A\mid B)=\frac{2/36}{6/36}=\frac13
Answer. \mathbf{1/3}.



Type 4 — Checking independence
How to recognise it: “are A and B independent?”
Recipe: compute P(A\cap B) and P(A)P(B). Equal means independent.


                  
                  Practice 4.1 
                  
                

(i) Given. P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, P(A\cup B)=0.7. Are A and B independent?
P(A\cap B)=0.4+0.5-0.7=0.2
P(A)\,P(B)=0.4\times0.5=0.2
Equal, so independent.
(ii) Given. A die is rolled. A = “even”, B = “at most 4”. Are they independent?
A\cap B=\{2,4\}, so
P(A\cap B)=\frac26=\frac13
P(A)\,P(B)=\frac12\cdot\frac46=\frac13
Equal, so independent.



Type 5 — Independent people or parts working together
How to recognise it: “three students try independently”, “the problem is solved if at least one solves it”.
Recipe:
P(\text{solved})=1-\prod P(\text{fails})
“Exactly one” is the sum of the “only this one” cases.


                  
                  Practice 5.1 
                  
                

Given. Three students solve a problem independently with probabilities \frac12,\frac13,\frac14. Find the probability that (i) the problem is solved, (ii) exactly one solves it.
Step 1 — (i) Nobody solves.
P(\text{none})=\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac34=\frac14
P(\text{solved})=1-\frac14=\frac34
Step 2 — (ii) Exactly one.
\begin{aligned}
P&=\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac34+\frac12\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac34+\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac14\\
&=\frac{6+3+2}{24}\\
&=\frac{11}{24}\approx0.458
\end{aligned}
Answer. (i) 3/4, (ii) 11/24 ≈ 0.458.



Extra practice


                  
                  Answers (try first) 
                  
                

1. Bag A: 4 white, 6 black; bag B: 5 white, 5 black. One ball moves from A to B, then a ball is drawn from B. P(white)?
Answer: \frac4{10}\cdot\frac6{11}+\frac6{10}\cdot\frac5{11}=\frac{54}{110}=\frac{27}{55}\approx0.491.
2. Machines produce 60% and 40% of output with defect rates 3% and 5%. An item is defective; P(from machine 2)?
Answer: 0.02/0.038=0.526.
3. P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.4, independent. Find P(A\cup B).
Answer: 0.58.
4. Two cards drawn without replacement. P(both hearts)?
Answer: \frac{13}{52}\cdot\frac{12}{51}=\frac1{17}.
5. Can A and B with P(A)=0.2, P(B)=0.3 be mutually exclusive and independent?
Answer: No, because 0\ne0.06.

1-Probability/P3-Random-Variables-PMF-PD.content:
P3 · Random Variables, PMF, PDF and CDF


                  
                  Why this matters for the TF 
                  
                

A “density function” question appears almost every year: 2020-21 Q6(b) (find k for k(3-x)^2), 2021-22 Q6(c) (build a distribution and F(x)), 2022-23 Q1(c) (CDF of an exponential density) and 2023-24 Q2(a) (probability using both the CDF and the pdf).
The last two are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions.
You need three skills: ==find k, compute a probability as a sum or an area, and move between f(x) and F(x)==.


Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize 
                  
                

Discrete X (counts)
Use \sum=1 to find k.
f(x)=P(X=x)\ge0
\sum_x f(x)=1
Continuous X (measurements)
Use the total area =1 to find k.
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1
Probability is area
P(a<X<b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
For continuous X, P(X=a)=0, so < and \le give the same answer.
CDF (definition)
Discrete: add f(t) for t\le x (a step function).
F(x)=P(X\le x)
CDF from a pdf
F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t)\,dt
pdf from a CDF
f(x)=F'(x)
Probability from a CDF
P(a<X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)




Problem types you will face
Type 1 — Find k in a pmf
How to recognise it: a table or formula with an unknown constant, for discrete values.
Recipe:

Add all probabilities.
Set the sum to 1 and solve for k.
Add the required values.



                  
                  Practice 1.1 
                  
                

Given. f(x)=k(x^2+1) for x=0,1,2,3. Find k and P(X\ge2).
Step 1 — Sum to 1.
k(1+2+5+10)=18k=1
k=\frac1{18}
Step 2 — Add the required values.
P(X\ge2)=f(2)+f(3)=\frac{5+10}{18}=\frac56
Answer. k=\mathbf{1/18}, P(X\ge2)=\mathbf{5/6}.




                  
                  Practice 1.2 
                  
                

Given. f(x)=kx for x=1,2,3,4. Find k and P(1<X\le3).
Step 1 — Sum to 1.
k(1+2+3+4)=10k=1
k=\frac1{10}
Step 2 — Add the required values.
P(1<X\le3)=f(2)+f(3)=\frac{2+3}{10}=0.5
Answer. k=\mathbf{1/10}, P=\mathbf{0.5}.



Type 2 — Find k in a pdf, then probabilities
How to recognise it: ”f(x)=k\cdot(\text{something}) on an interval, determine k … find the probability that …“.
Recipe:

Integrate over the whole range and set equal to 1.
For each probability, integrate over the required interval.
For “magnitude exceeds c”, use the complement:

P(|X|>c)=1-P(-c\le X\le c)


                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q6(b) (10 marks) — measurement error 
                  
                

Given. f(x)=k(3-x)^2 for -1\le x\le1, and 0 elsewhere.
Step 1 — (i) Find k.
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-1}^{1}k(3-x)^2\,dx&=k\left[-\frac{(3-x)^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{1}\\
&=k\cdot\frac{4^3-2^3}{3}\\
&=\frac{56k}{3}=1
\end{aligned}
k=\frac{3}{56}
Step 2 — (ii) Error less than \frac12, i.e. between -1 and \frac12.
\begin{aligned}
P\left(X<\tfrac12\right)&=\frac{3}{56}\cdot\frac{4^3-2.5^3}{3}\\
&=\frac{64-15.625}{56}\\
&=\frac{48.375}{56}=0.8638
\end{aligned}
Step 3 — (iii) Magnitude exceeds 0.8, i.e. |X|>0.8. First find the middle part.
\begin{aligned}
P(|X|\le0.8)&=\frac{3}{56}\cdot\frac{3.8^3-2.2^3}{3}\\
&=\frac{54.872-10.648}{56}\\
&=\frac{44.224}{56}=0.7897
\end{aligned}
P(|X|>0.8)=1-0.7897=0.2103
Answer. (i) k=\mathbf{3/56}, (ii) 0.8638, (iii) 0.2103.




                  
                  Practice 2.1 
                  
                

Given. f(x)=kx(2-x) for 0<x<2. Find k, P(X>1.5) and P(0.5<X<1).
Step 1 — Find k.
\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx=\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}3\right]_0^2=4-\frac83=\frac43
k=\frac34
Step 2 — P(X>1.5).
P(X>1.5)=\frac34\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{1.5}^{2}=\frac34\left(\frac43-1.125\right)=0.15625
Step 3 — P(0.5<X<1).
P(0.5<X<1)=\frac34\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0.5}^{1}=\frac34\left(\frac23-\frac{5}{24}\right)=0.34375
Answer. k=\mathbf{3/4}, 0.15625, 0.34375.




                  
                  Practice 2.2 
                  
                

Given. f(x)=ke^{-2x} for x>0. Find k and P(X>1).
Step 1 — Find k.
\int_0^\infty ke^{-2x}\,dx=\frac k2=1
k=2
Step 2 — P(X>1).
P(X>1)=\int_1^\infty 2e^{-2x}\,dx=e^{-2}=0.1353
Answer. k=\mathbf{2}, P(X>1)=\mathbf{0.1353}.



Type 3 — CDF from a pdf (and checking with both)
How to recognise it: “find the cumulative distribution function”, “use F(x) to find …“.
Recipe:

Integrate f from the left end of the support up to x.
Write F piecewise, with a 0 line and a 1 line.
Then P(a<X<b)=F(b)-F(a).



                  
                  Practice 3.1 
                  
                

Given. f(x)=\frac x2 for 0<x<2. Find F(x) and P(0.5<X<1.5).
Step 1 — Integrate up to x. For 0<x<2,
F(x)=\int_0^x\frac t2\,dt=\frac{x^2}{4}
Step 2 — Write F piecewise.
F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\le0\\ x^2/4,&0<x<2\\ 1,&x\ge2\end{cases}
Step 3 — Probability from the CDF.
P(0.5<X<1.5)=F(1.5)-F(0.5)=\frac{2.25-0.25}{4}=0.5
Step 4 — Check with the pdf.
\int_{0.5}^{1.5}\frac x2\,dx=0.5\ \checkmark
Answer. F(x)=x^2/4 on (0,2); P=\mathbf{0.5}.




                  
                  Practice 3.2 — piecewise (triangular) density 
                  
                

Given. f(x)=x for 0<x<1, f(x)=2-x for 1\le x<2, 0 elsewhere. Find F(x) and P(0.5<X<1.5).
Step 1 — First piece, 0<x<1.
F(x)=\int_0^x t\,dt=\frac{x^2}2
So F(1)=\frac12.
Step 2 — Second piece, 1\le x<2. Start from F(1).
F(x)=\frac12+\int_1^x(2-t)\,dt=1-\frac{(2-x)^2}{2}
Step 3 — Write F piecewise.
F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\le0\\ x^2/2,&0<x<1\\ 1-(2-x)^2/2,&1\le x<2\\ 1,&x\ge2\end{cases}
Step 4 — Probability.
P(0.5<X<1.5)=F(1.5)-F(0.5)=0.875-0.125=0.75
Answer. P=\mathbf{0.75}.




                  
                  Piecewise densities 
                  
                

When f changes formula at x=1, the CDF in the second piece must start from F(1), not from 0.



Type 4 — Given the CDF: probabilities and the pdf
How to recognise it: a CDF like F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x} is given (2023-24 Q2(a)), or a pdf like \frac{1}{\beta}e^{-x/\beta} is given and you must find F (2022-23 Q1(c)).
Recipe:

Convert units first.
Use P(X\le a)=F(a) and P(X>a)=1-F(a).
Differentiate F to get f, and confirm the same probability by integrating f.



                  
                  Practice 4.1 (same shape as 2023-24 Q2(a)) 
                  
                

Given. The waiting time in hours until a server receives a request has CDF F(x)=1-e^{-3x} for x\ge0. Find the probability of waiting less than 20 minutes, using both the CDF and the pdf.
Step 1 — Convert units. 20 minutes =\frac13 hour.
Step 2 — Using the CDF.
P\left(X<\tfrac13\right)=F\left(\tfrac13\right)=1-e^{-1}=0.6321
Step 3 — Using the pdf. Differentiate:
f(x)=F'(x)=3e^{-3x}
\int_0^{1/3}3e^{-3x}\,dx=\left[-e^{-3x}\right]_0^{1/3}=1-e^{-1}=0.6321
Answer. P=\mathbf{0.6321} by both methods.




                  
                  Practice 4.2 (same shape as 2022-23 Q1(c)) 
                  
                

Given. The lifetime (hours) of a component has f(x)=\frac1{50}e^{-x/50} for x\ge0. Find (i) the CDF, (ii) P(lasts more than 100 hours), (iii) P(fails between 20 and 60 hours), (iv) the median lifetime.
Step 1 — (i) CDF. For x\ge0 (and F=0 for x<0):
F(x)=\int_0^x\frac1{50}e^{-t/50}\,dt=1-e^{-x/50}
Step 2 — (ii) More than 100 hours.
P(X>100)=1-F(100)=e^{-2}=0.1353
Step 3 — (iii) Between 20 and 60 hours.
\begin{aligned}
P(20<X<60)&=F(60)-F(20)\\
&=e^{-0.4}-e^{-1.2}\\
&=0.6703-0.3012=0.3691
\end{aligned}
Step 4 — (iv) Median. Solve F(m)=0.5.
e^{-m/50}=0.5
m=50\ln2=34.66 \text{ hours}
Answer. (i) 1-e^{-x/50}, (ii) 0.1353, (iii) 0.3691, (iv) 34.66 hours.




                  
                  Units 
                  
                

If X is in hours and the question says minutes, convert first (12 minutes = 0.2 hour).



Type 5 — Distribution of a count from sampling without replacement, and its F(x)
How to recognise it: “a lot of N items contains k defective; n are taken; find the probability distribution of X = number defective, and F(x)“.
Recipe:

For each possible x, use

f(x)=\frac{\binom kx\binom{N-k}{n-x}}{\binom Nn}

Make a table.
Build the step CDF by running totals.



                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q6(c) (15 marks) — cars with paint blemishes 
                  
                

Given. 5 cars, 2 blemished; the agency receives 3. X = number of blemished cars received, X=0,1,2.
Step 1 — Total samples.
\binom53=10
Step 2 — The pmf.
f(x)=\frac{\binom2x\binom3{3-x}}{10}
f(0)=\frac1{10}
f(1)=\frac{6}{10}
f(2)=\frac{3}{10}

















x012f(x)1/106/103/10
Step 3 — The CDF (running totals).
F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0\\ 1/10,&0\le x<1\\ 7/10,&1\le x<2\\ 1,&x\ge2\end{cases}
Answer. The table and F(x) above.




                  
                  Practice 5.1 — markers 
                  
                

Given. A lot of 7 markers has 3 defective. A buyer takes 3 at random. Find the distribution of X = number of defective markers and F(x).
Step 1 — Total samples.
\binom73=35
Step 2 — The pmf. For x=0,1,2,3:
f(x)=\frac{\binom3x\binom4{3-x}}{35}



















x0123f(x)4/3518/3512/351/35
Step 3 — The CDF.
F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0\\ 4/35,&0\le x<1\\ 22/35,&1\le x<2\\ 34/35,&2\le x<3\\ 1,&x\ge3\end{cases}
Answer. The table and F(x) above.




                  
                  Practice 5.2 — coin tosses 
                  
                

Given. A coin is tossed 3 times; X = number of heads.
Step 1 — The pmf.
f(0)=\frac18
f(1)=\frac38
f(2)=\frac38
f(3)=\frac18
Answer. F jumps to \frac18,\frac48,\frac78,1 at x=0,1,2,3.




                  
                  Writing a discrete CDF 
                  
                

Use "\le" on the left and "<" on the right of each interval.
Always include the first line (F=0) and the last line (F=1).



Extra practice


                  
                  Answers (try first) 
                  
                

1. f(x)=cx^2 on 0<x<3. Find c and P(X>2).
Answer: c=\frac19; P=\frac{27-8}{27}=\frac{19}{27}\approx0.704.
2. F(x)=1-e^{-x/4} (x\ge0). Find f(x) and P(2<X<6).
Answer: f=\frac14e^{-x/4}; e^{-0.5}-e^{-1.5}=0.3834.
3. f(x)=\frac{x+1}{8} on 2<x<4. Show it is valid and find P(X<3.5).
Answer: \int_2^4\frac{x+1}8dx=1; P=\left[\frac{(x+1)^2}{16}\right]_2^{3.5}=\frac{4.5^2-3^2}{16}=0.7031.
4. A box has 6 good and 4 bad bulbs; 2 are taken. Distribution of the number of bad bulbs?
Answer: f(0)=\frac{15}{45}, f(1)=\frac{24}{45}, f(2)=\frac6{45}.
5. For a discrete CDF, what is the jump at x?
Answer: P(X=x).

1-Probability/P4-Joint-Marginal-and-Cond.content:
P4 · Joint, Marginal and Conditional Distributions


                  
                  Why this matters for the TF 
                  
                

Joint distributions were asked in 2020-21 Q5(c) (joint density k(x^2+y^2)), 2022-23 Q2(a) (density 10xy^2 on a triangle: marginals, conditional, conditional probability) and 2023-24 Q2(b) (20 marks: joint pmf from drawing pens, then P[(X,Y)\in A], marginals, variance and covariance).
The last two are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions.
Every one of those shapes is practised below.


Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize 
                  
                

Joint pmf (discrete)
f(x,y)=P(X=x,\ Y=y)
\sum_x\sum_y f(x,y)=1
P[(X,Y)\in A] is the sum of the cells in A.
Joint pdf (continuous)
Use the total =1 to find k.
\iint f(x,y)\,dx\,dy=1
P[(X,Y)\in A]=\iint_A f(x,y)\,dx\,dy
Marginals
Discrete: row and column totals. Continuous:
g(x)=\int f(x,y)\,dy
h(y)=\int f(x,y)\,dx
Conditional
f(y\mid x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{g(x)}
f(x\mid y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{h(y)}
P(a<Y<b\mid X=x)=\int_a^b f(y\mid x)\,dy
Independence
X and Y are independent if, for every (x,y),
f(x,y)=g(x)\,h(y)
If the support is not a rectangle (for example 0<x<y<1), X and Y are not independent.
Drawing objects of three colours (sample of size n)
Valid for x+y\le n.
f(x,y)=\frac{\binom{N_1}{x}\binom{N_2}{y}\binom{N_3}{n-x-y}}{\binom{N}{n}}



Problem types you will face
Type 1 — Joint pmf from drawing objects (the 2023-24 Q2(b) shape)
How to recognise it: “a bag contains … of three colours, n are selected; X = number of colour 1, Y = number of colour 2”.
Recipe:

List all pairs with x+y\le n.
Compute each cell with the three-colour formula.
Fill the table with row and column totals (the marginals) and check it adds to 1.
Answer P[(X,Y)\in A] by adding cells.
Find E(X), E(X^2) and \mathrm{Var}(X) from g(x); E(XY) from the table; then \mathrm{Cov}=E(XY)-E(X)E(Y).



                  
                  Practice 1.1 (full 2023-24 Q2(b) shape) 
                  
                

Given. A box has 4 red, 3 green and 2 white balls. Two balls are drawn at random. X = number of red, Y = number of green. (i) Find the joint distribution and plot it. (ii) Find P[(X,Y)\in A], A=\{(x,y): x+y\le1\}. (iii) Marginals. (iv) \mathrm{Var}(X). (v) \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y).
Step 1 — (i) Total samples.
\binom92=36
Step 2 — (i) Two sample cells.
f(1,1)=\frac{\binom41\binom31\binom20}{36}=\frac{12}{36}
f(0,0)=\frac{\binom22}{36}=\frac1{36}
All cells:








































f(x,y)y=0y=1y=2g(x)x=01/366/363/3610/36x=18/3612/36020/36x=26/36006/36h(y)15/3618/363/361
Plot. Draw the x and y axes on the floor and mark the six points (0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,0),(1,1),(2,0). Draw a vertical stick at each point with height f(x,y). The tallest stick is at (1,1), height \frac13.
Step 3 — (ii) Add the cells with x+y\le1: (0,0),(0,1),(1,0).
P[(X,Y)\in A]=\frac{1+6+8}{36}=\frac{15}{36}=\frac5{12}
Step 4 — (iii) Marginals (row and column totals).
g(0)=\frac5{18},\quad g(1)=\frac59,\quad g(2)=\frac16
h(0)=\frac5{12},\quad h(1)=\frac12,\quad h(2)=\frac1{12}
Step 5 — (iv) Variance of X.
E(X)=\frac59+2\cdot\frac16=\frac89
E(X^2)=\frac59+4\cdot\frac16=\frac{11}9
\mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{11}9-\frac{64}{81}=\frac{35}{81}\approx0.4321
Step 6 — (v) Covariance. Only the (1,1) cell has xy\ne0.
E(XY)=1\cdot1\cdot\frac{12}{36}=\frac13
E(Y)=\frac12+2\cdot\frac1{12}=\frac23
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)&=E(XY)-E(X)E(Y)\\
&=\frac13-\frac89\cdot\frac23\\
&=\frac{9-16}{27}=-\frac7{27}\approx-0.2593
\end{aligned}
Answer. (ii) 5/12, (iv) 35/81 ≈ 0.4321, (v) −7/27 ≈ −0.2593.
The negative covariance makes sense: more red balls leave less room for green ones.




                  
                  Common mistakes 
                  
                

Forgetting the third-colour factor \binom{N_3}{n-x-y}.
Including impossible cells such as (1,2) when only 2 items are drawn.
Always check the table totals 1.



Type 2 — Joint pmf given by a formula
How to recognise it: ”f(x,y)=k(\dots) for x=\dots, y=\dots“.
Recipe:

Add over all cells to find k.
Find the marginals by summing.
Conditional = cell ÷ marginal.
Check independence by comparing f with g\cdot h.



                  
                  Practice 2.1 
                  
                

Given. f(x,y)=k(x+y) for x=0,1,2 and y=0,1,2,3. Find (i) k, (ii) the marginals, (iii) P(X\le1,\,Y\ge2), (iv) f(y\mid x=1), (v) \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y).
Step 1 — (i) Find k.
\sum\sum(x+y)=4(0+1+2)+3(0+1+2+3)=12+18=30
k=\frac1{30}
Step 2 — (ii) Marginal of X.
g(x)=\sum_{y=0}^3\frac{x+y}{30}=\frac{4x+6}{30}
g(0)=\frac15,\quad g(1)=\frac13,\quad g(2)=\frac7{15}
Step 3 — (ii) Marginal of Y.
h(y)=\sum_{x=0}^2\frac{x+y}{30}=\frac{3+3y}{30}
h(0)=\frac1{10},\quad h(1)=\frac15,\quad h(2)=\frac3{10},\quad h(3)=\frac25
Step 4 — (iii) Add cells (0,2),(0,3),(1,2),(1,3).
P(X\le1,\ Y\ge2)=\frac{2+3+3+4}{30}=\frac{12}{30}=\frac25
Step 5 — (iv) Conditional. For y=0,1,2,3:
f(y\mid1)=\frac{(1+y)/30}{1/3}=\frac{1+y}{10}
Step 6 — (v) Covariance.
E(X)=\frac13+2\cdot\frac7{15}=\frac{19}{15}
E(Y)=\frac15+\frac{6}{10}+\frac{6}{5}=2
E(XY)=\sum\sum xy\,\frac{x+y}{30}=\frac{12}5
\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=\frac{12}{5}-\frac{19}{15}\cdot2=\frac{36-38}{15}=-\frac2{15}
Answer. k=\mathbf{1/30}, (iii) 2/5, (v) −2/15.
Since \mathrm{Cov}\ne0, X and Y are not independent (also f(0,0)=0\ne g(0)h(0)).



Type 3 — Joint pdf on a rectangle: find k and rectangle probabilities
How to recognise it: ”f(x,y)=k(\dots) for a\le x<b,\ c\le y<d“.
Recipe:

Integrate over y first (treat x as a constant), then over x.
Set the total to 1 to find k.
For each probability, use the same integral with the new limits.
Translate words into limits carefully (“underfilled” = below the target).



                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q5(c) (10 marks) — tyre pressures 
                  
                

Given. f(x,y)=k(x^2+y^2) for 30\le x<50, 30\le y<50.
Step 1 — (i) Inner integral. For fixed x:
\int_{30}^{50}(x^2+y^2)\,dy=20x^2+\frac{50^3-30^3}{3}=20x^2+\frac{98000}{3}
Step 2 — (i) Outer integral.
\int_{30}^{50}\left(20x^2+\frac{98000}3\right)dx=20\cdot\frac{98000}{3}+20\cdot\frac{98000}{3}=\frac{3{,}920{,}000}{3}
k=\frac{3}{3{,}920{,}000}\approx7.653\times10^{-7}
Step 3 — (ii) P(30\le X\le40,\ 40\le Y<50). For fixed x:
\int_{40}^{50}(x^2+y^2)\,dy=10x^2+\frac{61000}{3}
\int_{30}^{40}\left(10x^2+\frac{61000}3\right)dx=\frac{370000+610000}{3}=\frac{980000}3
P=\frac{980000}{3{,}920{,}000}=0.25
Step 4 — (iii) Both underfilled (30\le X<40, 30\le Y<40).
\int_{30}^{40}\!\!\int_{30}^{40}(x^2+y^2)\,dy\,dx=\frac{370000}{3}+\frac{370000}{3}=\frac{740000}{3}
P=\frac{740000}{3{,}920{,}000}=\frac{37}{196}\approx0.1888
Answer. (i) k=\mathbf{3/3{,}920{,}000}, (ii) 0.25, (iii) 0.1888.




                  
                  Practice 3.1 
                  
                

Given. f(x,y)=k(x+2y) for 0<x<1, 0<y<1. Find k, P(X<\frac12,Y<\frac12), the marginals, and check independence.
Step 1 — Find k.
\int_0^1\!\int_0^1(x+2y)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1(x+1)\,dx=\frac32
k=\frac23
Step 2 — Rectangle probability.
\begin{aligned}
P\left(X<\tfrac12,\ Y<\tfrac12\right)&=\frac23\int_0^{1/2}\!\!\int_0^{1/2}(x+2y)\,dy\,dx\\
&=\frac23\int_0^{1/2}\left(\frac x2+\frac14\right)dx\\
&=\frac23\cdot\frac{3}{16}=\frac18
\end{aligned}
Step 3 — Marginals.
g(x)=\frac23\int_0^1(x+2y)\,dy=\frac23(x+1)
h(y)=\frac23\int_0^1(x+2y)\,dx=\frac23\left(\frac12+2y\right)
Step 4 — Independence. The product g(x)h(y) is not \frac23(x+2y).
Answer. k=\mathbf{2/3}, P=\mathbf{1/8}, not independent.




                  
                  Practice 3.2 — an independent case 
                  
                

Given. f(x,y)=kxy for 0<x<1, 0<y<2. Find k and show X, Y are independent.
Step 1 — Find k.
k\int_0^1x\,dx\int_0^2y\,dy=k\cdot\frac12\cdot2=k=1
Step 2 — Marginals.
g(x)=\int_0^2xy\,dy=2x
h(y)=\int_0^1xy\,dx=\frac y2
Step 3 — Check.
g(x)\,h(y)=2x\cdot\frac y2=xy=f(x,y)
Answer. k=\mathbf{1}, and X, Y are independent.



Type 4 — Joint pdf on a triangle: marginals, conditional, conditional probability
How to recognise it: support like 0<x<y<1 (the 2022-23 Q2(a) shape).
Recipe:

Draw the region.
For g(x), integrate over y from the line to the edge.
For h(y), integrate over x.
f(y\mid x)=f/g.
Substitute the given x and integrate over the required y-range (keeping inside the support).




                  
                  Practice 4.1 
                  
                

Given. f(x,y)=8xy for 0<y<x<1. Find the marginals, f(y\mid x) and P(Y<\frac14\mid X=\frac12).
Step 1 — Limits. For fixed x, y runs from 0 to x. For fixed y, x runs from y to 1.
Step 2 — Marginal of X (0<x<1).
g(x)=\int_0^x8xy\,dy=4x^3
Step 3 — Marginal of Y (0<y<1).
h(y)=\int_y^18xy\,dx=4y(1-y^2)
Step 4 — Conditional (0<y<x).
f(y\mid x)=\frac{8xy}{4x^3}=\frac{2y}{x^2}
Step 5 — Conditional probability. At x=\frac12, f(y\mid\frac12)=8y on 0<y<\frac12.
P\left(Y<\tfrac14\mid X=\tfrac12\right)=\int_0^{1/4}8y\,dy=\frac14
Answer. g(x)=4x^3, h(y)=4y(1-y^2), f(y\mid x)=2y/x^2, P=\mathbf{1/4}.




                  
                  Practice 4.2 
                  
                

Given. f(x,y)=6x for 0<x<y<1. Find g(x), h(y), f(x\mid y), P(X<\frac14\mid Y=\frac12) and P(X+Y<1).
Step 1 — Marginal of X (0<x<1).
g(x)=\int_x^16x\,dy=6x(1-x)
Step 2 — Marginal of Y (0<y<1).
h(y)=\int_0^y6x\,dx=3y^2
Step 3 — Conditional (0<x<y).
f(x\mid y)=\frac{6x}{3y^2}=\frac{2x}{y^2}
Step 4 — Conditional probability. At y=\frac12, f(x\mid\frac12)=8x on 0<x<\frac12.
P\left(X<\tfrac14\mid Y=\tfrac12\right)=\int_0^{1/4}8x\,dx=\frac14
Step 5 — P(X+Y<1). Inside the triangle, x runs from 0 to \frac12 and y from x to 1-x.
\begin{aligned}
P(X+Y<1)&=\int_0^{1/2}\!\int_x^{1-x}6x\,dy\,dx\\
&=\int_0^{1/2}6x(1-2x)\,dx\\
&=6\left(\frac18-\frac1{12}\right)=\frac14
\end{aligned}
Answer. g=6x(1-x), h=3y^2, f(x\mid y)=2x/y^2, 1/4, 1/4.




                  
                  Limits on a triangle 
                  
                

Write the limits next to the sketch before integrating.
Marginals of triangle densities always have the variable in the limits, so they look like 6x(1-x) or \frac{10x}{3}(1-x^3), never a constant.



Extra practice


                  
                  Answers (try first) 
                  
                

1. From 3 red, 2 blue, 1 green pen, 2 are chosen. X = red, Y = blue. Find f(1,1) and P(X=0).
Answer: f(1,1)=\frac{3\cdot2}{15}=\frac25; P(X=0)=\frac{\binom32}{15}=\frac15.
2. f(x,y)=c\,xy for x=1,2, y=1,2,3. Find c.
Answer: c(1+2)(1+2+3)=18c=1, so c=\frac1{18} (and X, Y are independent).
3. f(x,y)=4xy on the unit square. Find P(X<\frac12,Y>\frac12).
Answer: \frac14\cdot\frac34=\frac3{16}.
4. f(x,y)=2 on 0<x<y<1. Find g(x) and f(y\mid x).
Answer: g(x)=2(1-x); f(y\mid x)=\frac1{1-x}, x<y<1.
5. Why can’t X, Y be independent on 0<x<y<1?
Answer: The support is not a rectangle.

1-Probability/P5-Expectation-Variance-Co.content:
P5 · Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Chebyshev’s Theorem


                  
                  Why this matters for the TF 
                  
                

These are quick, reliable marks.
2019-20 Q7(b) asked for E(e^{2X/3}); 2020-21 Q8(a) for E(X+4); 2022-23 Q2(b) for the mean and variance of 3X-2 and Q2(c) for P(\mu-2\sigma<X<\mu+2\sigma) compared with Chebyshev; 2023-24 Q2(b) for a variance and covariance, and Q3(a) for Chebyshev’s theorem in a job-selection story.
The 2022-23 and 2023-24 versions are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions.


Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize 
                  
                

Mean
E(X)=\sum x\,f(x)\quad\text{or}\quad\int x\,f(x)\,dx
Function of X
No need to find the distribution of g(X).
E[g(X)]=\sum g(x)\,f(x)\quad\text{or}\quad\int g(x)\,f(x)\,dx
Variance
\mathrm{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2
\sigma=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}
Linear rule for the mean
E(aX+b)=a\,E(X)+b
Linear rule for the variance
The constant b disappears and a is squared.
\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)
Covariance
\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=E(XY)-E(X)\,E(Y)
where E(XY)=\sum\sum xy\,f(x,y) or \iint xy\,f(x,y)\,dx\,dy. Independent implies \mathrm{Cov}=0 (not the other way round).
Correlation coefficient
\rho=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\,\sigma_Y}
Chebyshev
Use when only \mu and \sigma are known.
P(\mu-k\sigma<X<\mu+k\sigma)\ge1-\frac1{k^2}
Equivalently,
P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)\le\frac1{k^2}



Theory the TF actually asks
State Chebyshev’s theorem (2023-24 Q3(a))


                  
                  Exam answer 
                  
                

Chebyshev’s theorem. ==The probability that any random variable X will assume a value within k standard deviations of its mean is at least 1-\dfrac1{k^2}.==
That is, for any k>1,
P(\mu-k\sigma<X<\mu+k\sigma)\ge1-\frac1{k^2}
It holds for every distribution, whatever its shape, so it gives only a lower bound.
For k=2, at least 75% of the probability lies within 2\sigma of the mean. For k=3, at least 88.9\%.
If the distribution is symmetric, each tail gets at most half of the remaining probability:
P(X\ge\mu+k\sigma)\le\frac{1}{2k^2}



Problem types you will face
Type 1 — Mean and variance of a discrete variable
How to recognise it: a pmf table or a story (insurance, profit, defective items).
Recipe:

Make columns x, f(x), xf(x), x^2f(x) and add them.
Then \mathrm{Var}=E(X^2)-\mu^2.



                  
                  Practice 1.1 
                  
                

Given. f(0)=0.1,\ f(1)=0.3,\ f(2)=0.4,\ f(3)=0.2. Find the mean and SD.
Step 1 — Mean.
E(X)=0.3+0.8+0.6=1.7
Step 2 — E(X^2).
E(X^2)=0.3+1.6+1.8=3.7
Step 3 — Variance and SD.
\mathrm{Var}(X)=3.7-2.89=0.81
\sigma=\sqrt{0.81}=0.9
Answer. Mean 1.7, SD 0.9.




                  
                  Practice 1.2 — insurance 
                  
                

Given. An insurance company sells a one-year policy of Tk 50,000 for a premium of Tk 500. The probability that the holder dies during the year is 0.002. Find the company’s expected gain per policy.
Step 1 — Possible gains. The gain is 500 with probability 0.998, and 500-50000=-49500 with probability 0.002.
Step 2 — Expected gain.
\begin{aligned}
E(\text{gain})&=500(0.998)+(-49500)(0.002)\\
&=499-99\\
&=400
\end{aligned}
Answer. Expected gain Tk 400 per policy.




                  
                  Practice 1.3 — defective markers 
                  
                

Given. From the distribution in P3 Random Variables PMF PDF CDF (f(0)=\frac4{35}, f(1)=\frac{18}{35}, f(2)=\frac{12}{35}, f(3)=\frac1{35}), find the mean and variance of the number of defective markers.
Step 1 — Mean.
E(X)=\frac{0+18+24+3}{35}=\frac{45}{35}=\frac97
Step 2 — E(X^2).
E(X^2)=\frac{0+18+48+9}{35}=\frac{75}{35}=\frac{15}7
Step 3 — Variance.
\mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{15}{7}-\frac{81}{49}=\frac{24}{49}\approx0.490
Answer. Mean 9/7, variance 24/49 ≈ 0.490.



Type 2 — Mean and variance of a continuous variable, and E[g(X)]
How to recognise it: a pdf is given and the question asks for E(X), \mathrm{Var}(X), an “average”, or the expected value of some function.
Recipe: integrate x f, x^2 f, or g(x) f over the support.


                  
                  Past TF 2019-20 Q7(b) (18 marks) — E(e^{2X/3})
                  
                

Given. f(x)=e^{-x} for x>0.
Step 1 — Write the integral.
E\left(e^{2X/3}\right)=\int_0^\infty e^{2x/3}\,e^{-x}\,dx
Step 2 — Combine and integrate.
\begin{aligned}
E\left(e^{2X/3}\right)&=\int_0^\infty e^{-x/3}\,dx\\
&=\left[-3e^{-x/3}\right]_0^\infty\\
&=3
\end{aligned}
Answer. E(e^{2X/3})=\mathbf{3}.




                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q8(a) (10 marks) — average hospital stay 
                  
                

Given. Y=X+4 with f(x)=\dfrac{32}{(x+4)^3}, x>0.
Step 1 — Write the integral.
E(Y)=\int_0^\infty(x+4)\,\frac{32}{(x+4)^3}\,dx
Step 2 — Simplify and integrate.
\begin{aligned}
E(Y)&=32\int_0^\infty(x+4)^{-2}\,dx\\
&=32\left[-\frac1{x+4}\right]_0^\infty\\
&=\frac{32}{4}=8
\end{aligned}
Answer. The average stay is 8 days (equivalently E(X)=4 and E(Y)=E(X)+4).




                  
                  Practice 2.1 
                  
                

Given. f(x)=2(1-x) for 0<x<1. Find E(X), \mathrm{Var}(X) and E[(3X+2)^2].
Step 1 — Mean.
E(X)=\int_0^12x(1-x)\,dx=1-\frac23=\frac13
Step 2 — E(X^2).
E(X^2)=\int_0^12x^2(1-x)\,dx=\frac23-\frac12=\frac16
Step 3 — Variance.
\mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac16-\frac19=\frac1{18}
Step 4 — Expand (3X+2)^2 and take expectations.
\begin{aligned}
E[(3X+2)^2]&=9E(X^2)+12E(X)+4\\
&=\frac96+4+4\\
&=9.5
\end{aligned}
Answer. E(X)=\mathbf{1/3}, \mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathbf{1/18}, E[(3X+2)^2]=\mathbf{9.5}.



Type 3 — Mean and variance of Y=aX+b
How to recognise it: ”Y=3X-2 where X has density …, find the mean and variance of Y” (2022-23 Q2(b)).
Recipe: find E(X) and \mathrm{Var}(X) first, then apply the linear rules.


                  
                  Practice 3.1 
                  
                

Given. X has f(x)=\frac15e^{-x/5}, x>0 (exponential, mean 5). The cost is Y=4X+10. Find E(Y) and \mathrm{Var}(Y).
Step 1 — Moments of X. For this exponential (see P9 Uniform Exponential and Other Continuous Distributions):
E(X)=5
\mathrm{Var}(X)=25
Step 2 — Mean of Y.
E(Y)=4(5)+10=30
Step 3 — Variance and SD of Y.
\mathrm{Var}(Y)=16(25)=400
\sigma_Y=20
Answer. E(Y)=\mathbf{30}, \mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mathbf{400}.




                  
                  The classic slip 
                  
                

\mathrm{Var}(3X-2)=9\,\mathrm{Var}(X), not 3\,\mathrm{Var}(X)-2.



Type 4 — Covariance and correlation from a joint distribution
How to recognise it: a joint table or joint pdf and “find \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)” or "\rho".
Recipe:

Marginals → E(X), E(Y).
Table → E(XY).
\mathrm{Cov}=E(XY)-E(X)E(Y).
For \rho, also find the variances.



                  
                  Practice 4.1 
                  
                

Given. The joint pmf is:























f(x,y)x=1x=2x=3y=10.100.200.10y=20.200.100.30
Find \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) and \rho.
Step 1 — Marginals.
g(1)=0.3,\quad g(2)=0.3,\quad g(3)=0.4
h(1)=0.4,\quad h(2)=0.6
Step 2 — Means.
E(X)=0.3+0.6+1.2=2.1
E(Y)=0.4+1.2=1.6
Step 3 — E(XY).
E(XY)=1(0.1)+2(0.2)+3(0.1)+2(0.2)+4(0.1)+6(0.3)=3.4
Step 4 — Covariance.
\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=3.4-2.1(1.6)=0.04
Step 5 — Variances.
E(X^2)=0.3+1.2+3.6=5.1,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(X)=5.1-4.41=0.69
E(Y^2)=0.4+2.4=2.8,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y)=2.8-2.56=0.24
Step 6 — Correlation.
\rho=\frac{0.04}{\sqrt{0.69\times0.24}}=0.098
Answer. \mathrm{Cov}=\mathbf{0.04}, \rho=\mathbf{0.098}: a very weak positive relationship.




                  
                  Practice 4.2 — continuous 
                  
                

Given. f(x,y)=x+y for 0<x<1, 0<y<1. Find \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y).
Step 1 — Marginal and mean of X.
g(x)=x+\frac12
E(X)=\int_0^1x\left(x+\frac12\right)dx=\frac13+\frac14=\frac7{12}
By symmetry, E(Y)=\frac7{12}.
Step 2 — E(XY).
E(XY)=\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1xy(x+y)\,dx\,dy=\frac16+\frac16=\frac13
Step 3 — Covariance.
\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=\frac13-\frac{49}{144}=-\frac{1}{144}
Answer. \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbf{-1/144}.


A full covariance calculation for a “draw from a bag” table is in P4 Joint Marginal and Conditional Distributions.

Type 5 — Exact probability within \mu\pm k\sigma compared with Chebyshev
How to recognise it: “compute P(\mu-2\sigma<X<\mu+2\sigma) and compare with Chebyshev’s theorem” (2022-23 Q2(c)).
Recipe:

Find \mu and \sigma.
Form the interval (cut it at the support boundary).
Integrate f over it.
Compare with 1-\frac1{k^2}.



                  
                  Practice 5.1 
                  
                

Given. f(x)=3x^2 for 0<x<1.
Step 1 — Mean.
\mu=\int_0^13x^3\,dx=\frac34
Step 2 — Variance and SD.
E(X^2)=\int_0^13x^4\,dx=\frac35
\sigma^2=\frac35-\frac9{16}=\frac3{80}
\sigma=0.1936
Step 3 — The interval.
\mu\pm2\sigma=(0.3627,\ 1.1373)
Above 1 the density is zero, so integrate only up to 1.
Step 4 — Exact probability.
P=\int_{0.3627}^{1}3x^2\,dx=1-0.3627^3=0.9523
Step 5 — Compare. Chebyshev guarantees at least 1-\frac14=0.75.
Answer. Exact 0.9523 ≥ Chebyshev bound 0.75, consistent with the theorem (the bound is conservative).




                  
                  Practice 5.2 
                  
                

Given. f(x)=e^{-x}, x>0 (so \mu=1, \sigma=1). Find P(\mu-2\sigma<X<\mu+2\sigma) and compare.
Step 1 — The interval. (-1,3), effectively (0,3).
Step 2 — Exact probability.
P=1-e^{-3}=0.9502
Answer. 0.9502 ≥ 0.75.



Type 6 — Chebyshev applications (bounds, jobs, intervals)
How to recognise it: only \mu and \sigma are known, no distribution.
Recipe:

Compute

k=\frac{\text{distance from mean}}{\sigma}

Apply the bound.
Halve it if the distribution is symmetric and only one tail is wanted.
Multiply by the number of people if needed.



                  
                  Practice 6.1 (same logic as 2023-24 Q3(a)) — jobs 
                  
                

Given. 50 jobs, 800 applicants; test scores have mean 70 and SD 5, symmetric. Can a person who scores 85 count on a job?
Step 1 — Find k.
k=\frac{85-70}{5}=3
Step 2 — Chebyshev bound.
P(|X-70|\ge15)\le\frac19
Step 3 — One tail (symmetric).
P(X\ge85)\le\frac1{18}
Step 4 — Convert to people.
800\times\frac1{18}\approx44
Answer. At most about 44 applicants can score 85 or more. Since there are 50 jobs, yes, a score of 85 should get a job.




                  
                  Practice 6.2 — bounds 
                  
                

Given. X has mean 8 and variance 9 (distribution unknown). Find (i) a lower bound for P(-4<X<20), (ii) an upper bound for P(|X-8|\ge6).
\sigma=3.
Step 1 — (i) -4 and 20 are 12=4\sigma from the mean, so k=4.
P(-4<X<20)\ge1-\frac1{16}=\frac{15}{16}
Step 2 — (ii) 6=2\sigma, so k=2.
P(|X-8|\ge6)\le\frac14
Answer. (i) ≥ 15/16, (ii) ≤ 1/4.




                  
                  Practice 6.3 — reverse question 
                  
                

Given. Marks have mean 60 and SD 8. (i) At least what fraction lies between 40 and 80? (ii) Find an interval that contains at least 90% of the marks.
Step 1 — (i)
k=\frac{20}{8}=2.5
1-\frac1{6.25}=0.84
Step 2 — (ii) Solve for k.
1-\frac1{k^2}=0.9\ \Rightarrow\ k=\sqrt{10}=3.162
60\pm3.162(8)=(34.7,\ 85.3)
Answer. (i) at least 84%, (ii) (34.7, 85.3).




                  
                  Three-line Chebyshev answer 
                  
                

Compute k.
State the bound (halve it for one tail if symmetric).
Convert to people or compare with what is asked.



Extra practice


                  
                  Answers (try first) 
                  
                

1. E(X)=3, \mathrm{Var}(X)=2. Find E(4X+1) and \mathrm{Var}(4X+1).
Answer: 13 and 32.
2. f(x)=\frac{x}{2} on 0<x<2. Find E(X) and \mathrm{Var}(X).
Answer: \frac43; E(X^2)=2, so \mathrm{Var}=2-\frac{16}9=\frac29.
3. f(x)=2e^{-2x}, x>0. Find E(e^{X}).
Answer: \int_0^\infty2e^{-x}dx=2.
4. Mean 100, SD 10. Lower bound for P(80 < X < 120)?
Answer: k=2: at least 0.75.
5. If \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0, must X and Y be independent?
Answer: No.

1-Probability/P6-Bernoulli-Binomial-Mult.content:
P6 · Binomial Family: Problems First


                  
                  Why this matters for the TF 
                  
                

A binomial-type story problem appears in almost every paper: lottery tickets and delegates (2021-22 Q6), diodes and Valium prescriptions (2020-21 Q6–Q7), and recovery from a blood disease (2023-24 Q3(c), solved in TF 2023-24 Solutions).
These are quick, reliable marks once you can recognise the distribution and translate words like “at least” into x values.


Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize: the five distributions 
                  
                

Binomial
Use for a fixed number n of independent trials, two outcomes, constant p.
b(x;n,p)=\binom nx p^x q^{n-x}
\mu=np
\sigma^2=npq
Multinomial
Use when each trial has k outcomes, with \sum x_i=n.
P=\frac{n!}{x_1!\cdots x_k!}\,p_1^{x_1}\cdots p_k^{x_k}
Hypergeometric
Use when you draw n without replacement from N items containing k successes.
h(x)=\frac{\binom kx\binom{N-k}{n-x}}{\binom Nn}
\mu=\frac{nk}{N}
Geometric
Use for “the first success is on trial x“.
g(x)=p\,q^{x-1}
\mu=\frac1p
Negative binomial
Use for “the k-th success is on trial x“.
b^*(x;k,p)=\binom{x-1}{k-1}p^k q^{x-k}




                  
                  Translating words into x values
                  
                

“At least 10” is 1-P(X\le9).
“From 3 to 8” is P(X\le8)-P(X\le2).
“At most 2” is P(X\le2).
“Exactly 5 die” when X counts survivors out of 15 means exactly 10 survive.
Always write one sentence saying what X counts before you calculate.


Theory the TF may ask (short)
Only the mean and variance of the binomial are ever needed, and a two-line argument is enough.
X is the sum of n independent Bernoulli variables X_i, each equal to 1 with probability p and 0 with probability q.
Each Bernoulli variable:
E(X_i)=p
\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=p-p^2=pq
Means add, and for independent variables variances add, so:
Binomial mean:
E(X)=np
Binomial variance:
\mathrm{Var}(X)=npq

Problem types you will face
Type 1 — Binomial: “at least”, “between”, “exactly k fail”
Recognise it: a fixed number of people or items, each independently succeeding with the same probability.
Recipe:

Define X and write X\sim b(x;n,p).
Translate the words into x values.
Add the needed terms (use the complement when it has fewer terms).



                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q6(a) (10 marks) — lottery tickets 
                  
                

Given. Out of 500 tickets, 200 pay back at least their cost. You buy 5 tickets.
Step 1 — Define X. Let X be the number of tickets that win back at least their cost.
p=\frac{200}{500}=0.4,\qquad q=0.6,\qquad n=5
5 is tiny compared with 500, so the tickets are treated as independent. We need P(X\ge3).
Step 2 — The three terms.
P(X=3)=\binom53(0.4)^3(0.6)^2=10(0.064)(0.36)=0.2304
P(X=4)=\binom54(0.4)^4(0.6)=0.0768
P(X=5)=(0.4)^5=0.01024
Step 3 — Add.
P(X\ge3)=0.2304+0.0768+0.01024=0.3174
Answer. P(X\ge3)=\mathbf{0.3174}.




                  
                  Practice 1 (TF style, like 2023-24 Q3(c)) — recovery 
                  
                

Given. The probability that a patient recovers from an illness is 0.3. If 12 people have the illness, find the probability that (i) at least 8 recover, (ii) from 2 to 5 recover, (iii) exactly 4 die.
Step 1 — Define X. Let X = number who recover, X\sim b(x;12,0.3).
Step 2 — (i) At least 8 recover.
P(X\ge8)=\sum_{x=8}^{12}\binom{12}{x}(0.3)^x(0.7)^{12-x}=0.0095
Step 3 — (ii) From 2 to 5 recover.
P(2\le X\le5)=P(X\le5)-P(X\le1)=0.7971
Step 4 — (iii) Exactly 4 die means exactly 8 recover.
\begin{aligned}
P(X=8)&=\binom{12}{8}(0.3)^8(0.7)^4\\
&=495\times0.00006561\times0.2401\\
&=0.0078
\end{aligned}
Answer. (i) 0.0095, (ii) 0.7971, (iii) 0.0078.




                  
                  Practice 2 (TF style) — defective items 
                  
                

Given. 10% of the bolts made by a machine are defective. In a box of 10 bolts find the probability of (i) at most 2 defective, (ii) at least 2 defective, (iii) exactly 8 good bolts.
Step 1 — Define X. Let X = number of defectives, X\sim b(x;10,0.1).
Step 2 — The first three terms.
P(0)=(0.9)^{10}=0.3487
P(1)=10(0.1)(0.9)^9=0.3874
P(2)=45(0.01)(0.9)^8=0.1937
Step 3 — (i) At most 2.
P(X\le2)=0.3487+0.3874+0.1937=0.9298
Step 4 — (ii) At least 2. The complement is much shorter than adding 9 terms.
P(X\ge2)=1-P(0)-P(1)=1-0.3487-0.3874=0.2639
Step 5 — (iii) 8 good means 2 defective.
P(X=2)=0.1937
Answer. (i) 0.9298, (ii) 0.2639, (iii) 0.1937.




                  
                  Practice 3 (TF style) — a new drug 
                  
                

Given. A drug cures 70% of patients. It is given to 12 patients. Find (i) P(\text{at least 9 cured}), (ii) P(4\le X\le7), (iii) P(\text{exactly 3 not cured}).
Step 1 — Define X. X = number cured, X\sim b(x;12,0.7).
Step 2 — (i) At least 9.
P(9)=0.2397,\quad P(10)=0.1678,\quad P(11)=0.0712,\quad P(12)=0.0138
P(X\ge9)=0.2397+0.1678+0.0712+0.0138=0.4925
Step 3 — (ii) From 4 to 7.
P(4\le X\le7)=P(X\le7)-P(X\le3)=0.2763-0.0017=0.2747
Step 4 — (iii) 3 not cured means 9 cured.
P(X=9)=\binom{12}{9}(0.7)^9(0.3)^3=0.2397
Answer. (i) 0.4925, (ii) 0.2747, (iii) 0.2397.




                  
                  Practice 4 (TF style) — guessing a test 
                  
                

Given. A quiz has 6 multiple-choice questions with 4 options each. A student guesses every answer. Find the probability of getting at least 3 correct.
Step 1 — Define X. X\sim b(x;6,0.25).
Step 2 — The terms.
P(3)=0.1318,\quad P(4)=0.0330,\quad P(5)=0.0044,\quad P(6)=0.0002
Step 3 — Add.
P(X\ge3)=0.1694
Answer. \mathbf{0.1694}.



Type 2 — Binomial mean, variance and “nothing fails”
Recognise it: “what is the mean number of failures”, “the variance”, “the board works only if none is defective”.
Recipe:
\mu=np
\sigma^2=npq
P(\text{none})=P(X=0)=q^n


                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q7(a) (17 marks) — diode failures 
                  
                

Given. Each of the n=200 diodes fails independently with p=0.03, so X\sim b(x;200,0.03) with q=0.97.
Step 1 — (i) Mean.
\mu=np=200(0.03)=6 \text{ failures}
Step 2 — (ii) Variance.
\sigma^2=npq=200(0.03)(0.97)=5.82
\sigma=2.41
Step 3 — (iii) The board works only if no diode fails.
P(X=0)=(0.97)^{200}=0.00226
Answer. (i) 6, (ii) 5.82, (iii) 0.00226.
Comment. The board almost never works. The Poisson approximation with \lambda=6 gives e^{-6}=0.00248, which is close (see P7 Poisson Distribution and Poisson Process).




                  
                  Practice 5 (TF style) — resistors 
                  
                

Given. A resistor is faulty with probability 0.02. A circuit uses 400 resistors. Find the mean and SD of the number of faulty resistors and the probability that the circuit has no faulty resistor.
Step 1 — Mean.
\mu=400(0.02)=8
Step 2 — Variance and SD.
\sigma^2=400(0.02)(0.98)=7.84
\sigma=2.8
Step 3 — No faulty resistor.
P(X=0)=(0.98)^{400}=0.0003
Answer. Mean 8, SD 2.8, P(\text{none})=\mathbf{0.0003}. The circuit is practically certain to contain a faulty resistor.



Type 3 — Find n and p from the mean and variance
Recipe:

Divide the variance by the mean to get q:

q=\frac{npq}{np}

Then p=1-q.
Then n=\mu/p.



                  
                  Practice 6 (TF style) 
                  
                

Given. A binomial variable has mean 4 and variance 3.2. Find n, p and P(X=2).
Step 1 — Find q and p.
q=\frac{3.2}{4}=0.8
p=0.2
Step 2 — Find n.
n=\frac{4}{0.2}=20
Step 3 — P(X=2).
\begin{aligned}
P(X=2)&=\binom{20}{2}(0.2)^2(0.8)^{18}\\
&=190\times0.04\times0.01801\\
&=0.1369
\end{aligned}
Answer. n=\mathbf{20}, p=\mathbf{0.2}, P(X=2)=\mathbf{0.1369}.




                  
                  Check your answer 
                  
                

The variance of a binomial is always smaller than its mean (because q<1).
n must come out as a whole number. If either fails, re-read the question.



Type 4 — Multinomial
Recognise it: each trial has three or more outcomes and you want a given count of each.
Recipe:

Check the counts add to n.
Coefficient times product of powers.



                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q6(b) (10 marks) — how delegates arrived 
                  
                

Given. Probabilities: air 0.4, bus 0.2, automobile 0.3, train 0.1. We want 3, 3, 1, 2 out of n=9.
Step 1 — Check the counts. 3+3+1+2=9 ✓
Step 2 — Multinomial coefficient.
\frac{9!}{3!\,3!\,1!\,2!}=5040
Step 3 — Probability.
\begin{aligned}
P&=5040\,(0.4)^3(0.2)^3(0.3)(0.1)^2\\
&=5040\times1.536\times10^{-6}\\
&=0.00774
\end{aligned}
Answer. P=\mathbf{0.00774}.




                  
                  Practice 7 (TF style) — a die 
                  
                

Given. A fair die is rolled 6 times. Find the probability that a 1 or 2 appears twice, a 3, 4 or 5 appears three times, and a 6 appears once.
Step 1 — Outcome probabilities.
p_1=\frac13,\qquad p_2=\frac12,\qquad p_3=\frac16
Step 2 — Multinomial.
\begin{aligned}
P&=\frac{6!}{2!\,3!\,1!}\left(\tfrac13\right)^2\left(\tfrac12\right)^3\left(\tfrac16\right)\\
&=60\times\frac19\times\frac18\times\frac16\\
&=0.1389
\end{aligned}
Answer. \mathbf{0.1389}.




                  
                  Practice 8 (TF style) — blood groups 
                  
                

Given. In a population, blood groups O, A, B, AB occur with probabilities 0.45, 0.40, 0.11, 0.04. Among 8 randomly chosen donors, find the probability of 3 O, 3 A, 1 B and 1 AB.
Step 1 — Multinomial coefficient.
\frac{8!}{3!\,3!\,1!\,1!}=1120
Step 2 — Probability.
\begin{aligned}
P&=1120\,(0.45)^3(0.40)^3(0.11)(0.04)\\
&=1120\times(2.566\times10^{-5})\\
&=0.0287
\end{aligned}
Answer. \mathbf{0.0287}.



Type 5 — Hypergeometric: distribution and F(x)
Recognise it: “a lot/shipment of N contains k defective; n are chosen” (without replacement).
Recipe:

List all possible x.
Compute h(x) for each.
Build the cumulative F(x) as a step function.

The 2021-22 Q6(c) cars problem (N=5,k=2,n=3, giving \frac1{10},\frac35,\frac3{10}) is solved in P3 Random Variables PMF PDF CDF.


                  
                  Practice 9 (TF style) — a lot of 10 items 
                  
                

Given. A lot of 10 items contains 3 defectives. An inspector picks 4 at random. Find the probability distribution and the CDF of X, the number of defectives picked.
Step 1 — Total samples.
\binom{10}{4}=210
Step 2 — The pmf.
h(x)=\frac{\binom3x\binom7{4-x}}{210}


























x0123f(x)\frac{35}{210}=\frac16\frac{105}{210}=\frac12\frac{63}{210}=\frac{3}{10}\frac{7}{210}=\frac1{30}F(x)\frac16\frac23\frac{29}{30}1
Step 3 — The CDF.
F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0\\ 1/6,&0\le x<1\\ 2/3,&1\le x<2\\ 29/30,&2\le x<3\\ 1,&x\ge3\end{cases}
Step 4 — Check the mean.
\mu=\frac{nk}{N}=\frac{4\times3}{10}=1.2
Answer. The table and F(x) above.




                  
                  Practice 10 (TF style) — a committee 
                  
                

Given. A committee of 3 is chosen at random from 6 men and 4 women. Find the probability that at least 2 women are chosen.
Step 1 — Add the “2 women” and “3 women” cases.
\begin{aligned}
P&=\frac{\binom42\binom61+\binom43\binom60}{\binom{10}{3}}\\
&=\frac{36+4}{120}\\
&=\frac13
\end{aligned}
Answer. \mathbf{1/3\approx0.3333}.



Type 6 — Geometric and negative binomial
Recognise it: “the 5th prescription is the first/third …”, “the first success occurs on trial …“.
Recipe:

The last trial is a success.
Arrange the remaining k-1 successes among the first x-1 trials.



                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q6(c) (10 marks) — Valium prescriptions 
                  
                

Given. A prescription is for a woman (success) with p=\frac23, q=\frac13.
Step 1 — (i) Fifth prescription is the first for a woman (geometric, x=5).
g(5)=\left(\tfrac23\right)\left(\tfrac13\right)^4=\frac{2}{243}=0.00823
Step 2 — (ii) Fifth prescription is the third for a woman (negative binomial, k=3, x=5).
\begin{aligned}
b^*(5;3,\tfrac23)&=\binom42\left(\tfrac23\right)^3\left(\tfrac13\right)^2\\
&=6\cdot\frac{8}{27}\cdot\frac19\\
&=0.1975
\end{aligned}
Answer. (i) 0.00823, (ii) 0.1975.




                  
                  Common mistake 
                  
                

Do not use \binom53 in part (ii).
The last trial is forced to be a success, so only the first 4 trials are free, giving \binom42.




                  
                  Practice 11 (TF style) — oil drilling 
                  
                

Given. Each well drilled strikes oil with probability 0.3. Find the probability that (i) the first strike comes on the 4th well, (ii) the 3rd strike comes on the 7th well.
Step 1 — (i) Geometric.
g(4)=(0.7)^3(0.3)=0.1029
Step 2 — (ii) Negative binomial.
\begin{aligned}
b^*(7;3,0.3)&=\binom62(0.3)^3(0.7)^4\\
&=15\times0.027\times0.2401\\
&=0.0972
\end{aligned}
Answer. (i) 0.1029, (ii) 0.0972.




                  
                  Practice 12 (TF style) — free throws 
                  
                

Given. A player makes 80% of free throws. Find the probability that the 5th throw is the player’s second miss.
Step 1 — Define the success. A miss is the “success” here, so p=0.2.
Step 2 — Negative binomial.
\begin{aligned}
b^*(5;2,0.2)&=\binom41(0.2)^2(0.8)^3\\
&=4\times0.04\times0.512\\
&=0.0819
\end{aligned}
Answer. \mathbf{0.0819}.



Extra practice


                  
                  Answers (try first) 
                  
                

1. 5% of items are defective; in a sample of 8, find P(\text{at most 1 defective}).
Answer: (0.95)^8+8(0.05)(0.95)^7=0.6634+0.2793=0.9427.
2. Mean of a binomial is 6, SD is 2. Find n and p.
Answer: q=4/6, p=1/3, n=18.
3. A coin is tossed until the first head; probability it takes exactly 4 tosses?
Answer: (1/2)^4=1/16.
4. Mean and variance of b(x;20,0.25)?
Answer: 5 and 3.75.
5. From 5 cars of which 2 are blemished, 3 are bought. P(\text{no blemished car})?
Answer: \binom33/\binom53=1/10.
6. Multinomial coefficient for counts 2, 1, 1 out of 4?
Answer: 4!/(2!1!1!)=12.
