1-Probability/P7-Poisson-Distribution-an.content:
P7 · Poisson Distribution: Problems First


                  
                  Why this matters for the TF 
                  
                

Poisson appears in every recent paper: glass bubbles (2019-20 Q8(a)), tax-return errors plus two derivations (2022-23 Q3(a),(b)), and switchboard calls plus the binomial–Poisson relation (2023-24 Q3(b)).
The numerical parts are quick; the derivations below are pure memory marks.
The 2022-23 and 2023-24 parts are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions.


Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize: Poisson 
                  
                

Poisson pmf (x=0,1,2,\dots)
p(x;\mu)=\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^x}{x!}
Mean and variance are equal
E(X)=\mu
\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mu
Mean for a rate (use for counts in time or space)
Counts of events in time or space at an average rate: the rate times the length of the interval.
\mu=\lambda t
Mean for approximating a binomial (large n, small p)
\mu=np




                  
                  Fast calculation 
                  
                

Use the recursion, starting from p(0)=e^{-\mu}:
p(x)=p(x-1)\cdot\frac{\mu}{x}
It is faster and safer than recomputing every factorial.



Theory the TF actually asks (learn word for word)
Bernoulli process vs Poisson process (2022-23 Q3(a))


                  
                  Memorize: Bernoulli process 
                  
                

A Bernoulli process is a sequence of trials with three properties.

Each trial has only two outcomes (success or failure).
The probability of success p stays the same from trial to trial.
The trials are independent.

The number of successes in n trials of a Bernoulli process is binomial, b(x;n,p).




                  
                  Memorize: Poisson process 
                  
                

A Poisson process describes events occurring randomly in continuous time or space (calls at a switchboard, accidents, flaws along a cable). It has three properties.

The numbers of events in non-overlapping intervals are independent (no memory).
The probability of exactly one event in a very short interval is proportional to the length of the interval and does not depend on events outside it.
The probability of two or more events in a very short interval is negligible.

The number of events X in an interval of length t is then Poisson with mean \mu=\lambda t, where \lambda is the average rate per unit time.


A Poisson process can be viewed as a Bernoulli process in which time is cut into a huge number of tiny pieces. Each piece is a trial with a tiny chance of containing an event.
Deriving Poisson from binomial (2022-23 Q3(a), 2023-24 Q3(b) “establish the relation”)


                  
                  Memorize: Derivation 
                  
                

Let X\sim b(x;n,p) and let n\to\infty, p\to0 with np=\mu fixed.
Step 1 — Put p=\mu/n.
b(x;n,p)=\frac{n!}{x!\,(n-x)!}\left(\frac{\mu}{n}\right)^x\left(1-\frac{\mu}{n}\right)^{n-x}
Step 2 — Rearrange into four factors.
b(x;n,p)=\frac{\mu^x}{x!}\cdot\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-x+1)}{n^x}\cdot\left(1-\frac{\mu}{n}\right)^{n}\cdot\left(1-\frac{\mu}{n}\right)^{-x}
Step 3 — Take the limit of each factor as n\to\infty with x and \mu fixed.
The second factor is 1\cdot(1-\frac1n)\cdots(1-\frac{x-1}{n}), so
\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-x+1)}{n^x}\to1
The third factor:
\left(1-\frac{\mu}{n}\right)^{n}\to e^{-\mu}
The last factor:
\left(1-\frac{\mu}{n}\right)^{-x}\to1
Step 4 — Result. For x=0,1,2,\dots
\lim_{n\to\infty}b(x;n,p)=\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^x}{x!}=p(x;\mu)
==The Poisson distribution is the limiting form of the binomial when n is large, p is small and np=\mu is moderate.==
It is a valid distribution because
\sum_x \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^x}{x!}=e^{-\mu}e^{\mu}=1


Relation in words. Both count successes: the binomial in a fixed number of trials, the Poisson in a continuous interval.
The binomial has mean np and variance npq. As p\to0, q\to1, so the variance npq\to np. That is why the Poisson has equal mean and variance.
In practice, approximate the binomial by the Poisson when n\ge20 and p\le0.05, using \mu=np.
Mean and variance (2022-23 Q3(b) “calculate the variance”)


                  
                  Memorize: Mean 
                  
                

\begin{aligned}
E(X)&=\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}x\,\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^x}{x!}\\
&=\mu e^{-\mu}\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu^{x-1}}{(x-1)!}\\
&=\mu e^{-\mu}e^{\mu}\\
&=\mu
\end{aligned}




                  
                  Memorize: Variance (via E[X(X-1)])
                  
                

Step 1 — Find E[X(X-1)].
\begin{aligned}
E[X(X-1)]&=\sum_{x=2}^{\infty}x(x-1)\,\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^x}{x!}\\
&=\mu^2e^{-\mu}\sum_{x=2}^{\infty}\frac{\mu^{x-2}}{(x-2)!}\\
&=\mu^2
\end{aligned}
Step 2 — Find E(X^2).
E(X^2)=E[X(X-1)]+E(X)=\mu^2+\mu
Step 3 — Variance.
\mathrm{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2=\mu^2+\mu-\mu^2=\mu



Problem types you will face
Type 1 — A rate per unit time, scaled to the interval asked
Recognise it: “on average 0.5 calls per minute … in a five-minute period”.
Recipe:

Scale the rate to the interval (in matching units):

\mu=\text{rate}\times\text{interval length}

Use the Poisson formula.



                  
                  Common mistake: scaling the rate 
                  
                

If calls arrive at 0.5 per minute and the question is about 5 minutes, \mu=2.5, not 0.5.
If accidents happen 3 times per month and the question is about two months, \mu=6.




                  
                  Practice 1 (TF style, like 2023-24 Q3(b)) — server requests 
                  
                

Given. Requests reach a server at an average rate of 2 per minute. Find the probability that exactly 4 arrive in a 3-minute period.
Step 1 — Scale the rate.
\mu=2\times3=6
Step 2 — Poisson formula.
\begin{aligned}
P(X=4)&=\frac{e^{-6}6^4}{4!}\\
&=\frac{0.0024788\times1296}{24}\\
&=0.1339
\end{aligned}
Answer. \mathbf{0.1339}.




                  
                  Practice 2 (TF style) — factory accidents 
                  
                

Given. Accidents occur in a factory at an average of 3 per month. Find (i) the probability of no accident in a two-month period, (ii) the probability of at least 2 accidents in a month.
Step 1 — (i) Two months, so \mu=6.
P(X=0)=e^{-6}=0.0025
Step 2 — (ii) One month, so \mu=3.
\begin{aligned}
P(X\ge2)&=1-e^{-3}(1+3)\\
&=1-0.0498\times4\\
&=0.8009
\end{aligned}
Answer. (i) 0.0025, (ii) 0.8009.




                  
                  Practice 3 (TF style) — typing errors 
                  
                

Given. A typist makes on average 0.4 errors per page. Find the probability that a 5-page report has at most one error.
Step 1 — Scale the rate.
\mu=0.4\times5=2
Step 2 — At most one.
P(X\le1)=e^{-2}(1+2)=0.1353\times3=0.4060
Answer. \mathbf{0.4060}.



Type 2 — Poisson approximation to a binomial
Recognise it: “1 in every 1000 …”, a huge sample (n in thousands), “find the probability that 6, 7 or 8 …” or “fewer than 7”.
Recipe:

State that n is large and p small.
Put \mu=np.
Add the required Poisson terms (use the recursion).



                  
                  Past TF 2019-20 Q8(a) (10 marks) — glass bubbles 
                  
                

Given. On average 1 in 1000 items has bubbles, so p=0.001, with n=8000.
Step 1 — Justify the approximation. Since n is large and p small, X is approximately Poisson with
\mu=np=8000\times0.001=8
Step 2 — “Fewer than 7” means X\le6. Compute the terms:

























x0123456e^{-8}8^x/x!0.00030.00270.01070.02860.05730.09160.1221
Step 3 — Add.
P(X<7)=\sum_{x=0}^{6}\frac{e^{-8}8^x}{x!}=0.3134
Answer. \mathbf{0.3134}: about a 31% chance that fewer than 7 of the 8000 items have bubbles.




                  
                  Practice 4 (TF style, like 2022-23 Q3(b)) — misprinted tickets 
                  
                

Given. On average 1 ticket in 1000 is misprinted. If 5000 tickets are checked, find the probability that 3, 4 or 5 are misprinted.
Step 1 — Mean.
\mu=5000\times0.001=5
Step 2 — The terms (recursion).
p(3)=\frac{e^{-5}5^3}{3!}=0.1404
p(4)=p(3)\cdot\frac54=0.1755
p(5)=p(4)\cdot\frac55=0.1755
Step 3 — Add.
P(3\le X\le5)=0.1404+0.1755+0.1755=0.4913
Answer. \mathbf{0.4913}.




                  
                  Practice 5 (TF style) — defective chips 
                  
                

Given. A chip is defective with probability 0.002. In a batch of 1500 chips, find the probability of at least 2 defectives.
Step 1 — Mean.
\mu=1500\times0.002=3
Step 2 — At least 2.
P(X\ge2)=1-e^{-3}(1+3)=0.8009
Answer. \mathbf{0.8009}. (The exact binomial gives 0.8012, so the approximation is excellent.)



Type 3 — Find \mu from a relation between probabilities
Recognise it: “if P(X=1)=P(X=2), find the mean and SD”.
Recipe:

Write both sides with the formula.
Cancel e^{-\mu} and solve for \mu.
Then mean =\mu and SD =\sqrt\mu.



                  
                  Practice 6 (TF style) 
                  
                

Given. For a Poisson variable P(X=1)=P(X=2). Find the mean, SD and P(X\ge1).
Step 1 — Set up the equation.
e^{-\mu}\mu=\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^2}{2}
Step 2 — Solve.
\mu=2
Step 3 — SD and probability.
\sigma=\sqrt2=1.4142
P(X\ge1)=1-e^{-2}=0.8647
Answer. Mean 2, SD 1.4142, P(X\ge1)=\mathbf{0.8647}.




                  
                  Practice 7 (TF style) 
                  
                

Given. For a Poisson variable 3P(X=2)=2P(X=1). Find \mu and P(X=0).
Step 1 — Set up and cancel e^{-\mu}.
3\cdot\frac{\mu^2}{2}=2\mu
Step 2 — Solve.
\mu=\frac43
Step 3 — P(X=0).
P(X=0)=e^{-4/3}=0.2636
Answer. \mu=\mathbf{4/3}, P(X=0)=\mathbf{0.2636}.



Extra practice


                  
                  Answers (try first) 
                  
                

1. Calls arrive at 3 per hour. Probability of no call in 20 minutes?
Answer: \mu=1, so e^{-1}=0.3679.
2. 1 person in 500 has a rare blood type. Among 1000 donors, P(\text{exactly } 3)?
Answer: \mu=2, so e^{-2}2^3/6=0.1804.
3. Mean and variance of a Poisson with \mu=4?
Answer: Both 4.
4. Which limit is used in the derivation?
Answer: (1-\mu/n)^n\to e^{-\mu}.
5. Why compute E[X(X-1)] for the variance?
Answer: Because x(x-1) cancels with x!, giving \mu^2 directly.

1-Probability/P8-Normal-Distribution.content:
P8 · Normal Distribution: Problems First


                  
                  Why this matters for the TF 
                  
                

A normal-table calculation appears in every paper: mice lifetimes (2020-21 Q7(b)), ball bearings (2021-22 Q7(b)), the lawyer’s trip times (2022-23 Q3(c)) and bulb lives (2023-24 Q4(a)).
The newest papers also ask theory: properties of the normal curve and its mean, mode and SD (2022-23 Q4(a)) and ==show that the mode is \mu== (2023-24 Q4(a)).
Those two papers are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions.


Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize: Normal 
                  
                

Normal density (-\infty<x<\infty)
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}
Standardise
Use for every normal probability.
Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim N(0,1)
Less than (the table gives the left area)
P(X<a)=\Phi(z)
More than
P(X>a)=1-\Phi(z)
Between
P(a<X<b)=\Phi(z_2)-\Phi(z_1)
Negative z
\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)
Reverse lookup (find a cut-off value)
x=\mu+z\sigma
Empirical rule
Within \mu\pm\sigma, \mu\pm2\sigma, \mu\pm3\sigma: 68.27%, 95.45%, 99.73%.






                  
                  Always draw the curve 
                  
                

Sketch a bell curve, mark \mu and your x values, shade the wanted area and write the z values under them.
Ten seconds of drawing prevents the most common error: taking the wrong side.



Theory the TF actually asks (learn word for word)
Properties of the normal curve (2022-23 Q4(a))


                  
                  Memorize: Properties 
                  
                


The normal curve is ==bell-shaped and symmetric about x=\mu, so mean = median = mode = \mu==.
Its highest point is at x=\mu, with height \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}.
It has points of inflection at x=\mu\pm\sigma.
It approaches the x-axis asymptotically on both sides but never touches it.
The total area under the curve is 1.
About 68.27%, 95.45% and 99.73% of the area lies within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean.
Its skewness is 0 and \beta_2=3 (mesokurtic).
The two parameters \mu and \sigma determine the curve completely: \mu fixes the centre, and a larger \sigma gives a lower, wider curve.



The mode is \mu (2023-24 Q4(a))
Step 1 — Differentiate the density with the chain rule.
f'(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}\cdot\left(-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\right)
f'(x)=-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\,f(x)
Step 2 — Set f'(x)=0. Since f(x)>0 always, f'(x)=0 gives
x=\mu
Step 3 — Second derivative.
f''(x)=\frac{f(x)}{\sigma^2}\left[\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2}-1\right]
f''(\mu)=-\frac{f(\mu)}{\sigma^2}<0
Conclusion. f has its maximum at x=\mu: ==the mode of the normal distribution is \mu==.
(Also, f''(x)=0 at x=\mu\pm\sigma, which proves the points of inflection.)
The mean is \mu and the SD is \sigma (2022-23 Q4(a))
Substitution. Put z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}, so x=\mu+\sigma z and dx=\sigma\,dz.
Mean:
\begin{aligned}
E(X)&=\mu\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}\,dz+\sigma\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{z}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}\,dz\\
&=\mu(1)+\sigma(0)\\
&=\mu
\end{aligned}
The first integral is the total area under the standard normal curve (1). The second is 0 because z\,e^{-z^2/2} is an odd function.
Variance:
\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sigma^2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{z^2}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}\,dz
Integrate by parts with u=z, dv=z\,e^{-z^2/2}dz (so v=-e^{-z^2/2}):
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}z^2e^{-z^2/2}\,dz&=\Big[-z\,e^{-z^2/2}\Big]_{-\infty}^{\infty}+\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-z^2/2}\,dz\\
&=0+\sqrt{2\pi}
\end{aligned}
So \mathrm{Var}(X)=\sigma^2 and the SD is \sigma.


                  
                  Memorize: Standard normal 
                  
                

Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma} has mean 0 and variance 1.
E(Z)=\frac{E(X)-\mu}{\sigma}=0
\mathrm{Var}(Z)=\frac{\mathrm{Var}(X)}{\sigma^2}=1
Its density is
\phi(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}
Every normal probability can be read from this one table.



Problem types you will face
Type 1 — Forward probabilities: less than, more than, between
Recipe:

Compute z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} (2 decimals).
Read \Phi from the table.
Use the left/right/between rule.



                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q7(b) (18 marks) — mice lifetimes 
                  
                

Given. X\sim N(40,\ 6.3^2) months.
Step 1 — (i) More than 32 months.
z=\frac{32-40}{6.3}=-1.27
P(X>32)=1-\Phi(-1.27)=1-0.1020=0.8980
Step 2 — (ii) Between 37 and 49 months.
z_1=\frac{37-40}{6.3}=-0.48
z_2=\frac{49-40}{6.3}=1.43
P(37<X<49)=\Phi(1.43)-\Phi(-0.48)=0.9236-0.3156=0.6080
Answer. (i) 0.8980, (ii) 0.6080.
(Without rounding z the answer is 0.6065; both are accepted when the table values are shown.)




                  
                  Practice 1 (TF style, like 2023-24 Q4(a)) — three questions at once 
                  
                

Given. X\sim N(50,\ 10^2). Find P(X<45), P(X>62) and P(42<X<64).
Step 1 — Less than 45. z=-0.50.
P(X<45)=\Phi(-0.50)=0.3085
Step 2 — More than 62. z=1.20.
P(X>62)=1-\Phi(1.20)=1-0.8849=0.1151
Step 3 — Between 42 and 64. z_1=-0.80, z_2=1.40.
P(42<X<64)=\Phi(1.40)-\Phi(-0.80)=0.9192-0.2119=0.7073
Answer. 0.3085, 0.1151, 0.7073.




                  
                  Practice 2 (TF style) — exam scores 
                  
                

Given. Scores are N(500,\ 50^2). Find P(450<X<620).
Step 1 — z values.
z_1=\frac{450-500}{50}=-1.00
z_2=\frac{620-500}{50}=2.40
Step 2 — Between.
P=\Phi(2.40)-\Phi(-1.00)=0.9918-0.1587=0.8331
Answer. \mathbf{0.8331}.




                  
                  Common mistake 
                  
                

In “between” questions subtract the areas \Phi(z_2)-\Phi(z_1), never the z values.
In “more than” questions remember 1-\Phi(z).



Type 2 — “What percentage of the time” / “how many out of N”
Recipe: find the probability as in Type 1, then multiply by 100 (percentage) or by N (count).


                  
                  Practice 3 (TF style) — 1000 students 
                  
                

Given. Marks of 1000 students are N(60,\ 8^2). How many students score (i) above 72, (ii) between 50 and 70?
Step 1 — (i) Above 72.
z=\frac{72-60}{8}=1.50
P=1-0.9332=0.0668
1000\times0.0668\approx67
Step 2 — (ii) Between 50 and 70. z=\pm1.25.
P=\Phi(1.25)-\Phi(-1.25)=0.8944-0.1056=0.7888
1000\times0.7888\approx789
Answer. (i) about 67 students, (ii) about 789 students.




                  
                  Practice 4 (TF style, like 2022-23 Q3(c)(i)) — late for class 
                  
                

Given. A student’s travel time is N(25,\ 4^2) minutes. Class starts at 10:00 and the student leaves at 9:30. What percentage of days is the student late?
Step 1 — Translate. Late means the trip takes more than 30 minutes.
Step 2 — Probability.
z=\frac{30-25}{4}=1.25
P(X>30)=1-\Phi(1.25)=1-0.8944=0.1056
Answer. The student is late on about 10.6% of days.



Type 3 — Reverse lookup: find the cut-off value
Recognise it: “find the score above which the top 10% lie”, “the time above which the slowest 15% of trips lie”, “minimum mark for an A”.
Recipe:

Convert to a left area.
Find z inside the table.
Then x=\mu+z\sigma.



                  
                  Practice 5 (TF style) — top 12% get an A 
                  
                

Given. Grades are N(74,\ 7^2). If the top 12% get an A, find the lowest A mark.
Step 1 — Left area. 1-0.12=0.88.
Step 2 — Find z. The table gives \Phi(1.17)=0.8790 and \Phi(1.18)=0.8810, so z\approx1.175.
Step 3 — Convert back.
x=74+1.175(7)=82.2
Answer. The lowest A is about 82.




                  
                  Practice 6 (TF style, like 2022-23 Q3(c)(ii)) — slowest 10% of trips 
                  
                

Given. Trip times are N(30,\ 4^2). Find the time above which the slowest 10% of trips lie.
Step 1 — Left area. 0.90, so z=1.28.
Step 2 — Convert back.
x=30+1.28(4)=35.12
Answer. 35.12 minutes.




                  
                  Practice 7 (TF style) — top 10% of scores 
                  
                

Given. Scores are N(500,\ 50^2). Find the score that cuts off the top 10%.
Step 1 — Left area. \Phi(1.28)\approx0.90, so z=1.28.
Step 2 — Convert back.
x=500+1.28(50)=564
Answer. 564.



Type 4 — Find \mu or \sigma from given percentages
Recipe: each given percentage gives one equation x=\mu+z\sigma; solve the pair.


                  
                  Practice 8 (TF style) 
                  
                

Given. In a normal distribution, 10% of values are below 35 and 5% are above 85. Find \mu and \sigma.
Step 1 — z values. Below 35 with left area 0.10 gives z=-1.28. Above 85 with left area 0.95 gives z=1.645.
Step 2 — Two equations.
35=\mu-1.28\sigma
85=\mu+1.645\sigma
Step 3 — Subtract and solve.
50=2.925\sigma\ \Rightarrow\ \sigma=17.09
\mu=35+1.28(17.09)=56.88
Answer. \mu=\mathbf{56.88}, \sigma=\mathbf{17.09}.



Type 5 — Normal combined with binomial
Recognise it: “find the probability that 2 of the next 3 trips take at least half an hour”.
Recipe:

Find p for one item from the normal table.
Use the binomial with that p.



                  
                  Practice 9 (TF style, like 2022-23 Q3(c)(iii)) — underweight packets 
                  
                

Given. Packet weights are N(500,\ 10^2) grams. A packet is underweight if it weighs less than 485 g. Among 4 packets, find the probability that exactly one is underweight.
Step 1 — Probability for one packet.
p=P(X<485)=\Phi(-1.50)=0.0668
Step 2 — Binomial.
P(\text{exactly 1 of 4})=\binom41(0.0668)(0.9332)^3=0.2172
Answer. \mathbf{0.2172}.



Type 6 — Specification limits and scrap rate
Recipe: “accepted” means inside the limits, so
P(\text{scrapped})=1-P(\text{inside})


                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q7(b) (15 marks) — ball bearings scrapped 
                  
                

Given. X\sim N(3.0,\ 0.005^2); accepted if 2.99\le X\le3.01.
Step 1 — z values.
z_1=\frac{2.99-3.0}{0.005}=-2.0
z_2=\frac{3.01-3.0}{0.005}=2.0
Step 2 — Both tails (symmetric).
P(\text{scrapped})=2\,\Phi(-2.0)=2(0.0228)=0.0456
Answer. On average 4.56% of the bearings will be scrapped.




                  
                  Practice 10 (TF style) — off-centre process 
                  
                

Given. Resistors must be 100\pm2 ohms. The process gives N(100.5,\ 1^2). What fraction is rejected?
Step 1 — z values.
z_1=\frac{98-100.5}{1}=-2.50
z_2=\frac{102-100.5}{1}=1.50
Step 2 — Accepted fraction.
P(\text{accepted})=\Phi(1.50)-\Phi(-2.50)=0.9332-0.0062=0.9270
Answer. 7.3% are rejected. (Because the process is not centred, the two tails are unequal; do not just double one tail.)



Type 7 — Normal approximation to the binomial
Recipe:

Use \mu=np and \sigma=\sqrt{npq}.
Apply the continuity correction (\pm0.5).
Read the table.

Use it when np\ge5 and nq\ge5.


                  
                  Memorize: Continuity correction 
                  
                

At most a
P(X\le a)\approx\Phi\!\left(\frac{a+0.5-np}{\sqrt{npq}}\right)
At least a
P(X\ge a)\approx1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{a-0.5-np}{\sqrt{npq}}\right)




                  
                  Practice 11 (TF style) 
                  
                

Given. 30% of a population has a certain trait. In a sample of 100, find P(X\le25).
Step 1 — Mean and SD.
\mu=30
\sigma=\sqrt{21}=4.583
Step 2 — Continuity correction.
P(X\le25)\approx\Phi\!\left(\frac{25.5-30}{4.583}\right)=\Phi(-0.98)=0.1635
Answer. \mathbf{0.1635} (exact binomial: 0.1631).




                  
                  Practice 12 (TF style) 
                  
                

Given. A process gives 40% success; n=60. Find P(20\le X\le30).
Step 1 — Mean and SD.
\mu=24
\sigma=\sqrt{14.4}=3.795
Step 2 — Continuity correction. The interval becomes 19.5 to 30.5.
z_1=-1.19
z_2=1.71
Step 3 — Between.
P=0.9564-0.1170=0.8394
Answer. \mathbf{0.8394} (exact: 0.8386).



Extra practice


                  
                  Answers (try first) 
                  
                

1. X\sim N(25,9); find k with P(X<k)=0.95.
Answer: \sigma=3, k=25+1.645(3)=29.9.
2. X\sim N(800,40^2); P(X>860)?
Answer: z=1.5, so 0.0668.
3. Weights N(70,5^2); what percentage lie between 65 and 75?
Answer: 68.26%.
4. \Phi(-1.5) in terms of \Phi(1.5)?
Answer: 1-\Phi(1.5).
5. Continuity-corrected form of P(X\ge40)?
Answer: 1-\Phi\big((39.5-np)/\sqrt{npq}\big).

1-Probability/P9-Uniform-Exponential-and.content:
P9 · Exponential and Uniform: Problems First


                  
                  Why this matters for the TF 
                  
                

Exponential waiting times appear in four of the five papers: fire-station calls (2019-20 Q8(b), 25 marks), the DVD component (2022-23 Q1(c)), Y=3X-2 (2022-23 Q2(b)) and the radar speeders (2023-24 Q2(a)).
These questions are almost pure calculation, so they are safe marks once you handle units correctly.
The 2022-23 and 2023-24 parts are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions.


Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize: Exponential (mean \beta, rate \lambda=1/\beta)
                  
                

Density (x>0)
f(x)=\frac1\beta e^{-x/\beta}=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}
CDF
Use for “fails before / within x“.
F(x)=1-e^{-x/\beta}
Survival
Use for “lasts more than x“.
P(X>x)=e^{-x/\beta}
Mean
E(X)=\beta=\frac1\lambda
Variance
\mathrm{Var}(X)=\beta^2=\frac1{\lambda^2}
Memoryless
P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)
Poisson link
If events occur at rate \lambda, the waiting time is exponential with rate \lambda, and
P(\text{no event in time } t)=e^{-\lambda t}




                  
                  Memorize: Uniform on [A,B]
                  
                

Density
f(x)=\frac{1}{B-A}
Mean
\mu=\frac{A+B}{2}
Variance
\sigma^2=\frac{(B-A)^2}{12}
Probability
P(c<X<d)=\frac{d-c}{B-A}





                  
                  Identify the parameter first 
                  
                

\frac{1}{2000}e^{-x/2000} means mean \beta=2000.
8e^{-8x} or F(x)=1-e^{-8x} means rate \lambda=8, mean \frac18.
Once you know \beta, every answer follows from the box.




                  
                  Units, units, units 
                  
                

Mixing units is the number-one error.
If the rate is per day and the question says 15 minutes, convert: 15 minutes =\frac{1}{96} day.
If the CDF is in hours and the question says 12 minutes, use x=0.2.
Write the conversion in your answer.


Theory the TF may ask (minimal)
CDF from the pdf (x>0):
\begin{aligned}
F(x)&=\int_0^x\frac1\beta e^{-t/\beta}\,dt\\
&=\Big[-e^{-t/\beta}\Big]_0^x\\
&=1-e^{-x/\beta}
\end{aligned}
Mean and variance. These follow from the integral
\int_0^\infty x^n e^{-x/\beta}\,dx=n!\,\beta^{n+1}
E(X)=\beta
E(X^2)=2\beta^2
\mathrm{Var}(X)=2\beta^2-\beta^2=\beta^2
Memoryless property:
\begin{aligned}
P(X>s+t\mid X>s)&=\frac{P(X>s+t)}{P(X>s)}\\
&=\frac{e^{-(s+t)/\beta}}{e^{-s/\beta}}\\
&=e^{-t/\beta}=P(X>t)
\end{aligned}
The \chi^2, t and F distributions are only needed as tables for tests.
\chi^2 (non-negative, right-skewed) is used for goodness-of-fit and contingency tests.
t (like Z but with heavier tails) is used for small-sample means.
F (a ratio of variances) is used for comparing variances and for ANOVA.
See S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests, S9 Chi-Square Tests and S10 ANOVA One-Way and Two-Way.

Problem types you will face
Type 1 — Find the CDF from the pdf, then probabilities
Recognise it: “find the cumulative distribution function”, “probability it lasts more than … / fails before …“.
Recipe:

Integrate to get F(x)=1-e^{-x/\beta} (state F(x)=0 for x<0).
Use the rules below.

P(X\le a)=F(a)
P(X>a)=1-F(a)
P(a<X<b)=F(b)-F(a)


                  
                  Practice 1 (TF style, like 2022-23 Q1(c)) 
                  
                

Given. A component’s life in years has f(x)=\frac13e^{-x/3}, x>0. Find the CDF, P(X>6) and P(1<X<4).
Step 1 — CDF. For x\ge0 (and F(x)=0 for x<0):
F(x)=\int_0^x\frac13e^{-t/3}\,dt=1-e^{-x/3}
Step 2 — More than 6 years.
P(X>6)=e^{-6/3}=e^{-2}=0.1353
Step 3 — Between 1 and 4 years.
\begin{aligned}
P(1<X<4)&=F(4)-F(1)\\
&=e^{-1/3}-e^{-4/3}\\
&=0.7165-0.2636=0.4529
\end{aligned}
Answer. F(x)=1-e^{-x/3}; 0.1353; 0.4529.




                  
                  Practice 2 (TF style, like 2023-24 Q2(a)) — CDF given, unit change 
                  
                

Given. The waiting time in hours between buses has CDF F(x)=1-e^{-5x}, x\ge0. Find the probability of waiting less than 6 minutes, using the CDF and then the pdf.
Step 1 — Convert units. 6 minutes =0.1 hour.
Step 2 — Using the CDF.
P(X<0.1)=1-e^{-0.5}=0.3935
Step 3 — Using the pdf.
f(x)=F'(x)=5e^{-5x}
\int_0^{0.1}5e^{-5x}\,dx=\big[-e^{-5x}\big]_0^{0.1}=1-e^{-0.5}=0.3935
Answer. \mathbf{0.3935}; both methods agree.



Type 2 — Lifetimes with a given mean


                  
                  Practice 3 (TF style) 
                  
                

Given. The life of a battery is exponential with mean 5 years. Find the probability that it (i) fails within 2 years, (ii) lasts more than 8 years.
Step 1 — (i) Fails within 2 years.
P(X\le2)=1-e^{-2/5}=1-0.6703=0.3297
Step 2 — (ii) Lasts more than 8 years.
P(X>8)=e^{-8/5}=0.2019
Answer. (i) 0.3297, (ii) 0.2019.



Type 3 — Memoryless questions
Recognise it: “it has already worked for 500 hours”, “no call so far, 15 minutes to go”.
Recipe: the past does not matter; answer as if starting fresh.


                  
                  Practice 4 (TF style) 
                  
                

Given. A bulb’s life is exponential with mean 1000 hours. It has already burned for 500 hours. Find the probability that it lasts at least another 1000 hours.
Step 1 — Apply the memoryless property.
P(X>1500\mid X>500)=P(X>1000)
Step 2 — Compute.
P(X>1000)=e^{-1000/1000}=e^{-1}=0.3679
Answer. \mathbf{0.3679}.



Type 4 — Rate of events: “no event in a period”, several periods
Recipe:

Use P(\text{no event in time } t)=e^{-\lambda t}, with \lambda t in matching units.
For several non-overlapping periods, multiply (independence).



                  
                  Past TF 2019-20 Q8(b) (25 marks) — calls to a fire station 
                  
                

Given. The rate is \lambda=1.8 calls per day (equivalently 0.075 per hour).
Step 1 — (i) A call within the next 15 minutes. 15 minutes =\frac{1}{96} day.
\begin{aligned}
P\left(T\le\tfrac{1}{96}\right)&=1-e^{-1.8/96}\\
&=1-e^{-0.01875}\\
&=0.0186
\end{aligned}
Step 2 — (ii) No call so far, 15 minutes left. By the memoryless property the answer is the same: \mathbf{0.0186}.
Step 3 — (iii) No calls in a 10-hour shift. Mean number of calls in the shift:
1.8\times\frac{10}{24}=0.75
P(\text{no call})=e^{-0.75}=0.4724
Step 4 — (iv) No calls in four successive shifts. Non-overlapping shifts are independent.
P=(e^{-0.75})^4=e^{-3}=0.0498
Step 5 — (v) In 10% of shifts there is a call in the first x hours.
1-e^{-0.075x}=0.1
x=\frac{-\ln0.9}{0.075}=\frac{0.10536}{0.075}=1.40 \text{ hours}
Answer. (i) 0.0186, (ii) 0.0186, (iii) 0.4724, (iv) 0.0498, (v) 1.4 hours.




                  
                  Practice 5 (TF style) — website errors 
                  
                

Given. Errors occur on a website at 0.6 per day. Find (i) the probability of no error in a 5-day week, (ii) the probability of at least one error on each of 3 given days.
Step 1 — (i) No error in 5 days.
e^{-0.6\times5}=e^{-3}=0.0498
Step 2 — (ii) At least one error on one day.
P(\text{at least one})=1-e^{-0.6}=0.4512
Step 3 — Three independent days.
(0.4512)^3=0.0918
Answer. (i) 0.0498, (ii) 0.0918.




                  
                  Practice 6 (TF style) — customers 
                  
                

Given. Customers arrive at 4 per hour. Find the probability that the time to the next arrival is (i) more than 30 minutes, (ii) between 10 and 20 minutes.
Step 1 — Rate in minutes.
\lambda=\frac{4}{60}=\frac1{15}\text{ per minute},\qquad \beta=15 \text{ minutes}
Step 2 — (i) More than 30 minutes.
P(T>30)=e^{-30/15}=e^{-2}=0.1353
Step 3 — (ii) Between 10 and 20 minutes.
\begin{aligned}
P(10<T<20)&=e^{-10/15}-e^{-20/15}\\
&=0.5134-0.2636\\
&=0.2498
\end{aligned}
Answer. (i) 0.1353, (ii) 0.2498.



Type 5 — Solve for x given a percentage (percentile, median)
Recipe: set 1-e^{-x/\beta}=p and take logs.
x=-\beta\ln(1-p)


                  
                  Practice 7 (TF style) 
                  
                

Given. Component life is exponential with mean 400 hours. Find (i) the time by which 20% of components fail, (ii) the median life.
Step 1 — (i) 20% fail.
x=-400\ln0.8=89.26 \text{ hours}
Step 2 — (ii) Median.
1-e^{-x/400}=0.5
x=400\ln2=277.26 \text{ hours}
Answer. (i) 89.26 hours, (ii) 277.26 hours. (The median is less than the mean because the distribution is skewed right.)



Type 6 — Mean and variance of Y=aX+b
Recipe:

Identify E(X)=\beta and \mathrm{Var}(X)=\beta^2.
Apply the linear rules (the constant b does not affect variance). See P5 Expectation Variance Covariance and Chebyshev.

E(Y)=a\,E(X)+b
\mathrm{Var}(Y)=a^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)


                  
                  Practice 8 (TF style, like 2022-23 Q2(b)) 
                  
                

Given. Processing time is Y=2X+5 minutes, where f(x)=\frac13e^{-x/3}, x>0. Find E(Y), \mathrm{Var}(Y) and P(Y>11).
Step 1 — Moments of X. \beta=3.
E(X)=3
\mathrm{Var}(X)=9
Step 2 — Mean of Y.
E(Y)=2(3)+5=11
Step 3 — Variance of Y.
\mathrm{Var}(Y)=2^2(9)=36
Step 4 — P(Y>11). Y>11 means X>3.
P(Y>11)=P(X>3)=e^{-1}=0.3679
Answer. E(Y)=\mathbf{11}, \mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mathbf{36}, P(Y>11)=\mathbf{0.3679}.



Type 7 — Uniform distribution


                  
                  Practice 9 (TF style) — conference room 
                  
                

Given. A reservation lasts X\sim U[0,4] hours.
Step 1 — Probability.
P(X\ge3)=\frac{4-3}{4}=0.25
Step 2 — Mean.
\mu=\frac{0+4}{2}=2 \text{ hours}
Step 3 — Variance.
\sigma^2=\frac{16}{12}=\frac43
Answer. 0.25, mean 2 hours, variance 4/3.




                  
                  Practice 10 (TF style) — bus wait 
                  
                

Given. A bus comes every 20 minutes, and your waiting time is uniform on [0,20]. Find P(\text{wait}>5), the mean and the variance.
Step 1 — Probability.
P(X>5)=\frac{20-5}{20}=0.75
Step 2 — Mean.
\mu=10 \text{ minutes}
Step 3 — Variance.
\sigma^2=\frac{400}{12}=33.33
Answer. 0.75, mean 10 minutes, variance 33.33.



Extra practice


                  
                  Answers (try first) 
                  
                

1. Mean and variance of f(x)=\frac1{500}e^{-x/500}?
Answer: 500 and 250,000.
2. Calls arrive at 2 per hour; probability of no call in 30 minutes?
Answer: e^{-1}=0.3679.
3. f(x)=\frac15e^{-x/5} and Y=4X-3: E(Y) and \mathrm{Var}(Y)?
Answer: 17 and 400.
4. Life is exponential with mean 2500 hours; P(\text{fails before }1000)?
Answer: 1-e^{-0.4}=0.3297.
5. Mean of U(2,10)?
Answer: 6.
6. Which distribution is used to compare two variances?
Answer: F.

S1 · Introduction to Statistics, Data and Sampling
Why this matters for the TF. This is the one statistics chapter where the term final asks theory instead of calculations, so these are easy marks if you have the answers ready. The papers have asked about statistical data and its sources in Bangladesh (2022-23 Q5a, 10 marks), stratified random sampling with an example (2023-24 Q6c), and statistic versus parameter (2022-23 Q7a). Each of those answers is written below in exam form, followed by the few small calculation types (allocating a stratified sample, systematic sampling, classifying variables) that go with them. The real papers are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions.

Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize 
                  
                

Proportional allocation in stratified sampling (use it whenever a question gives stratum sizes and a total sample size):
n_h = n\times\frac{N_h}{N}
Systematic sampling interval (use it when you take every k-th unit from a list):
k=\frac{N}{n}
Random start — pick one number at random:
r\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}
Units selected:
r,\quad r+k,\quad r+2k,\quad \dots
Parameter vs statistic: Parameter describes the Population (Greek letters \mu,\ \sigma,\ P).
Statistic describes the Sample (Latin letters \bar x,\ s,\ \hat p).



Theory the TF actually asks
Statistics, population and sample (2-3 mark definitions)
Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, summarizing, analyzing and interpreting data, and of drawing conclusions from data in the presence of uncertainty. A population is the complete set of individuals or objects under study, and a sample is the part of it that we actually observe. Collecting data from every member of the population is a census. Descriptive statistics only summarizes the data in hand (tables, graphs, mean, SD), while inferential statistics uses a sample to draw conclusions about the population (estimation and hypothesis testing), so it needs probability.
Statistic vs parameter (2022-23 Q7a)


                  
                  Exam answer: Statistic and parameter 
                  
                

A parameter is a numerical characteristic of a population, such as the population mean \mu, variance \sigma^2 or proportion P. It is a fixed constant, but usually unknown.
A statistic is a numerical characteristic calculated from a sample, such as the sample mean \bar x, variance s^2 or proportion \hat p. It is known once the sample is drawn, but it changes from sample to sample, so it is a random variable. Statistics are used to estimate and test parameters.
Example: the mean GPA of all students of a college (\mu) is a parameter; the mean GPA of 40 randomly chosen students (\bar x=2.8) is a statistic.


Statistical data: meaning, production, need and sources in Bangladesh (2022-23 Q5a)


                  
                  Exam answer: What is statistical data? 
                  
                

Statistical data are aggregates of facts, expressed numerically or classified into categories, collected systematically for a pre-determined purpose, and affected by many causes. A single number such as “Rahim is 170 cm tall” is not statistical data, but the heights of 500 students collected to study average height are. Statistical data must be numerical, reasonably accurate, collected systematically and comparable with each other.


How they are produced. Primary data are collected for the first time by the investigator for a specific purpose, by personal interview, questionnaires, enumerators filling schedules, direct observation and measurement, or designed experiments (for example testing bulb life in a laboratory). Secondary data were already collected by someone else and are taken from published or unpublished sources such as government reports, yearbooks, journals and company records. Many data also come from administrative records such as birth and death registration, tax, hospital, school and banking records. Data are produced either by a census (all units) or a sample survey (selected units), and either by observation or by experiment.
Why we need them. Decisions need facts rather than guesses. The government needs population, income and price data to plan schools, hospitals and the budget and to measure poverty, inflation and unemployment. Businesses need sales and cost data to forecast demand and control quality. Engineers and scientists need data to compare designs, test claims and measure reliability, and in computer science data are needed to measure system performance and to train and evaluate machine-learning models.


                  
                  Exam answer: Sources of statistical data in Bangladesh 
                  
                

The main source is the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), the national statistical office under the Ministry of Planning. It conducts the Population and Housing Census (every 10 years, latest 2022), the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) for poverty and income, the Labour Force Survey for employment, the Agriculture and Economic Censuses, and the MICS survey with UNICEF. It publishes the Statistical Yearbook of Bangladesh, the Monthly Statistical Bulletin, GDP estimates and the consumer price index.
Other sources: Bangladesh Bank (money supply, interest and exchange rates, remittances, reserves); the Ministry of Finance (Bangladesh Economic Review); DGHS (health statistics) and NIPORT (Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey); BANBEIS (education statistics); research institutes icddr,b and BIDS; the Export Promotion Bureau, National Board of Revenue and BTRC; and international bodies such as the World Bank, WHO and UNICEF.


In the exam, write the BBS part in detail and then name at least four other organizations with one line each.
Stratified random sampling with an example (2023-24 Q6c)


                  
                  Exam answer: Stratified random sampling 
                  
                

In stratified random sampling the population is first divided into non-overlapping groups called strata, each as homogeneous as possible with respect to the characteristic being studied (for example level, gender or region). A simple random sample is then drawn from every stratum separately, usually in proportion to the stratum size (n_h=nN_h/N), and the samples are combined.
Example. A CSE department has 600 students: 180 in Level 1, 160 in Level 2, 140 in Level 3 and 120 in Level 4. To estimate average daily screen time with a sample of 60, we take 60\times180/600=18, 16, 14 and 12 students from the four levels, each chosen at random within its level.
Advantages: every stratum is represented in the right proportion, estimates are more precise than a simple random sample of the same size, and separate estimates are available for each stratum. Disadvantage: the stratum of every unit and the stratum sizes must be known in advance.


For contrast, in simple random sampling every unit has the same chance and we pick n numbers at random from a numbered list. In systematic sampling we take every k-th unit after a random start. In cluster sampling we pick some whole groups (clusters, which are mixed inside) at random and study all units in them.


                  
                  Strata vs clusters 
                  
                

Strata are homogeneous inside and we sample from every stratum. Clusters are heterogeneous inside and we sample only some clusters.



Problem types you will face
Type 1 — Identify parameter, statistic and type of variable
Recognise it: a short story with a number, and you are asked which quantity is a parameter or statistic, or whether a variable is qualitative, discrete or continuous. Recipe: ask “is this number about everyone (parameter) or about the observed part (statistic)?”, and “is the variable counted (discrete), measured (continuous) or a category (qualitative)?“.


                  
                  Practice 1 (TF style) 
                  
                

A mobile operator says its average download speed across Bangladesh is 25 Mbps. A researcher tests 120 random connections and finds an average of 21.4 Mbps, and 18% of them drop at least once. Identify the parameters and statistics.
Solution. The operator’s 25 Mbps refers to all connections, so it is a claimed value of the parameter \mu. The true proportion of all connections that drop is the parameter P. The 21.4 Mbps is the sample mean \bar x and the 18% is the sample proportion \hat p=0.18; both are statistics because they come from the 120 tested connections.




                  
                  Practice 2 (TF style) 
                  
                

Classify each variable: (a) number of students absent today, (b) time taken to compile a program, (c) operating system used, (d) a student’s grade A/B/C, (e) monthly income in Tk.
Solution. (a) quantitative discrete, because it is counted; (b) quantitative continuous, because it is measured; (c) qualitative (nominal), because it is a category with no order; (d) qualitative (ordinal), because the categories have an order; (e) quantitative continuous (money is often treated as continuous because it is measured on a fine scale).


Type 2 — Allocate a stratified sample
Recognise it: stratum sizes and a total sample size are given. Recipe: n_h=n\times N_h/N for each stratum, round to whole numbers so the total stays n, then say “select each by simple random sampling within the stratum”.


                  
                  Practice 3 (TF style) 
                  
                

An online shop has 2400 customers: 1200 in Dhaka, 720 in Chattogram and 480 in Sylhet. A sample of 150 customers is needed to estimate the mean delivery time. Allocate it proportionally and explain why stratifying by city is sensible.
Given. N=2400 and n=150, so the sampling fraction is 150/2400=1/16.
Step 1 — Dhaka:
n_{\text{Dhaka}}=150\times\frac{1200}{2400}=75
Step 2 — Chattogram:
n_{\text{Ctg}}=150\times\frac{720}{2400}=45
Step 3 — Sylhet:
n_{\text{Syl}}=150\times\frac{480}{2400}=30
Check. 75+45+30=150.
Answer. 75 from Dhaka, 45 from Chattogram, 30 from Sylhet.
Why stratify? Delivery time depends strongly on the city, so customers within one city are similar to each other (homogeneous strata). Stratifying guarantees every city is represented in its true proportion and gives a more precise estimate than choosing 150 customers completely at random.




                  
                  Practice 4 (TF style, rounding needed) 
                  
                

A factory has 350 day-shift, 250 evening-shift and 100 night-shift workers. Allocate a sample of 50 proportionally.
Given. N=700, n=50.
Step 1 — exact shares:
n_{\text{day}} &= 50\times\tfrac{350}{700}=25\\
n_{\text{evening}} &= 50\times\tfrac{250}{700}=17.86\\
n_{\text{night}} &= 50\times\tfrac{100}{700}=7.14
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 2 — round so the total stays 50:** $25,\ 18,\ 7$.

**Answer.** **25 day, 18 evening and 7 night-shift workers.**


Type 3 — Systematic sample
Recognise it: “every k-th item”, or a list of N items and a sample of n. Recipe: k=N/n, pick a random start between 1 and k, then add k repeatedly.


                  
                  Practice 5 (TF style) 
                  
                

From a list of 1200 transactions a sample of 40 is needed. With random start 13, write the first five selected transactions and the last one.
Step 1 — interval:
k=\frac{1200}{40}=30
Step 2 — first five: 13,\ 43,\ 73,\ 103,\ 133.
Step 3 — last (the 40th):
13+39\times30=1183
Answer. 13, 43, 73, 103, 133, …, 1183.



Extra practice


                  
                  Answers 
                  
                

1. A survey of 400 voters finds 52% support a candidate. Name the parameter and the statistic. — Parameter: the true proportion P of all voters; statistic: \hat p=0.52.
2. A university has 3000 science, 2000 engineering and 1000 arts students. Allocate a stratified sample of 120. — 60, 40 and 20.
3. Why is a census not used to find the mean life of bulbs? — Testing life destroys the bulb, so a census would destroy the whole production; a sample is used.
4. Name the BBS survey that measures poverty, and the one that measures unemployment. — HIES and the Labour Force Survey.
5. A list has 500 names and a sample of 25 is needed; the random start is 9. Give the third and the last selected names. — k=20; third is 49, last is 9+24\times20=489.
6. In one sentence each, distinguish primary and secondary data. — Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator for the current purpose; secondary data were collected earlier by someone else and are reused from published or recorded sources.

2-Statistics/S10-ANOVA-One-Way-and-Two-W.title: S10 · ANOVA: One-Way and Two-Way
2-Statistics/S10-ANOVA-One-Way-and-Two-W.content:
S10 · ANOVA: One-Way and Two-Way
Why this matters for the TF. ANOVA appeared in 2021-22 Q8(b) (three salesmen, unequal sizes), 2022-23 Q8(b) (one-way, four bulb brands) and Q8(c) (two-way, soil blocks × corn types), and 2023-24 Q8(b) (one-way, prices in three cities, 20 marks).
The calculation is long but purely mechanical, so a practised student collects full marks. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 questions are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions.

Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize: one-way ANOVA ( k groups, N observations in total)
                  
                

G is the grand total, T_i the total of group i and n_i its size.
Correction term:
CT=\frac{G^2}{N}
Total sum of squares:
S_T=\sum\sum x^2-CT
Between-groups sum of squares:
S_B=\sum_i\frac{T_i^2}{n_i}-CT
Within-groups (error) sum of squares:
S_W=S_T-S_B
F ratio:
F=\frac{S_B/(k-1)}{S_W/(N-k)}\sim F_{k-1,\ N-k}
==Reject H_0 (all means equal) if F_{cal}>F_{\alpha}(k-1,N-k).==




                  
                  Memorize: two-way ANOVA ( r blocks/rows × c treatments/columns, one value per cell)
                  
                

Correction term:
CT=\frac{G^2}{rc}
Total sum of squares:
S_T=\sum x^2-CT
Rows (blocks) sum of squares:
S_R=\frac{\sum R_i^2}{c}-CT
Columns (treatments) sum of squares:
S_C=\frac{\sum C_j^2}{r}-CT
Error sum of squares:
S_E=S_T-S_R-S_C
F ratio for rows:
F_R=\frac{S_R/(r-1)}{S_E/[(r-1)(c-1)]}
F ratio for columns:
F_C=\frac{S_C/(c-1)}{S_E/[(r-1)(c-1)]}




                  
                  Memorize: ANOVA table layout (always draw it) 
                  
                


































SourcedfSSMS = SS/dfFBetween groups (or rows / columns)k-1S_BMS_BMS_B/MS_WWithin (error)N-kS_WMS_WTotalN-1S_T




                  
                  Minimal theory 
                  
                

ANOVA tests H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\dots=\mu_k against H_1: at least two means differ.
It assumes independent random samples from normal populations with a common variance. The test is always right-tailed.




                  
                  Coding trick 
                  
                

Subtracting a constant from every value changes nothing.
Dividing every value by h divides every SS by h^2 but leaves F unchanged.
Use this to keep numbers small.



Problem types you will face
Type 1 — one-way ANOVA, equal group sizes
Recipe: totals T_i → G → CT → \sum x^2 → S_T, S_B, S_W → ANOVA table → compare with F_\alpha → comment.


                  
                  Practice 1 (TF style): yield of three reactors 
                  
                

A: 72, 75, 78, 74, 76. B: 65, 68, 70, 72, 69. C: 78, 82, 85, 88, 90. Test at 5% (F_{0.05}(2,12)=3.89).
Hypothesis. H_0:\mu_A=\mu_B=\mu_C against H_1: at least two means differ.
Level of significance. \alpha=0.05.
Step 1 — totals.


























ABCT_i375344423G=1142\sum x^228145236943587787716
N=15, k=3.
Step 2 — correction term.
CT=\frac{1142^2}{15}=86944.27
Step 3 — total SS.
S_T=87716-86944.27=771.73
Step 4 — between SS.
S_B=\frac{375^2+344^2+423^2}{5}-86944.27=633.73
Step 5 — within SS.
S_W=771.73-633.73=138.00
Step 6 — ANOVA table.

































SourcedfSSMSFBetween reactors2633.73316.8727.55Within12138.0011.50Total14771.73
Decision. 27.55>3.89, so reject H_0.
Comment. The mean yields of the reactors differ significantly. Reactor C (mean 84.6) is the highest.



Type 2 — one-way ANOVA, unequal group sizes
Use T_i^2/n_i with each group’s own n_i. Nothing else changes.


                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q8(b) (18 marks): three salesmen 
                  
                

Given. Sales in Tk thousand. A: 300, 400, 300, 500, 0. B: 600, 300, 300, 400. C: 700, 300, 400, 600, 500. F_{0.05}(2,11)=3.98.
Hypothesis. H_0:\mu_A=\mu_B=\mu_C against H_1: at least two differ.
Level of significance. \alpha=0.05.
Step 1 — coding. Divide by 100 (this does not change F).



































ABCCoded values3, 4, 3, 5, 06, 3, 3, 47, 3, 4, 6, 5n_i545T_i151625\sum x^25970135
N=14 and G=56.
Step 2 — correction term.
CT=\frac{56^2}{14}=224
Step 3 — total SS.
S_T=264-224=40
Step 4 — between SS.
S_B &= \frac{15^2}{5}+\frac{16^2}{4}+\frac{25^2}{5}-224\\
&= 45+64+125-224\\
&= 10
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 5 — within SS.**

$$S_W=40-10=30$$

**Step 6 — ANOVA table.**

| Source | df | SS | MS | $F$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Between salesmen | 2 | 10 | 5.000 | 1.83 |
| Within | 11 | 30 | 2.727 | |
| Total | 13 | 40 | | |

**Decision.** $1.83<3.98$, so do not reject $H_0$.

**Comment.** The salesmen's average sales do not differ significantly. In original units every SS is multiplied by $100^2$, but $F$ is the same.




                  
                  Practice 2 (TF style): three catalysts, unequal sizes 
                  
                

A: 68, 70, 73, 75. B: 72, 74, 76, 78, 77. C: 75, 78, 80, 82, 85, 88. Test at 5% (F_{0.05}(2,12)=3.89).
Step 1 — totals.

































ABCn_i456N=15T_i286377488G=1151\sum x^220478284493980288729
Step 2 — correction term.
CT=\frac{1151^2}{15}=88320.07
Step 3 — total SS.
S_T=88729-88320.07=408.93
Step 4 — between SS.
S_B=\frac{286^2}{4}+\frac{377^2}{5}+\frac{488^2}{6}-88320.07=245.40
Step 5 — within SS.
S_W=408.93-245.40=163.53
Step 6 — ANOVA table.

































SourcedfSSMSFBetween2245.40122.709.00Within12163.5313.63Total14408.93
Decision. 9.00>3.89, so reject H_0.
Comment. The catalysts give significantly different mean yields.



Type 3 — large numbers: code first


                  
                  Practice 3 (TF style): output of three machines 
                  
                

M1: 1505, 1512, 1498, 1510. M2: 1520, 1515, 1525, 1518. M3: 1500, 1495, 1508, 1502. Test at 5% (F_{0.05}(2,9)=4.26).
Step 1 — code by subtracting 1500.
M1: 5, 12, −2, 10. M2: 20, 15, 25, 18. M3: 0, −5, 8, 2.
Step 2 — totals. Group totals 25, 78 and 5, so G=108. Sums of squares 273, 1574 and 93, which add to 1940. N=12.
Step 3 — correction term.
CT=\frac{108^2}{12}=972
Step 4 — total SS.
S_T=1940-972=968
Step 5 — between SS.
S_B=\frac{25^2+78^2+5^2}{4}-972=711.5
Step 6 — within SS.
S_W=968-711.5=256.5
Step 7 — F ratio.
F=\frac{711.5/2}{256.5/9}=\frac{355.75}{28.5}=12.48
Decision. 12.48>4.26, so reject H_0.
Comment. The machines’ mean outputs differ (M2 is highest).



Type 4 — two-way ANOVA (blocks × treatments)
Recognise it: a table where rows are blocks (soil, workers, days) and columns are treatments (varieties, machines), with one value per cell, and the question asks about both factors.
Recipe: row totals, column totals, CT, S_T, S_R, S_C, S_E by subtraction, then two F ratios, each compared with its own critical value.


                  
                  Practice 4 (TF style): soil plots × fertilizers 
                  
                

Given. Yields (kg):















































PlotF1F2F3R_iP1454351139P2474652145P3485055153P4423749128C_j182176207G=565
F_{0.05}(3,6)=4.76 and F_{0.05}(2,6)=5.14.
Hypotheses. H_{01}: the soil plots do not differ. H_{02}: the fertilizers do not differ.
Level of significance. \alpha=0.05.
Here r=4, c=3, and \sum x^2=26867.
Step 1 — correction term.
CT=\frac{565^2}{12}=26602.08
Step 2 — total SS.
S_T=26867-26602.08=264.92
Step 3 — rows (plots) SS.
S_R=\frac{139^2+145^2+153^2+128^2}{3}-CT=110.92
Step 4 — columns (fertilizers) SS.
S_C=\frac{182^2+176^2+207^2}{4}-CT=135.17
Step 5 — error SS.
S_E=264.92-110.92-135.17=18.83
Step 6 — ANOVA table.








































SourcedfSSMSFPlots (rows)3110.9236.9711.78Fertilizers (columns)2135.1767.5821.53Error618.833.139Total11264.92
Decision. 11.78>4.76 and 21.53>5.14, so both hypotheses are rejected.
Comment. Yields differ significantly between plots and between fertilizers. F3 is the best fertilizer.




                  
                  Practice 5 (TF style): workers × machines 
                  
                

Output of 4 workers (rows) on 3 machines (columns): W1: 22, 26, 24. W2: 18, 24, 20. W3: 25, 27, 29. W4: 20, 23, 23. Test both factors at 5% (F_{0.05}(3,6)=4.76, F_{0.05}(2,6)=5.14).
Step 1 — totals. Row totals: 72, 62, 81, 66. Column totals: 85, 100, 96. G=281 and \sum x^2=6689.
Step 2 — correction term.
CT=\frac{281^2}{12}=6580.08
Step 3 — total SS.
S_T=6689-6580.08=108.92
Step 4 — rows (workers) SS.
S_R=\frac{72^2+62^2+81^2+66^2}{3}-CT=68.25
Step 5 — columns (machines) SS.
S_C=\frac{85^2+100^2+96^2}{4}-CT=30.17
Step 6 — error SS.
S_E=108.92-68.25-30.17=10.50
Step 7 — ANOVA table.








































SourcedfSSMSFWorkers368.2522.7513.00Machines230.1715.088.62Error610.501.75Total11108.92
Decision. 13.00>4.76 and 8.62>5.14.
Comment. Both workers and machines differ significantly in output.



Type 5 — F-test for two variances
Recipe: put the larger variance on top:
F=\frac{\text{larger } s^2}{\text{smaller } s^2}
with df (numerator n-1, denominator n-1). For a two-tailed test at \alpha, compare with F_{\alpha/2}.


                  
                  Practice 6 (TF style): two filling machines 
                  
                

Machine A (n=8): 52, 55, 50, 54, 53, 56, 51, 57. Machine B (n=10): 48, 49, 47, 50, 46, 51, 45, 49, 48, 47. Are the variances equal, at 5%?
Step 1 — variance of A. \sum x=428 and \sum x^2=22940:
s_A^2=\frac{22940-428^2/8}{7}=\frac{42}{7}=6.0
Step 2 — variance of B. \sum x=480 and \sum x^2=23070:
s_B^2=\frac{23070-480^2/10}{9}=\frac{30}{9}=3.33
Hypothesis. H_0:\sigma_A^2=\sigma_B^2 against H_1:\sigma_A^2\ne\sigma_B^2.
Calculated value.
F=\frac{6.0}{3.333}=1.80
Critical region. F>F_{0.025}(7,9)=4.20.
Decision. 1.80<4.20, so do not reject H_0.
Comment. The variances can be regarded as equal.



Extra practice


                  
                  Extra practice (try first, then open for answers) 
                  
                

E1. Groups: (8, 10, 12), (12, 14, 13), (6, 7, 8). One-way ANOVA at 5% (F_{0.05}(2,6)=5.14).
Answer: G=90, CT=900, S_T=66, S_B=54, S_W=12, so F=27/2=13.5>5.14. Reject.
E2. With k=4 groups and N=20, what are the df of the F ratio?
Answer: (3, 16).
E3. In a two-way table with 5 blocks and 4 treatments, what are the error df?
Answer: (5-1)(4-1)=12.
E4. Every observation is divided by 10. What happens to SS and to F?
Answer: every SS is divided by 100, and F is unchanged.
E5. s_1^2=80.9 with n_1=7 and s_2^2=19.1 with n_2=8. Is there a difference in variation at 10% (F_{0.05}(6,7)=3.87)?
Answer: F=4.23>3.87, so reject: the variances differ.

2-Statistics/S2-Frequency-Distributions-.title: S2 · Frequency Distributions and Graphs
2-Statistics/S2-Frequency-Distributions-.content:
S2 · Frequency Distributions and Graphs
Why this matters for the TF. A table-and-graph question appears every year.
2023-24 asked how to make a stem-and-leaf plot (Q5a) and to interpret a scatter plot (Q5b). 2022-23 asked for a Sturges’ rule table, histogram and ogive from 60 raw values (Q5b), and a stem-and-leaf plot with median, mode and range (Q6b). 2021-22 asked for an ogive with the median and a count in an interval (Q5a), and for class limits and marks (Q5b-i).
The 2021-22 questions are solved below. The newer two papers are in TF 2023-24 Solutions and TF 2022-23 Solutions, and the practice problems below are built in exactly their shape.

Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize 
                  
                

Sturges’ rule — use when asked “how many classes”:
K=1+3.322\log_{10}N
Class width — round up so that the largest value fits:
h\approx\frac{\text{Largest}-\text{Smallest}}{K}
Class boundaries (integer data) — use to draw histograms and ogives:
\text{boundary}=\text{limit}\mp0.5
Class mark — use as the x value of a class:
\text{mark}=\frac{\text{lower limit}+\text{upper limit}}{2}
Width = difference of consecutive lower boundaries.
Median from grouped data — use to verify an ogive reading:
\text{Median}=L+\frac{N/2-F}{f}\times h
Quartiles and percentiles — same formula, only the position changes:
Q_1:\ \frac N4 \qquad\qquad Q_3:\ \frac{3N}4 \qquad\qquad P_k:\ \frac{kN}{100}
L = lower boundary of the class holding that position, F = cumulative frequency before it, f = its frequency, h = its width.
Less-than ogive — plot cumulative frequency against the upper boundary, starting at (first lower boundary, 0).



Theory the TF actually asks
Stem-and-leaf plot (2023-24 Q5a, 10 marks)


                  
                  Exam answer: Stem-and-leaf plot 
                  
                

A stem-and-leaf plot displays quantitative data by splitting each value into a stem (the leading digit or digits) and a leaf (the last digit).
Stems are written once in a column in increasing order. The leaves of all values with that stem are written in a row beside it, in increasing order.
It looks like a histogram turned on its side, but it keeps every original value. So the exact median, mode and range can be read, and the shape (symmetry, skewness, gaps, outliers) is visible.
How to create it.
Step 1. Choose the split: for two-digit data the tens digit is the stem and the units digit the leaf; for data like 17.4 the integer part is the stem and the decimal digit the leaf.
Step 2. Write all stems from smallest to largest, including empty ones.
Step 3. Write each leaf next to its stem.
Step 4. Arrange each row’s leaves in increasing order.
Step 5. Add a key such as “4 | 2 means 42”.
Example. Scores 42, 57, 38, 61, 45, 49, 53, 66, 71, 58:
Stem | Leaf     (Key: 4 | 2 means 42)
  3  | 8
  4  | 2 5 9
  5  | 3 7 8
  6  | 1 6
  7  | 1


Scatter plot (2023-24 Q5b)


                  
                  Exam answer: Scatter plot 
                  
                

A scatter plot is a graph of paired data (x,y) in which each pair is one point. The explanatory variable goes on the x-axis and the response on the y-axis.
It shows whether a relationship exists, and its:
Direction — points rising = positive, falling = negative.
Form — straight-line or curved.
Strength — tight band = strong, wide cloud = weak.
It also reveals outliers. It is the first step before computing correlation or fitting a regression line (S6 Correlation and Regression).



When you interpret a plot in the exam, write three things: the direction, the strength, and what it means in the story. Support it with r if you can.
Remember that a curved pattern can give r\approx 0 even when the variables are strongly related.
Other graphs (one line each if they come up):
A histogram has touching bars over class boundaries (height = frequency).
A frequency polygon joins frequencies plotted at class marks.
A bar chart has separated bars for categories.
A pie chart uses angles
\text{angle}=\frac{f}{N}\times360^\circ
A box plot shows the five-number summary (min, Q_1, median, Q_3, max). Outliers lie beyond
Q_1-1.5\,IQR \qquad\text{or}\qquad Q_3+1.5\,IQR


Problem types you will face
Type 1 — Class limits, boundaries and class marks
Recognise it: you are told where classes start and how wide they are, or given limits, and asked for boundaries or marks.
Recipe: for integer data, lower limit = lower boundary + 0.5 and upper limit = upper boundary − 0.5. The mark is the midpoint. Each next class adds the width.


                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q5(b)(i): class limits and class marks 
                  
                

Given. 34 integer observations from 201 to 337; seven classes of width 20, the first beginning at 199.5.
Step 1 — boundaries. 199.5 is a boundary, so the boundaries are:
199.5–219.5, 219.5–239.5, 239.5–259.5, 259.5–279.5, 279.5–299.5, 299.5–319.5, 319.5–339.5.
Step 2 — limits. Because the data are integers, the class limits are:
200–219, 220–239, 240–259, 260–279, 280–299, 300–319, 320–339.
Step 3 — class marks. The first mark is
\frac{200+219}{2}=209.5
and then 20 more each time:
209.5, 229.5, 249.5, 269.5, 289.5, 309.5, 329.5.
Check. 200 to 339 contains the smallest value 201 and the largest value 337, so all 34 observations fit.




                  
                  Practice 1 (TF style) 
                  
                

Weights recorded to one decimal place are grouped as 40.0–44.9, 45.0–49.9, 50.0–54.9. Find the boundaries, marks and width.
Step 1 — boundaries. The gap between 44.9 and 45.0 is 0.1, so boundaries are limits \mp0.05:
39.95–44.95, 44.95–49.95, 49.95–54.95.
Step 2 — marks.
\frac{40.0+44.9}{2}=42.45
then 47.45 and 52.45.
Step 3 — width.
44.95-39.95=5



Type 2 — Build a frequency table from raw data with Sturges’ rule
Recognise it: a block of raw numbers and “use Sturges’ rule” or “construct a frequency table”.
Recipe: find N, min, max. Compute K and h (round h up so that min +Kh passes the max). Write the classes, tally, check the total equals N. Add boundaries, marks and cumulative frequency.


                  
                  Practice 2 (TF style, like 2022-23 Q5b) 
                  
                

The response times (ms) of 40 server requests are:
52, 61, 47, 58, 66, 73, 55, 49, 62, 68, 57, 44, 71, 59, 63, 50, 54, 77, 65, 60, 48, 56, 69, 62, 53, 58, 64, 41, 75, 61, 57, 67, 51, 63, 59, 70, 46, 60, 55, 64.
Make a frequency table using Sturges’ rule, then describe the histogram and ogive.
Step 1 — basic facts. N=40, smallest =41, largest =77, range =36.
Step 2 — number of classes.
K &= 1+3.322\log_{10}40\\
&= 1+3.322(1.6021)\\
&= 6.32\approx 6
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 3 — width.** $36/6=6$, but six classes of width 6 starting at 41 end at 76 and would miss 77. So we round the width up to

$$h=7$$

(This "round up so the largest value fits" step is exactly where marks are lost.)

**Step 4 — tally** into classes 41–47, 48–54, … :

| Class | Boundaries | Mark | $f$ | Cum. $f$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 41–47 | 40.5–47.5 | 44 | 4 | 4 |
| 48–54 | 47.5–54.5 | 51 | 7 | 11 |
| 55–61 | 54.5–61.5 | 58 | 13 | 24 |
| 62–68 | 61.5–68.5 | 65 | 10 | 34 |
| 69–75 | 68.5–75.5 | 72 | 5 | 39 |
| 76–82 | 75.5–82.5 | 79 | 1 | 40 |

The total is 40, as it must be.

**Step 5 — histogram.** Bars over the boundaries 40.5, 47.5, …, 82.5 with heights 4, 7, 13, 10, 5, 1. The tallest bar (54.5–61.5) is the modal class. The shape is roughly symmetric with a slightly longer right tail.

**Step 6 — ogive.** The less-than ogive plots

(40.5, 0), (47.5, 4), (54.5, 11), (61.5, 24), (68.5, 34), (75.5, 39), (82.5, 40)

and joins them. The real 2022-23 version has the same layout, and its drawn graphs are in [[TF 2022-23 Solutions]].




Type 3 — Ogive: read the median, quartiles and “how many between”
Recognise it: “draw a suitable diagram and read the median”, “how many lie between a and b”, or unequal class widths.
Recipe: make the cumulative table and plot against upper boundaries. Read at N/2 (median), N/4, 3N/4, and verify with the formula. For “between a and b”, take full classes plus a proportional part of the partial class.


                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q5(a) (18 marks): ogive, median, workers between 2000 and 2170 Tk 
                  
                

Given. 1900–1950: 6, 1950–2000: 10, 2000–2050: 22, 2050–2100: 30, 2100–2150: 16, 2150–2200: 12, 2200–2400: 15.
Step 1 — choice of diagram. The last class is four times wider than the others, so a histogram would mislead. We need the median and a count, so the suitable diagram is the less-than ogive.
Step 2 — cumulative table.



























Wages (less than)19001950200020502100215022002400Cumulative no. of workers061638688496111

Step 3 — median from the graph. N/2=55.5. The horizontal line at 55.5 meets the ogive above about Tk 2079.
Step 4 — verify by formula. The 55.5-th worker is in 2050–2100, so L=2050, F=38, f=30, h=50.
\text{Median} &= 2050+\frac{55.5-38}{30}\times50\\
&= 2050+29.17\\
&= 2079.17\ \text{Tk}
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 5 — between 2000 and 2170 Tk.** Full classes 2000–2050, 2050–2100 and 2100–2150 give

$$22+30+16=68$$

From 2150–2200 we need only 2150 to 2170, which is $20/50$ of the class:

$$12\times\frac{20}{50}=4.8$$

**Answer.** Median **= Tk 2079.17**; workers between 2000 and 2170 Tk **= 72.8 ≈ 73**.




                  
                  Practice 3 (TF style) 
                  
                

Marks of 80 students: 0–10: 5, 10–20: 9, 20–30: 14, 30–40: 20, 40–50: 16, 50–60: 10, 60–70: 6. Find the median, Q_1, Q_3 and the 90th percentile, and estimate how many students scored between 25 and 47.
Step 1 — cumulative frequencies (less than 10, 20, …, 70): 5, 14, 28, 48, 64, 74, 80.
Step 2 — median. N/2=40, class 30–40, F=28, f=20:
\text{Median}=30+\frac{40-28}{20}\times10=36
Step 3 — Q_1. N/4=20, class 20–30, F=14, f=14:
Q_1=20+\frac{20-14}{14}\times10=24.29
Step 4 — Q_3. 3N/4=60, class 40–50, F=48, f=16:
Q_3=40+\frac{60-48}{16}\times10=47.5
Step 5 — P_{90}. 0.9N=72, class 50–60, F=64, f=10:
P_{90}=50+\frac{72-64}{10}\times10=58
Step 6 — between 25 and 47.
\text{half of }20\text{–}30 &: 14\times0.5=7\\
\text{all of }30\text{–}40 &: 20\\
\tfrac{7}{10}\text{ of }40\text{–}50 &: 16\times0.7=11.2\\
\text{Total} &= 38.2
\end{aligned}$$

**Answer.** Median **36**, $Q_1$ **24.29**, $Q_3$ **47.5**, $P_{90}$ **58**, and about **38 students** between 25 and 47.



Type 4 — Stem-and-leaf, then median, mode and range
Recognise it: a short list of raw values and “use a stem-and-leaf plot”.
Recipe: choose the stem/leaf split and write the ordered plot with a key. Count leaves to the middle position for the median. The most repeated value is the mode (report all if tied). Range = largest − smallest.


                  
                  Practice 4 (TF style, two-digit data) 
                  
                

Ages of 20 club members: 23, 31, 45, 28, 37, 42, 31, 56, 38, 29, 44, 31, 50, 35, 27, 41, 39, 48, 33, 52.
Step 1 — the plot.
Stem | Leaf           (Key: 3 | 1 means 31 years)
  2  | 3 7 8 9
  3  | 1 1 1 3 5 7 8 9
  4  | 1 2 4 5 8
  5  | 0 2 6
Step 2 — median. n=20, so the median is the mean of the 10th and 11th values. Stem 2 holds 4 values, so these are the 6th and 7th leaves of stem 3: 37 and 38.
\text{Median}=\frac{37+38}{2}=37.5
Step 3 — mode. The value 31 appears three times.
Step 4 — range.
56-23=33
Answer. Median 37.5 years, mode 31 years, range 33 years. The distribution is slightly skewed to the right (longer tail of larger ages).




                  
                  Practice 5 (TF style, decimal data like 2022-23 Q6b) 
                  
                

Lengths (cm) of 14 bolts: 9.8, 10.4, 11.2, 10.4, 9.5, 10.9, 11.6, 10.1, 10.4, 9.9, 11.0, 10.7, 11.6, 10.2.
Step 1 — the plot.
Stem | Leaf           (Key: 10 | 4 means 10.4 cm)
  9  | 5 8 9
 10  | 1 2 4 4 4 7 9
 11  | 0 2 6 6
Step 2 — median. n=14, so the median is the mean of the 7th and 8th values. Stem 9 has 3 values, so these are the 4th and 5th leaves of stem 10, both 10.4.
Step 3 — mode. 10.4 appears three times (11.6 only twice).
Step 4 — range.
11.6-9.5=2.1
Answer. Median 10.4 cm, mode 10.4 cm, range 2.1 cm.



Type 5 — Interpret a scatter plot
Recognise it: a small table of paired values and “draw/explain the scatter plot” or “is there any relationship”.
Recipe: plot the points with labelled axes. State direction, strength and form, and back it with r.


                  
                  Practice 6 (TF style) 
                  
                

Age of six used cars (years) and price (lakh Tk): (2, 78), (3, 74), (5, 65), (6, 60), (8, 52), (9, 47). Interpret the scatter plot.
Step 1 — plot. Age on the x-axis, price on the y-axis.
Step 2 — read the pattern. The points fall steadily from left to right and lie almost on a straight line.
Step 3 — support with r.
r=-0.9997
Answer. There is a strong negative linear relationship: older cars sell for less, losing roughly 4.4 lakh per year.




                  
                  Practice 7 (TF style, the curved trap) 
                  
                

Hours of daily exercise x=1,\dots,7 and a fatigue score y = 12, 18, 22, 23, 22, 18, 12. Interpret.
Step 1 — read the pattern. The points rise and then fall symmetrically, forming an arch.
Step 2 — compute r. The rising and falling halves cancel, so
r=0
Answer. There is a clear non-linear relationship but no linear one. y clearly depends on x; a straight line is the wrong model here.



Extra practice


                  
                  Answers 
                  
                

1. Classes 15–19, 20–24, 25–29 (integer data): boundaries and marks?
14.5–19.5, 19.5–24.5, 24.5–29.5; marks 17, 22, 27; width 5.
2. Sturges’ rule for N=100 and N=60?
K=7.64\approx8 and K=6.91\approx7.
3. In a less-than ogive, against what is cumulative frequency plotted?
The upper class boundary, starting at the first lower boundary with 0.
4. From Practice 3, how many students scored less than 45?
48+16\times0.5=56.
5. Values 3.2, 3.5, 3.5, 4.1, 4.4, 4.4, 4.8: median, mode, range?
Median 4.1; modes 3.5 and 4.4 (bimodal); range 1.6.
6. Why is a stem-and-leaf plot preferred to a histogram for small data?
It shows the shape like a histogram but keeps every original value, so exact median, mode and range can be read.
