2-Statistics/S9-Chi-Square-Tests.content:
S9 · Chi-Square Tests
Why this matters for the TF. Both MATH 243 papers had a chi-square contingency question: a 3×3 table on education and job performance (2023-24 Q8a, 15 marks, the lecture example) and a 2×2 table on a drug and typhoid (2022-23 Q8a). 2023-24 Q7(a) also asked a short note on goodness of fit.
These questions are completely mechanical, so they are safe marks. The two papers are solved in TF 2023-24 Solutions and TF 2022-23 Solutions.

Core tools (memorize)


                  
                  Memorize 
                  
                

Chi-square statistic — use in all chi-square tests:
\chi^2=\sum\frac{(O-E)^2}{E}
Shortcut form (same value):
\chi^2=\sum\frac{O^2}{E}-N
Goodness of fit — use when asked whether counts follow a given distribution or ratio:
E_i=Np_i
with df =k-1-m, where m is the number of parameters estimated from the data.
Contingency table, r\times c — use when asked whether two attributes are associated:
E_{ij}=\frac{R_i\times C_j}{N}
with df =(r-1)(c-1).
2×2 table with Yates’ correction (cells a,b,c,d), df =1:
\chi^2=\frac{N\left(\lvert ad-bc\rvert-\frac N2\right)^2}{(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)}
Decision. The test is always right-tailed. Reject H_0 if \chi^2_{cal}\ge\chi^2_{\alpha,\,df}.
Critical values at 5%:
df 1: 3.84 · df 2: 5.99 · df 3: 7.81 · df 4: 9.49 · df 5: 11.07




                  
                  Minimal theory 
                  
                

H_0 always says “no association” (independence) or “the data fit the stated distribution”.
The test needs random samples and every expected frequency at least 5; merge small classes otherwise.
A large \chi^2 means observed and expected frequencies disagree.




                  
                  Common mistakes 
                  
                

Expected frequencies must be computed from the totals, never copied from the observed table.
Check that every row of E adds up to the row total.
Use frequencies, never percentages.



Problem types you will face
Type 1 — r\times c contingency table (test of independence)
Recipe: write H_0/H_1. Compute every E_{ij}=R_iC_j/N (put them in brackets in the table). Make a table of (O-E)^2/E, sum it, and compare with \chi^2_{\alpha,(r-1)(c-1)}.


                  
                  Practice 1 (TF style): gender and first-choice major (4×2) 
                  
                

Given.









































MajorMaleFemaleTotalMathematics122941Biology271643Physics151934Chemistry91423Total6378141
Hypothesis. H_0: gender and choice of major are independent. H_1: they are associated.
Level of significance. \alpha=0.05.
Step 1 — expected frequencies.
E_{11}=\frac{41\times63}{141}=18.32
E_{12}=\frac{41\times78}{141}=22.68
The other rows follow in the same way: Biology 19.21 and 23.79, Physics 15.19 and 18.81, Chemistry 10.28 and 12.72.
Step 2 — chi-square table.

































































CellOE(O-E)^2/EMath, M1218.322.180Math, F2922.681.761Bio, M2719.213.156Bio, F1623.792.549Phys, M1515.190.002Phys, F1918.810.002Chem, M910.280.159Chem, F1412.720.128Total1411419.94
Critical region. df =(4-1)(2-1)=3, so reject if \chi^2\ge\chi^2_{0.05,3}=7.81.
Calculated value. \chi^2=9.94.
Decision. 9.94>7.81, so reject H_0.
Comment. Choice of major is associated with gender. Males lean towards biology and females towards mathematics.




                  
                  Practice 2 (TF style): immunization and mother's education (2×4) 
                  
                

Given.





































IlliteratePrimarySecondaryHigherTotalImmunized1501008070400Not immunized40302010100Total19013010080500
Hypothesis. H_0: the immunization rate does not depend on education.
Level of significance. \alpha=0.05.
Step 1 — expected frequencies.
Row 1: 400\times190/500=152, then 104, 80, 64.
Row 2: 38, 26, 20, 16.
Step 2 — chi-square.
\chi^2=\frac{4}{152}+\frac{16}{104}+0+\frac{36}{64}+\frac{4}{38}+\frac{16}{26}+0+\frac{36}{16}
\chi^2=0.026+0.154+0+0.563+0.105+0.615+0+2.25=3.71
Critical region. df =(2-1)(4-1)=3; critical value 7.81.
Decision. 3.71<7.81, so do not reject H_0.
Comment. Immunization rates do not differ significantly across education levels.



Type 2 — 2×2 table (use Yates’ correction)
Recipe: label the cells a,b (row 1) and c,d (row 2), find the four margins, and use the shortcut formula. Compare with 3.84 at 5%.
If the question does not mention Yates, it is safest to show the corrected value and mention the uncorrected one.


                  
                  Practice 3 (TF style): smoking and lung disease 
                  
                

Given.





























DiseaseNo diseaseTotalSmoker36 (a)14 (b)50Non-smoker18 (c)32 (d)50Total5446100
Hypothesis. H_0: lung disease is independent of smoking.
Level of significance. \alpha=0.05; critical value \chi^2_{0.05,1}=3.84.
Step 1 — cross-product difference.
ad-bc=36\times32-14\times18=1152-252=900
Step 2 — calculated value.
\chi^2=\frac{100\,(900-50)^2}{50\times50\times54\times46}=\frac{72{,}250{,}000}{6{,}210{,}000}=11.63
Decision. 11.63>3.84, so reject H_0.
Comment. Lung disease is associated with smoking. (Without Yates’ correction \chi^2=13.04, which gives the same decision.)




                  
                  Practice 4 (TF style): online course and passing 
                  
                

Given.





























PassedFailedTotalUsed course421860Did not use303060Total7248120
Step 1 — cross-product difference.
ad-bc=42\times30-18\times30=720
Step 2 — calculated value.
\chi^2=\frac{120\,(720-60)^2}{60\times60\times72\times48}=\frac{52{,}272{,}000}{12{,}441{,}600}=4.20
Decision. 4.20>3.84, so reject H_0.
Comment. Using the course is associated with passing.




                  
                  Practice 5 (TF style): gender and job type 
                  
                

Given. Male: 40 technical, 20 non-technical. Female: 25 technical, 35 non-technical. N=120.
Step 1 — cross-product difference.
ad-bc=40\times35-20\times25=900
Step 2 — calculated value.
\chi^2=\frac{120\,(900-60)^2}{60\times60\times65\times55}=6.58
Decision. 6.58>3.84, so reject H_0.
Comment. Job type depends on gender.



Type 3 — goodness of fit
Recipe: compute expected counts from the hypothesised probabilities (E=Np), then \chi^2. Use df =k-1, or fewer if parameters were estimated from the data.


                  
                  Practice 6 (TF style): is the die fair? 
                  
                

120 throws give the faces 1 to 6 with frequencies 25, 17, 15, 23, 24, 16. Test at 5%.
Hypothesis. H_0: the die is fair, so p_i=1/6 and every E_i=20.
Step 1 — chi-square table.









































Face123456O251715232416E202020202020(O-E)^2/E1.250.451.250.450.800.80
Calculated value.
\chi^2=5.00
Critical region. df =6-1=5; critical value 11.07.
Decision. 5.00<11.07, so do not reject H_0.
Comment. The die can be regarded as fair.




                  
                  Practice 7 (TF style): fit to a 9:3:3:1 ratio 
                  
                

Observed pea types: 315, 108, 101, 32 (total 556). Do they fit the 9:3:3:1 ratio, at 5%?
Step 1 — expected frequencies.
556\times\frac{9}{16}=312.75
556\times\frac{3}{16}=104.25\ \text{(twice)}
556\times\frac{1}{16}=34.75
Step 2 — calculated value.
\chi^2 &= \frac{2.25^2}{312.75}+\frac{3.75^2}{104.25}+\frac{3.25^2}{104.25}+\frac{2.75^2}{34.75}\\
&= 0.016+0.135+0.101+0.218\\
&= 0.47
\end{aligned}$$

**Critical region.** df $=3$; critical value 7.81.

**Decision.** $0.47<7.81$, so do not reject $H_0$.

**Comment.** The data fit the 9:3:3:1 ratio very well.



Extra practice


                  
                  Extra practice (try first, then open for answers) 
                  
                

E1. 200 births: 115 boys and 85 girls. Are boys and girls equally likely, at 5%?
Answer: E=100 each, \chi^2=2.25+2.25=4.5>3.84, so reject: they are not equally likely.
E2. 2×2 table with a=20, b=30, c=40, d=10. Test independence at 5% with Yates’ correction.
Answer: |ad-bc|=1000, N=100, \chi^2=15.04>3.84, so reject.
E3. What is the df for a 3×4 contingency table?
Answer: (3-1)(4-1)=6.
E4. A cell has R=60, C=50, N=200. Find E.
Answer: 60\times50/200=15.
E5. Why is the chi-square test always right-tailed?
Answer: because \chi^2\ge0, and only large values show disagreement with H_0.

Exam Answer Templates and Strategy
This page is about how to write answers so that you collect full marks, and how to decide quickly which method a question wants.
Most marks in MATH 243 are lost not because a student does not know the formula. They are lost because the student picks the wrong distribution or test, skips a step the examiner expects, or forgets to write a conclusion in words.
Read this page once at the start of your preparation and once again just before the exam.
Time and question choice
The paper carries 210 marks in 3 hours. You answer three questions from Section A and three from Section B, so each full question is worth 35 marks.
That gives you about 28 minutes per question, leaving roughly 10 minutes to read the paper and check.
When you first open the paper, spend two or three minutes marking every part you can do with confidence. Choose questions where the big-mark parts are ones you are sure of. A 15 or 20-mark calculation you know is safer than three small theory parts you half remember.
In Section B, the ANOVA, chi-square and moments questions are long but completely mechanical. That makes them excellent choices if you have practised them, since there is no guesswork involved.


                  
                  Use separate scripts 
                  
                

The paper says “use separate scripts for each section”. Section A answers go in one answer script and Section B answers in another. Mixing them can cost you marks.


Choosing the right distribution
Most probability questions are a short story, and the first job is to recognise which model the story describes.
The flowchart below captures the decision. The key questions are: is the variable a count or a measurement, is the number of trials fixed, and are we sampling with or without replacement?
flowchart TD
    A[Read the story] --> B{Is X a count<br/>or a measurement?}
    B -->|Measurement: time, length, weight| C{What is given?}
    C -->|mean and SD, bell shape| N[Normal: use Z = X - μ / σ]
    C -->|waiting time between events, rate λ| E[Exponential: P X > x = e^-λx]
    C -->|a formula f x is given| D[Integrate the given pdf]
    B -->|Count| F{Fixed number of trials n?}
    F -->|Yes, with replacement or independent, constant p| G{Two outcomes?}
    G -->|Yes| BI[Binomial]
    G -->|More than two| MU[Multinomial]
    F -->|Yes, without replacement from a small lot| H[Hypergeometric]
    F -->|No: wait until a success| I{First success or k-th?}
    I -->|First| GE[Geometric]
    I -->|k-th| NB[Negative binomial]
    F -->|No: events in time or space, average rate| P[Poisson]
    BI -->|n large, p small| P



                  
                  Signal words 
                  
                

“On average … per minute / per day / per page” → Poisson.
“Time between calls” or “time to failure” with a mean → exponential.
“Probability of … is 0.4, if 15 people …” → binomial.
“Lot of 5 contains 2 defective, choose 3” → hypergeometric.
“The fifth prescription is the first/third …” → geometric / negative binomial.
“Normally distributed with mean … and SD …” → normal.


Choosing the right test
flowchart TD
    A[What is being compared?] --> B{Means?}
    B -->|One mean vs a claimed value| C{σ known or n ≥ 30?}
    C -->|Yes| Z1[z-test]
    C -->|No, small sample| T1[t-test, df = n-1]
    B -->|Two independent means| D{Both samples large?}
    D -->|Yes| Z2[two-sample z-test]
    D -->|No| T2[pooled t-test, df = n1+n2-2]
    B -->|Same subjects measured twice| T3[paired t-test]
    B -->|Three or more means| AN[ANOVA F-test]
    A --> P{Proportions?}
    P -->|one or two proportions| ZP[z-test for proportions]
    A --> Q{Frequencies in categories?}
    Q -->|Fit to a model| GF[chi-square goodness of fit]
    Q -->|Two attributes in a table| CT[chi-square contingency test]
    A --> V{Two variances?}
    V --> FT[F = larger s² / smaller s²]

Template 1: any hypothesis test
The course lectures always use the same layout, and examiners expect it. Write every heading, even when the step is obvious, because each line carries marks.


                  
                  Memorize this layout 
                  
                

Hypothesis.
H_0:\ \mu=\mu_0 \quad\text{against}\quad H_1:\ \mu\ne\mu_0
(or > or < — read the question’s wording).
Level of significance. \alpha=0.05 (or as given).
Test statistic. Write the general formula and state its distribution, for example
t=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}
Critical region. For example, reject H_0 if
t<-t_{0.05,\,11}=-1.796
Calculated value. Substitute the numbers and compute.
Decision. “Since the calculated value falls in the critical region, we reject H_0 at 5% level of significance” (or “falls in the acceptance region, so we do not reject H_0”).
Comment. Translate back into the story in plain words, for example “the new procedure has reduced the mean waiting time”.


The direction of H_1 comes from the question’s words.
One-tailed wording: “has the machine improved”, “is it less than”, “is there reason to believe \mu<40”, “greater than 220 mg”.
Two-tailed wording: “is the difference significant”, “does it differ”, “can it be regarded as coming from a population with mean …“.


                  
                  P-value questions 
                  
                

If the question says “use a P-value”, compute it from z_{cal}.
Left-tailed test:
p=\Phi(z_{cal})
Right-tailed test:
p=1-\Phi(z_{cal})
Two-tailed test:
p=2\left[1-\Phi(\lvert z_{cal}\rvert)\right]
Then reject H_0 if p\le\alpha.
If no \alpha is given, say “the P-value is very small (less than 0.01), so the evidence against H_0 is strong”.


Template 2: total probability and Bayes
Step 1 — Name the events in words. Half the marks are for setting up the problem correctly. For example: “Let B_1, B_2, B_3 be the events that the product is made by machine 1, 2, 3, and let D be the event that it is defective.”
Step 2 — Write the given probabilities with symbols, for example P(B_1)=0.30 and P(D\mid B_1)=0.02. A tree diagram earns marks and prevents mistakes.
Step 3 — Total probability:
P(D)=\sum_i P(B_i)\,P(D\mid B_i)
Step 4 — Bayes for each cause:
P(B_i\mid D)=\frac{P(B_i)\,P(D\mid B_i)}{P(D)}
Step 5 — Check that the posterior probabilities add up to 1.
Template 3: a grouped-data statistics question
Step 1 — Build a full calculation table with these columns: class, mid value x, frequency f, u, fu, fu^2, fu^3, fu^4 (and cumulative frequency if medians or quantiles are needed). The step deviation is
u=\frac{x-A}{h}
Step 2 — Choose A as the mid value of the class with the highest frequency, or one near the middle. This keeps the numbers small.
Step 3 — Write the totals in the last row.
Step 4 — Write each formula, substitute, and give the result with units.
Step 5 — Finish with an interpretation sentence about the shape (skewness and kurtosis) or the comparison (which group is more consistent).
Template 4: interpretation sentences
Interpretation lines are short but carry real marks.
Correlation. Say whether r is positive or negative, and whether it is weak (about 0 to 0.3), moderate (0.3 to 0.7) or strong (above 0.7). Then say what that means in the story.
CV. “The group with the smaller CV is more consistent (less variable).”
Skewness. “Since \gamma_1>0, the distribution is positively skewed, meaning a longer tail to the right and mean greater than mode.”
Kurtosis. “Since \beta_2<3, the distribution is platykurtic, flatter than the normal curve.”
R^2. “About 93% of the variation in yield is explained by the fitted model.”
Reading the statistical tables
Normal table. It gives the area to the left of z:
\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)
For a right tail use
P(Z>z)=1-\Phi(z)
and for a negative z use
\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)
For a reverse question such as “find the time above which the slowest 15% of trips lie”, look inside the table for 0.85 and read off z\approx1.04.
t-table. Degrees of freedom are on the left and the tail area is at the top. For a two-tailed 5% test you need the column for 0.025.
Chi-square and F tables. These are always used as one-tailed (right tail). For F_{\alpha}(\nu_1,\nu_2), \nu_1 is the numerator df (between groups) and \nu_2 is the denominator df (within groups or error).
In many questions the examiner simply gives you the critical value, so read the question carefully before looking for a table.


                  
                  Critical values that appeared in past papers 
                  
                

Chi-square: \chi^2_{0.05,4}=9.49 and \chi^2_{0.05,1}=3.84.
t (two-tailed): t_{0.05}(13)=2.16 and t_{0.05}(9)=2.262.
t (one-tailed): t_{0.05}(11)=1.796 and t_{0.05}(19)=1.729.
F at 5%: F(2,9)=4.26, F(2,11)=3.98, F(3,8)=4.07, F(4,12)=3.26, F(3,12)=3.49.
F at 1%: F(3,8)=7.59.


Final-week plan
First pass. Read the probability notes P1 to P9 and the statistics notes S1 to S10 in order, solving every “Past TF” example yourself before reading its solution.
Second pass. Use the TF Question Map to attempt every 2019-20, 2020-21 and 2021-22 question under time pressure.
Third pass. Sit the 2022-23 and 2023-24 papers as mock exams with a timer, and only then compare with TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions.
Read the Formula Sheet every day.

3-Exam-Toolkit/Formula-Sheet.content:
Formula Sheet
This is the page to read on the last evening and on the morning of the exam.
Every formula here has been used in at least one of the last five term finals, or is needed to reach one. Each formula has a one-line “use when”, because knowing when is as important as knowing the formula.
If a formula feels unfamiliar, click the linked note and read the explanation again.


                  
                  The five things students most often forget 
                  
                

1. Skewness by moments is positive for positive (right) skew:
\gamma_1=\frac{\mu_3}{\mu_2^{3/2}}
2. With step deviations u=\dfrac{x-A}{h}, the r-th moment must be multiplied by h^r.
3. The sample variance in tests divides by n-1:
s^2=\frac{\sum (x-\bar x)^2}{n-1}
4. The normal table gives the left area:
\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)
5. In rank correlation with ties, add \dfrac{m^3-m}{12} for every tied group in both variables.



1. Basic probability — P1 Probability Basics and Counting
Use these whenever you count outcomes or combine events.
Addition rule — use when you need “A or B”:
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)
Complement rule — use for “at least one” questions:
P(A^c)=1-P(A)
Addition rule for three events:
P(A\cup B\cup C)=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)-P(AB)-P(AC)-P(BC)+P(ABC)
Permutation — use when order matters (arrangements, posts):
{}^nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}
Combination — use when order does not matter (selections, committees, drawing balls):
{}^nC_r=\binom{n}{r}=\frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}
De Morgan’s laws:
(A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c
(A\cap B)^c=A^c\cup B^c
Odds — if the odds in favour of A are a:b, then
P(A)=\frac{a}{a+b}

2. Conditional probability and Bayes — P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes
Use the multiplication law when events happen one after another. Use total probability when the final event can happen through several routes. Use Bayes when you are asked “given the result, what is the probability of the cause”.
Conditional probability:
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}
Multiplication law:
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B\mid A)
Independence test:
A,\ B \text{ independent}\iff P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)
Total probability — the final event can happen through causes A_1, A_2, \dots:
P(B)=\sum_i P(A_i)\,P(B\mid A_i)
Bayes’ theorem — the result B is known, find the probability of cause A_k:
P(A_k\mid B)=\frac{P(A_k)\,P(B\mid A_k)}{\sum_i P(A_i)\,P(B\mid A_i)}


                  
                  Mutually exclusive is not independent 
                  
                

If P(A)>0, P(B)>0 and A\cap B=\varnothing, then
P(A\cap B)=0\ne P(A)P(B)
so the events are dependent. Two events can be both mutually exclusive and independent only if one of them has probability zero.



3. Random variables — P3 Random Variables PMF PDF CDF and P4 Joint Marginal and Conditional Distributions
To find an unknown constant k, set the total probability equal to 1.
Discrete pmf:
P(X=x)=f(x),\qquad \sum_x f(x)=1
Continuous pdf — probability is an area:
P(a<X<b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx=1
Cumulative distribution function (CDF):
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t)\,dt
pdf from CDF:
f(x)=F'(x)
Probability from CDF:
P(a<X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)
Marginal of X — integrate out y:
g(x)=\int f(x,y)\,dy
Marginal of Y — integrate out x:
h(y)=\int f(x,y)\,dx
Conditional density of Y given X=x:
f(y\mid x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{g(x)}
Independence of X and Y:
f(x,y)=g(x)\,h(y)

4. Expectation — P5 Expectation Variance Covariance and Chebyshev
Mean:
E(X)=\sum x f(x)\quad\text{or}\quad \int x f(x)\,dx
Mean of a function — use for E(X^2), E(e^{X}), etc.:
E[g(X)]=\sum g(x)f(x)\quad\text{or}\quad \int g(x)f(x)\,dx
Variance:
\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2
Linear change — use for Y=aX+b:
E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b
\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)
Covariance:
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E(XY)-E(X)E(Y)
Variance of a combination:
\operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)=a^2\sigma_X^2+b^2\sigma_Y^2+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)


                  
                  Chebyshev's theorem 
                  
                

For any distribution with mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma:
P(\mu-k\sigma<X<\mu+k\sigma)\ \ge\ 1-\frac{1}{k^2}
Equivalently, the probability of falling far from the mean is small:
P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)\ \le\ \frac{1}{k^2}
With k=2, at least 75% lies within two SDs. With k=3, at least 88.9%.
If the distribution is symmetric, each tail gets at most half:
P(X\ge \mu+k\sigma)\le \frac{1}{2k^2}



5. Discrete distributions — P6 Bernoulli Binomial Multinomial Hypergeometric Geometric and P7 Poisson Distribution and Poisson Process





























































DistributionpmfMeanVarianceUse it whenBernoullip^x q^{1-x}ppqone trial, success or failureBinomial\binom{n}{x}p^x q^{n-x}npnpqfixed n independent trials, constant pMultinomialsee belownp_inp_i(1-p_i)each trial has k outcomesHypergeometricsee below\frac{nk}{N}see belowsampling without replacementGeometricq^{x-1}p\frac1p\frac{q}{p^2}trial on which the first success occursNegative binomial\binom{x-1}{k-1}p^k q^{x-k}\frac kp\frac{kq}{p^2}trial on which the k-th success occursPoisson\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}\lambda\lambdacounts in time/space; or binomial with large n, small p
Multinomial pmf — n trials, outcome i happens x_i times:
P=\frac{n!}{x_1!\,x_2!\cdots x_k!}\;p_1^{x_1}p_2^{x_2}\cdots p_k^{x_k}
Hypergeometric pmf — choose n from N items, of which k are “successes”:
P(X=x)=\frac{\binom{k}{x}\binom{N-k}{n-x}}{\binom{N}{n}}
Hypergeometric variance:
\sigma^2=\frac{N-n}{N-1}\cdot n\cdot\frac{k}{N}\left(1-\frac{k}{N}\right)
Poisson approximation to binomial — when n is large and p is small:
\lambda=np

6. Continuous distributions — P8 Normal Distribution and P9 Uniform Exponential and Other Continuous Distributions
Uniform on (A,B)
pdf:
f(x)=\frac{1}{B-A},\qquad A<x<B
Mean:
\mu=\frac{A+B}{2}
Variance:
\sigma^2=\frac{(B-A)^2}{12}
Exponential with rate \lambda (mean \beta=1/\lambda)
pdf:
f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x},\qquad x\ge 0
CDF — probability of happening within time x:
F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}
Survival — probability of lasting beyond x:
P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}
Mean:
\mu=\frac1\lambda
Variance:
\sigma^2=\frac1{\lambda^2}
Memoryless property:
P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)
Normal N(\mu,\sigma^2)
pdf:
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}
Standardising — always the first step:
Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim N(0,1)
Probability between two values:
P(a<X<b)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{b-\mu}{\sigma}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{a-\mu}{\sigma}\right)
Negative z:
\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)
Normal approximation to binomial — when np\ge5 and nq\ge5, use a continuity correction of \pm0.5 with
\mu=np,\qquad \sigma=\sqrt{npq}


                  
                  Normal-table values to know by heart 
                  
                

\Phi(1)=0.8413
\Phi(1.645)=0.95
\Phi(1.96)=0.975
\Phi(2)=0.9772
\Phi(2.33)=0.99
\Phi(2.58)=0.995
\Phi(3)=0.9987
Within 1\sigma, 2\sigma, 3\sigma of the mean: 68.27%, 95.45%, 99.73%.



7. Frequency tables — S2 Frequency Distributions and Graphs
Sturges’ rule — number of classes:
K=1+3.322\log_{10}N
Class width:
h\approx\frac{\text{Largest}-\text{Smallest}}{K}
Class mark (mid-value):
x=\frac{\text{lower limit}+\text{upper limit}}{2}
Class boundaries lie halfway between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.

8. Central tendency — S3 Measures of Central Tendency
Step deviation:
u=\frac{x-A}{h}
Mean (grouped data):
\bar x=\frac{\sum fx}{N}=A+\frac{\sum fu}{N}\times h
Median:
\text{Median}=L+\frac{\frac N2-F}{f_m}\times h
Mode:
\text{Mode}=L+\frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta_1+\Delta_2}\times h
where \Delta_1=f_m-f_{m-1} and \Delta_2=f_m-f_{m+1}.
Quartiles:
Q_i=L+\frac{\frac{iN}{4}-F}{f}\times h
Deciles:
D_i=L+\frac{\frac{iN}{10}-F}{f}\times h
Percentiles:
P_i=L+\frac{\frac{iN}{100}-F}{f}\times h
In these, L is the lower boundary of the class containing the position, F is the cumulative frequency before that class, f is its frequency, and h is its width.
Combined mean:
\bar x=\frac{n_1\bar x_1+n_2\bar x_2}{n_1+n_2}

9. Dispersion — S4 Measures of Dispersion
Variance (grouped data):
\sigma^2=\frac{\sum f x^2}{N}-\bar x^2
Variance with step deviations:
\sigma^2=h^2\left[\frac{\sum fu^2}{N}-\left(\frac{\sum fu}{N}\right)^2\right]
Coefficient of variation — larger CV means more variable (less consistent):
CV=\frac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100\%
Corrected mean and SD — first rebuild the totals, then remove the wrong values and add the right ones:
\sum x=N\bar x
\sum x^2=N(\sigma^2+\bar x^2)

10. Moments, skewness, kurtosis — S5 Moments Skewness and Kurtosis
Raw moments about A:
\mu_r'=\frac{\sum f u^r}{N}\times h^r
Central moments from raw moments:
\mu_2=\mu_2'-\mu_1'^2
\mu_3=\mu_3'-3\mu_2'\mu_1'+2\mu_1'^3
\mu_4=\mu_4'-4\mu_3'\mu_1'+6\mu_2'\mu_1'^2-3\mu_1'^4
Skewness by moments:
\beta_1=\frac{\mu_3^2}{\mu_2^3}
\gamma_1=\frac{\mu_3}{\mu_2^{3/2}}
Kurtosis by moments:
\beta_2=\frac{\mu_4}{\mu_2^2}
\gamma_2=\beta_2-3
\beta_2>3 leptokurtic (peaked), \beta_2=3 mesokurtic (normal), \beta_2<3 platykurtic (flat).
Pearson’s coefficient of skewness:
SK_P=\frac{\text{Mean}-\text{Mode}}{\sigma}
Bowley’s coefficient of skewness (quartiles):
SK_B=\frac{Q_3+Q_1-2Q_2}{Q_3-Q_1}
Kelly’s coefficient of skewness (percentiles):
SK_K=\frac{P_{90}-2P_{50}+P_{10}}{P_{90}-P_{10}}

11. Correlation and regression — S6 Correlation and Regression
Corrected sums of squares and products:
S_{xx}=\sum x^2-\frac{(\sum x)^2}{n}
S_{yy}=\sum y^2-\frac{(\sum y)^2}{n}
S_{xy}=\sum xy-\frac{\sum x\sum y}{n}
Pearson’s correlation coefficient:
r=\frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}}
Regression coefficient of Y on X:
b_{yx}=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}
Regression coefficient of X on Y:
b_{xy}=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}}
Link between them:
r=\pm\sqrt{b_{yx}\,b_{xy}}
Regression line of Y on X — use to predict y from x:
y-\bar y=b_{yx}(x-\bar x)
Regression line of X on Y — use to predict x from y:
x-\bar x=b_{xy}(y-\bar y)
Sums of squares:
SST=S_{yy}
SSR=b_{yx}S_{xy}
SSE=SST-SSR
Coefficient of determination:
R^2=\frac{SSR}{SST}\quad(=r^2\text{ for a straight line})
Spearman’s rank correlation with ties:
r_s=1-\frac{6\left[\sum D^2+\sum\frac{m^3-m}{12}\right]}{n(n^2-1)}
Second-degree fit y=a+bx+cx^2 — solve these three normal equations:
\sum y=na+b\sum x+c\sum x^2
\sum xy=a\sum x+b\sum x^2+c\sum x^3
\sum x^2y=a\sum x^2+b\sum x^3+c\sum x^4

12. Sampling and estimation — S7 Sampling Distributions CLT and Confidence Intervals
Central limit theorem (large n):
\bar X\approx N\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
Standard error of the mean:
SE(\bar x)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
Confidence interval, \sigma known or n\ge30:
\bar x\pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
Confidence interval, small n:
\bar x\pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,\frac{s}{\sqrt n}

13. Hypothesis tests — S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests, S9 Chi-Square Tests, S10 ANOVA One-Way and Two-Way




























































SituationTest statisticDistributionOne mean, \sigma known or n\ge30z=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}N(0,1)One mean, small n, \sigma unknownt=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}t_{n-1}Two means, large samplesz=\frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}N(0,1)Two means, small samples, equal variancest=\frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2}}t_{n_1+n_2-2}Paired samplest=\frac{\bar d}{s_d/\sqrt n}t_{n-1}One proportionz=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0q_0/n}}N(0,1)Two proportionsz=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p\hat q(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}N(0,1)Goodness of fit / contingency\chi^2=\sum\frac{(O-E)^2}{E}\chi^2_{k-1} or \chi^2_{(r-1)(c-1)}2×2 table (Yates)see below\chi^2_1Two variancesF=\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2} (larger on top)F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}
Pooled variance — for the small-sample two-mean t-test:
s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}
Pooled proportion — for the two-proportion z-test:
\hat p=\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2},\qquad \hat q=1-\hat p
Expected frequency in a contingency table:
E=\frac{R\times C}{N}
2×2 table with Yates’ correction:
\chi^2=\frac{N\left(\lvert ad-bc\rvert-\frac N2\right)^2}{(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)}


                  
                  Critical values of z
                  
                

Two-tailed: 1.96 at 5%, 2.58 at 1%.
One-tailed: 1.645 at 5%, 2.33 at 1%.
A left-tailed test uses the negative value.




                  
                  One-way ANOVA 
                  
                

Correction term:
CT=\frac{G^2}{N}
Total sum of squares:
SST=\sum\sum x^2-CT
Between-groups sum of squares:
SSB=\sum\frac{T_i^2}{n_i}-CT
Within-groups sum of squares:
SSW=SST-SSB
F statistic:
F=\frac{SSB/(k-1)}{SSW/(N-k)}\sim F_{k-1,\ N-k}




                  
                  Two-way ANOVA ( r blocks, c treatments)
                  
                

Rows (blocks):
SSR=\sum\frac{R_i^2}{c}-CT
Columns (treatments):
SSC=\sum\frac{C_j^2}{r}-CT
Error:
SSE=SST-SSR-SSC
Error degrees of freedom are (r-1)(c-1).

TF Question Map (2019-20 to 2023-24)
This page maps every probability and statistics question from the last five term finals to the note where the concept is taught and, for the older papers, where the question is solved in full. Use it in two ways. Before studying a topic, look at how it has been asked so you know what to focus on. After studying a topic, come back here and make sure you can solve every question listed for it without looking.


                  
                  Read this first: what the papers look like 
                  
                

The 2022-23 and 2023-24 papers are MATH 243 (Probability and Statistics). Both sections (A and B) are probability and statistics, 8 questions in total, and you answer any three from each section. The 2019-20, 2020-21 and 2021-22 papers are MATH 245 (Complex Variable and Statistics). In those papers Section A was complex variables, which is not in your syllabus, so only their Section B (Q5 to Q8) matters for you. That is why the newest two papers are solved separately in TF 2023-24 Solutions and TF 2022-23 Solutions, while the Section B questions of the older three papers are solved inside the topic notes as worked “Past TF” examples.

What keeps coming back
Looking across all five papers, some question types appear almost every year, so they deserve the most practice. Bayes' theorem and total probability appears in four of the five papers (truth serum, machines, party supporters, ball transfer). Binomial, Poisson and normal probability calculations appear in every paper, usually with a real-life story, so you must be fast at choosing the right distribution and reading the normal table. Joint and continuous densities (finding k, marginals, conditional density, expected values) appear in every MATH 243 paper and in 2020-21.
On the statistics side, ==moments about an assumed mean with \beta_1,\beta_2 or \gamma_1,\gamma_2 appears in 2019-20, 2022-23 and 2023-24, and two of those are the exact examples from the lecture slides. Regression lines and correlation (including rank correlation with ties and a second-degree polynomial fit) appear every single year. Hypothesis testing is guaranteed: a z-test or t-test for a mean every year, plus a chi-square contingency test and a one-way ANOVA== in both MATH 243 papers. Finally, the newest papers have started asking short theory questions (CLT and its use in computer science, stratified sampling, stem-and-leaf plots, sources of statistical data in Bangladesh, differences between testing concepts), so do not skip the theory paragraphs in S1 Introduction to Statistics Data and Sampling, S2 Frequency Distributions and Graphs, S7 Sampling Distributions CLT and Confidence Intervals and S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests.


                  
                  Lecture examples come back word for word 
                  
                

2023-24 Q4(c) (nitrogen dose and rice yield), 2023-24 Q8(a) (job performance vs education), 2022-23 Q4(b) (Bangla and English marks) and 2022-23 Q6(c) and 2019-20 Q5(b) (moments) are copied directly from the lecture slides. Practising the lecture examples is therefore directly practising the exam.

Term Final 2022-23 — Complete Solutions
This file contains the full solution of every part of the MATH 243 (Probability and Statistics) term final of 2022-23. The questions are not repeated, so keep your printed paper beside you.
Try each part on your own first, then check your work against the steps here.
Notice how each answer is presented: what is given, the formula, the substitution, and then a clear one-line conclusion. Copy that habit on your own script.


                  
                  Final answers at a glance 
                  
                

Q1(a) P(\text{black})=38/63=0.6032
Q1(b) P(D)=0.0245; P(B_1\mid D)=0.2449, P(B_2\mid D)=0.5510, P(B_3\mid D)=0.2041
Q1(c) F(x)=1-e^{-x/2000}; P(X>1000)=0.6065; P(X<2000)=0.6321
Q2(a) g(x)=\frac{10x}{3}(1-x^3), h(y)=5y^4, f(y\mid x)=\frac{3y^2}{1-x^3}; probability =8/9
Q2(b) E(Y)=10, \operatorname{Var}(Y)=144
Q2(c) 0.9839, compared with Chebyshev’s bound \ge0.75
Q3(b) 0.0631+0.0901+0.1126=0.2657
Q3(c) P(X\ge30)=0.0571; late 99.11% of the time; 27.95 min; 0.0092
Q4(b) r_s=0 (no rank correlation)
Q4(c) y=0.7895+0.8158x, x=1.6429+1.1071y; husband ≈ 34.86 yrs; wife ≈ 21.18 yrs; r=0.95
Q5(b) 7 classes of width 6 starting from 18
Q5(c) A: mean 2146.67, CV 11.01%; B: mean 2070, CV 7.65%; prefer A (longer average life)
Q6(b) median 17.65, modes 17.4 and 19.0, range 2.6
Q6(c) \mu_2=152.04, \mu_3=21.312, \mu_4=47327.5; \gamma_1=0.011, \gamma_2=-0.95
Q7(b) z=7.23, reject; 99% CI (2.657,\ 2.943)
Q7(c) t=-2.33<-1.796, reject; mean now less than 50
Q8(a) \chi^2=220>3.84, drug effective
Q8(b) F=1.67, not significant at 5% or 1%
Q8(c) blocks F=0.65 (not significant); corn F=5.83 (significant)



SECTION A
Q1(a) — Transferring a ball between bags (8 marks)
Given / setup. Bag 1 has 4 white and 3 black (7 balls). Bag 2 has 3 white and 5 black (8 balls); after one ball is added it has 9 balls.
Let W_1 = the transferred ball is white, B_1 = it is black, and B = the ball finally drawn from bag 2 is black.
Step 1 — Probabilities of the transferred ball.
P(W_1)=\frac47
P(B_1)=\frac37
Step 2 — Conditional probabilities for the second draw.
If a white ball was transferred, bag 2 has 4 white and 5 black:
P(B\mid W_1)=\frac59
If a black ball was transferred, bag 2 has 3 white and 6 black:
P(B\mid B_1)=\frac69
Step 3 — Theorem of total probability.
\begin{aligned}
P(B)&=P(W_1)P(B\mid W_1)+P(B_1)P(B\mid B_1)\\
&=\frac47\cdot\frac59+\frac37\cdot\frac69\\
&=\frac{20+18}{63}\\
&=\frac{38}{63}
\end{aligned}


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

P(\text{black from second bag})=\dfrac{38}{63}\approx0.6032


Concept: P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes

Q1(b) — Bayes’ theorem: which machine made the defective item? (15 marks)
Given / setup. Let B_1,B_2,B_3 be the events that a product is made by machines B_1,B_2,B_3, and D the event that it is defective.
Prior probabilities (share of production):
P(B_1)=0.30,\quad P(B_2)=0.45,\quad P(B_3)=0.25
Defective rates of each machine:
P(D\mid B_1)=0.02,\quad P(D\mid B_2)=0.03,\quad P(D\mid B_3)=0.02
Step 1 — Total probability of a defective.
\begin{aligned}
P(D)&=\sum_i P(B_i)P(D\mid B_i)\\
&=0.30(0.02)+0.45(0.03)+0.25(0.02)\\
&=0.0060+0.0135+0.0050\\
&=0.0245
\end{aligned}
Step 2 — Bayes’ theorem.
P(B_i\mid D)=\frac{P(B_i)P(D\mid B_i)}{P(D)}
Machine B_1:
P(B_1\mid D)=\frac{0.0060}{0.0245}=0.2449
Machine B_2:
P(B_2\mid D)=\frac{0.0135}{0.0245}=0.5510
Machine B_3:
P(B_3\mid D)=\frac{0.0050}{0.0245}=0.2041
Check: 0.2449+0.5510+0.2041=1 ✓
graph LR
  S((Product)) -->|0.30| B1[B1]
  S -->|0.45| B2[B2]
  S -->|0.25| B3[B3]
  B1 -->|0.02| D1[Defective: 0.0060]
  B2 -->|0.03| D2[Defective: 0.0135]
  B3 -->|0.02| D3[Defective: 0.0050]



                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

P(B_1\mid D)=0.2449
P(B_2\mid D)=0.5510
P(B_3\mid D)=0.2041
A defective item most likely came from B_2.


Concept: P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes

Q1(c) — Time to failure of a DVD component (12 marks)
Given / setup. The density is an exponential distribution with mean \beta=2000 hours:
f(x)=\frac{1}{2000}e^{-x/2000},\qquad x\ge0
(i) CDF. For x<0, F(x)=0. For x\ge0:
\begin{aligned}
F(x)&=\int_0^x\frac1{2000}e^{-t/2000}\,dt\\
&=\Big[-e^{-t/2000}\Big]_0^x\\
&=1-e^{-x/2000}
\end{aligned}
So F(x)=1-e^{-x/2000} for x\ge0, and F(x)=0 for x<0.
(ii) Lasts more than 1000 hours.

Q2(a) — Marginal and conditional densities (15 marks)
Given / setup. f(x,y)=10xy^2 on the triangle 0<x<y<1.

Step 1 — Marginal of X. For fixed x, y runs from x to 1:
\begin{aligned}
g(x)&=\int_x^1 10xy^2\,dy\\
&=10x\left[\frac{y^3}{3}\right]_x^1\\
&=\frac{10x}{3}(1-x^3),\qquad 0<x<1
\end{aligned}
Step 2 — Marginal of Y. For fixed y, x runs from 0 to y:
\begin{aligned}
h(y)&=\int_0^y 10xy^2\,dx\\
&=10y^2\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^y\\
&=5y^4,\qquad 0<y<1
\end{aligned}
Check: \int_0^1 5y^4\,dy=1 ✓
Step 3 — Conditional density of Y given X=x.
\begin{aligned}
f(y\mid x)&=\frac{f(x,y)}{g(x)}\\
&=\frac{10xy^2}{\frac{10x}{3}(1-x^3)}\\
&=\frac{3y^2}{1-x^3},\qquad x<y<1
\end{aligned}
Step 4 — (ii) The conditional probability. “Spectrum shifts more than half” means Y>\frac12. “Temperature increased by 0.25 unit” means X=0.25.
At x=0.25:

Therefore:

&=\frac{64}{63}\Big[y^3\Big]_{1/2}^1\\
&=\frac{64}{63}\cdot\frac78\\
&=\frac89
\end{aligned}

g(x)=\frac{10x}{3}(1-x^3) for 0<x<1
h(y)=5y^4 for 0<y<1

Q3(a) — Bernoulli and Poisson processes; deriving the Poisson distribution (10 marks)
Bernoulli process. A Bernoulli process is a sequence of repeated trials with these properties.
The experiment consists of n repeated trials. Each trial results in only two outcomes, called success and failure. The probability of success p stays the same from trial to trial, and the trials are independent.
The number of successes X in n Bernoulli trials is a binomial random variable:
b(x;n,p)=\binom nx p^xq^{n-x}
Example: tossing a coin 10 times and counting heads.
Poisson process. Experiments that count the number of events in a given interval of time (or region of space) form a Poisson process if the following hold.
The numbers of events in non-overlapping intervals are independent (no memory). The probability of exactly one event in a very short interval of length \Delta t is proportional to its length, about \lambda\Delta t, and does not depend on events outside it. The probability of more than one event in such a short interval is negligible.
The number of events X in an interval of length t is then a Poisson random variable with mean \lambda t. Examples: calls arriving at a switchboard per hour, typing errors per page, accidents per month.
Derivation of the Poisson distribution (as a limit of the binomial).
Divide the interval into n tiny sub-intervals. Each is a Bernoulli trial with success probability p=\lambda/n, where \lambda is the mean number of events in the interval.
Step 1 — Write the binomial probability.
P(X=x)=\binom nx\left(\frac\lambda n\right)^x\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^{n-x}
Step 2 — Rearrange the factors.
P(X=x)=\frac{\lambda^x}{x!}\cdot\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-x+1)}{n^x}\cdot\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^n\cdot\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^{-x}
Step 3 — Take the limit n\to\infty of each factor.
\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-x+1)}{n^x}=1\left(1-\frac1n\right)\cdots\left(1-\frac{x-1}n\right)\to1
\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^{-x}\to1
\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^n\to e^{-\lambda}
Step 4 — Result.
p(x;\lambda)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!},\qquad x=0,1,2,\dots
This is the Poisson distribution. It is a valid pmf because:
\sum_{x=0}^\infty\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}=e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda}=1
Concept: P7 Poisson Distribution and Poisson Process

E(X)&=\sum_{x=0}^\infty x\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}\\

Q4(a) — Properties of the normal curve; mean, mode and SD (10 marks)
The normal density:
f(x)=\frac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}},\qquad -\infty<x<\infty
Properties of the normal curve.
The curve is bell-shaped and symmetric about the vertical line x=\mu. Its mean, median and mode are all equal to \mu, and the maximum height \frac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} occurs at x=\mu.
The curve approaches the horizontal axis asymptotically on both sides but never touches it. It has points of inflection at x=\mu\pm\sigma, being concave downward between them and concave upward outside.
The total area under the curve is 1. About 68.27%, 95.45% and 99.73% of the area lies within \mu\pm\sigma, \mu\pm2\sigma and \mu\pm3\sigma respectively.
Its skewness is 0 and \beta_2=3 (mesokurtic). Changing \mu shifts the curve left or right; a larger \sigma makes it flatter and wider.
Mean. Put z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}, so x=\mu+\sigma z and dx=\sigma\,dz:
\begin{aligned}
E(X)&=\int_{-\infty}^\infty x f(x)\,dx\\
&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\mu+\sigma z)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}\,dz\\
&=\mu\underbrace{\int\frac{e^{-z^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}dz}_{=1}+\sigma\underbrace{\int z\frac{e^{-z^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}dz}_{=0\ (\text{odd})}\\
&=\mu
\end{aligned}
Mode. Differentiate the density:
f'(x)=-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}f(x)=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=\mu
f''(\mu)=-\frac{f(\mu)}{\sigma^2}<0
So f is maximum at x=\mu: mode =\mu.
Standard deviation. Using integration by parts with u=z, dv=ze^{-z^2/2}dz:
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(X)&=E(X-\mu)^2\\
&=\int_{-\infty}^\infty \sigma^2z^2\frac{e^{-z^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dz\\
&=\sigma^2\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\left\{\Big[-ze^{-z^2/2}\Big]_{-\infty}^{\infty}+\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}dz\right\}\\
&=\sigma^2(0+1)\\
&=\sigma^2
\end{aligned}
So the SD is \sigma.
Standard normal variable. If Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}, then:
E(Z)=\frac{E(X)-\mu}{\sigma}=0
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\sigma^2}=1
So the standard normal variable always has mean 0 and variance 1, Z\sim N(0,1). This is why a single table of \Phi(z) serves all normal distributions.
Concept: P8 Normal Distribution

Q4(b) — Correlation vs regression; rank correlation of Bangla and English marks (12 marks)
Correlation vs regression.
Correlation analysis measures the degree and direction of the relationship between two variables using a single number (such as r, between −1 and +1). Both variables are treated alike as random, and r_{xy}=r_{yx}.
Regression analysis finds the actual average functional relationship (an equation such as y=a+bx) between a dependent variable and an independent variable, so that the dependent variable can be predicted. The two variables play different roles, and the regression of Y on X is different from that of X on Y.
Correlation is a pure number without units, while regression coefficients have units. Correlation does not imply cause and effect, whereas regression is generally used where one variable is considered to influence the other.

Q5(a) — Statistical data, how produced, why needed, and sources in Bangladesh (10 marks)
Statistical data. Statistical data are numerical facts (measurements or counts) about a group of individuals or items, collected in a systematic way for a definite purpose, which can be compared and analysed.
A single number is not statistical data; an aggregate of related facts is. For example, the monthly incomes of 500 households of Dhaka, or the yearly rice production of each district, are statistical data.
How they are produced. Data are produced either as primary data or as secondary data.
Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator for the specific purpose, through a census (complete enumeration of every unit), a sample survey, direct observation, interviews, questionnaires or experiments.
Secondary data are data already collected by some other agency and taken from published or unpublished records, reports, journals, websites and administrative registers.
Data are also produced continuously as administrative records (birth and death registrations, tax returns, customs records, hospital records) and automatically by digital systems (sensors, transactions, web logs).
Why we need them. Without data we cannot describe a situation accurately or make objective decisions.
Government needs data for planning (budgets, schools, hospitals, food and energy supply) and for measuring progress such as GDP growth, inflation, poverty and literacy. Businesses need data for market research, production planning, quality control and forecasting demand. Researchers need data to test hypotheses and build models.
In short, statistical data turn guesswork into evidence-based decision-making.
Usual sources of statistical data in Bangladesh.
The main official source is the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS). It conducts the Population and Housing Census, the Agriculture Census, the Economic Census, the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) and the Labour Force Survey, and publishes the Statistical Yearbook of Bangladesh, national accounts (GDP) and the consumer price index (inflation).
Other sources are Bangladesh Bank (money, banking, exchange rate, remittance, balance of payments), the Ministry of Finance (Bangladesh Economic Review, budget documents), and the Export Promotion Bureau and National Board of Revenue (trade and tax data).
Health and population data come from the Directorate General of Health Services and NIPORT (Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey). The Bangladesh Election Commission holds voter data and BANBEIS holds education statistics.
Research institutes such as BIDS and icddr,b, and international organizations such as the World Bank, UNDP, UNICEF and WHO, are further sources.

Q6(a) — Definitions with examples (10 marks)
For the examples below, take the small data set 2, 4, 6, 8 with mean \bar x=5.
(i) Standard deviation. The standard deviation is the positive square root of the mean of the squared deviations of the observations from their arithmetic mean:
\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}{n}}
It measures, in the same units as the data, how far the observations typically lie from the mean.
For the example, the deviations are −3, −1, 1, 3 and their squares add to 20, so:
\sigma=\sqrt{20/4}=\sqrt5=2.236
(ii) Variance. The variance is the mean of the squared deviations from the mean, i.e. the square of the standard deviation:
\sigma^2=\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}{n}
The sample variance uses divisor n-1:
s^2=\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}{n-1}
For the example, \sigma^2=20/4=5 and s^2=20/3=6.67. A larger variance means the data are more spread out.
(iii) Skewness. Skewness means lack of symmetry in a distribution.
If the longer tail is on the right, the distribution is positively skewed and mean > median > mode (e.g. income of people in a country). If the longer tail is on the left, it is negatively skewed and mean < median < mode (e.g. marks in an easy exam).
It is measured by Karl Pearson’s coefficient:
Sk_p=\frac{\text{Mean}-\text{Mode}}{\sigma}
or by Bowley’s coefficient:
Sk_B=\frac{Q_3+Q_1-2Q_2}{Q_3-Q_1}
or by the moment measure:
\gamma_1=\frac{\mu_3}{\mu_2^{3/2}}
The example 2, 4, 6, 8 is symmetric, so its skewness is 0.
(iv) Kurtosis. Kurtosis is the degree of peakedness or flatness of a frequency curve compared with the normal curve. It is measured by:
\beta_2=\frac{\mu_4}{\mu_2^2}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\gamma_2=\beta_2-3
If \beta_2=3 the curve is mesokurtic (normal). If \beta_2>3 it is leptokurtic (more peaked, e.g. daily stock returns). If \beta_2<3 it is platykurtic (flatter, e.g. a uniform distribution, which has \beta_2=1.8).
(v) Moments. The r-th moment is the average of the r-th powers of the deviations of the observations from a fixed point.
Moments about an arbitrary point A are raw moments:
\mu'_r=\frac{\sum f(x-A)^r}{N}
Moments about the mean are central moments:
\mu_r=\frac{\sum f(x-\bar x)^r}{N}
The first raw moment about zero is the mean, the second central moment is the variance, the third central moment measures skewness and the fourth measures kurtosis.
For the example:
\mu_2=5
\mu_3=\frac{-27-1+1+27}{4}=0
\mu_4=\frac{81+1+1+81}{4}=41

Q7(a) — Differentiate the pairs of concepts (10 marks)
(i) Statistic and parameter.
A parameter is a numerical characteristic of a population, such as the population mean \mu, variance \sigma^2 or proportion P. It is usually fixed but unknown.
A statistic is a numerical characteristic computed from a sample, such as \bar x, s^2 or p. It is known once the sample is drawn but varies from sample to sample, and it is used to estimate the parameter.
(ii) Critical region and acceptance region.
The set of possible values of the test statistic is divided into two parts. The critical (rejection) region is the part for which the null hypothesis is rejected; its probability under H_0 equals the level of significance \alpha.
The acceptance region is the complementary part, for which H_0 is not rejected; its probability under H_0 is 1-\alpha.
For a two-tailed z-test at 5%, the critical region is |z|>1.96 and the acceptance region is -1.96\le z\le1.96.
(iii) Exact and inexact hypothesis.
An exact (simple) hypothesis specifies the parameter as a single exact value and so completely specifies the distribution, e.g. H:\mu=50.
An inexact (composite) hypothesis specifies a range of values for the parameter, e.g. H:\mu>50 or \mu\neq50. The null hypothesis is usually exact, while the alternative is usually inexact.
(iv) Unidirectional and non-directional test.
A unidirectional (one-tailed) test is one where the alternative hypothesis specifies a direction (H_1:\mu>\mu_0 or \mu<\mu_0), so the whole critical region lies in one tail.
A non-directional (two-tailed) test is one where the alternative is H_1:\mu\neq\mu_0, so the critical region is divided equally between the two tails, \alpha/2 in each.
(v) Level of significance and p-value.
The level of significance \alpha is the maximum probability of a Type I error (rejecting a true H_0) that we are willing to accept. It is fixed before the test (commonly 0.05 or 0.01).
The p-value is the probability, computed from the sample assuming H_0 is true, of getting a test statistic as extreme as or more extreme than the one observed. We reject H_0 when p-value \le\alpha.
Concept: S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests

2.657<\mu<2.943

                  Answer 
                  
                

t=-2.33<-1.796 ⇒ reject H_0
The mean waiting time is now less than 50 minutes.

Term Final 2023-24 — Complete Solutions
This file solves every part of the MATH 243 (Probability and Statistics) term final of 2023-24. The questions are not repeated, so keep your printed question paper next to you.
Try each part yourself on paper first, then come here and compare step by step.
Pay attention to how each answer is written, not only to the final number. The layout used here (setup, then formula, then substitution, then a clear conclusion) is exactly what earns full marks.


                  
                  Final answers at a glance 
                  
                

Q1(a) No — two events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.
Q1(b) P(\text{red}) = 103/144 = 0.7153
Q1(c) P(A\mid \bar V)=0.504, P(B\mid \bar V)=0.256, P(C\mid \bar V)=0.240

SECTION A
Q1(a) — Can events be mutually exclusive and independent at the same time? (6 marks)
Definitions.
Two events A and B are mutually exclusive when they cannot occur together, that is A\cap B=\varnothing. Then
P(A\cap B)=0
Two events are independent when the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other. Then
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)
Step 1 — Assume both hold. If A and B are both mutually exclusive and independent, the two equations above give
P(A)\,P(B)=0
Step 2 — Conclude. This is only possible when P(A)=0 or P(B)=0.
So if both events have positive probability, they cannot be mutually exclusive and independent at the same time.
In fact, mutually exclusive events are strongly dependent. If A happens, we know for certain that B did not happen, so
P(B\mid A)=0\neq P(B)
The only exception is the trivial case where at least one event is impossible (probability zero).
Example. In one toss of a die, let A=\{1\} and B=\{2\}. They are mutually exclusive, so P(A\cap B)=0. But
P(A)\,P(B)=\tfrac16\cdot\tfrac16=\tfrac1{36}\neq 0
so they are not independent.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

No. Mutually exclusive means P(A\cap B)=0; independence means P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B).
Both can hold only if P(A)=0 or P(B)=0. For events with non-zero probability, it is impossible.


Concept: P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes
Q1(b) — Multiplication law and the ball-transfer problem (12 marks)
Multiplication law of probability. For any two events A and B, the probability that both occur equals the probability of one of them multiplied by the conditional probability of the other, given that the first has occurred:
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B\mid A)=P(B)\,P(A\mid B)
If A and B are independent, this reduces to
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)
For three events:
P(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3)=P(A_1)\,P(A_2\mid A_1)\,P(A_3\mid A_1\cap A_2)
Given / setup. Box A has 5 white and 7 red balls (12 in total). Box B has 3 white and 8 red balls (11 in total). One ball is moved from A to B, so B then has 12 balls.
Let W_1 = the transferred ball is white, R_1 = the transferred ball is red, and R = the ball finally drawn from box B is red.
Step 1 — Probabilities of the transfer.
P(W_1)=\frac{5}{12}
P(R_1)=\frac{7}{12}
Step 2 — Conditional probabilities of drawing red.
If a white ball is transferred, box B has 4 white and 8 red:
P(R\mid W_1)=\frac{8}{12}
If a red ball is transferred, box B has 3 white and 9 red:
P(R\mid R_1)=\frac{9}{12}
Step 3 — Total probability. W_1 and R_1 are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so we apply the multiplication law on each path and add:
P(R)&=P(W_1)\,P(R\mid W_1)+P(R_1)\,P(R\mid R_1)\\
&=\frac{5}{12}\cdot\frac{8}{12}+\frac{7}{12}\cdot\frac{9}{12}\\
&=\frac{40+63}{144}\\
&=\frac{103}{144}
\end{aligned}$$

> [!success] Answer
> 
> $$P(\text{red ball from box } B)=\frac{103}{144}\approx 0.7153$$

Concept: [[P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes]]

## Q1(c) — Bayes' theorem: who is the non-voter? (17 marks)

**Given / setup.** Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be the events that a randomly chosen city dweller supports party $A$, party $B$, or the other parties. Let $\bar V$ be the event that the person did **not** vote.

**Step 1 — Prior probabilities.**

$$P(A)=0.45$$

$$P(B)=0.40$$

$$P(C)=0.15$$

**Step 2 — Probabilities of not voting.** The turn-out rates are 65%, 80% and 50%, so

$$P(\bar V\mid A)=0.35$$

$$P(\bar V\mid B)=0.20$$

$$P(\bar V\mid C)=0.50$$

**Step 3 — Total probability of not voting.**

$$\begin{aligned}
P(\bar V)&=P(A)P(\bar V\mid A)+P(B)P(\bar V\mid B)+P(C)P(\bar V\mid C)\\
&=0.45(0.35)+0.40(0.20)+0.15(0.50)\\
&=0.1575+0.0800+0.0750\\
&=0.3125
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 4 — Bayes' theorem.**

$$P(A\mid\bar V)=\frac{P(A)\,P(\bar V\mid A)}{P(\bar V)}=\frac{0.1575}{0.3125}=0.504$$

$$P(B\mid\bar V)=\frac{0.0800}{0.3125}=0.256$$

$$P(C\mid\bar V)=\frac{0.0750}{0.3125}=0.240$$

**Check:** $0.504+0.256+0.240=1$ ✓

> [!success] Answer
> 
> Given that the person did not vote:
>
> $P(A)=0.504$, $P(B)=0.256$, $P(C)=0.240$.
>
> The non-voter is most likely a supporter of party $A$.

Concept: [[P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes]]

---

## Q2(a) — Waiting time between speeders (15 marks)

**Given / setup.** The CDF is

$$F(x)=\begin{cases}1-e^{-8x}, & x\ge 0\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

where $x$ is in **hours**. Since 12 minutes $=\frac{12}{60}=0.2$ hour, we need $P(X<0.2)$.

**Step 1 — Using the CDF.** For a continuous random variable, $P(X<a)=F(a)$:

$$\begin{aligned}
P(X<0.2)&=F(0.2)\\
&=1-e^{-8(0.2)}\\
&=1-e^{-1.6}\\
&=1-0.2019\\
&=0.7981
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 2 — Find the PDF.** The density is the derivative of the CDF:

$$f(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\left(1-e^{-8x}\right)=8e^{-8x},\qquad x\ge 0$$

and $f(x)=0$ otherwise.

**Step 3 — Using the PDF.**

$$\begin{aligned}
P(X<0.2)&=\int_0^{0.2}8e^{-8x}\,dx\\
&=\Big[-e^{-8x}\Big]_0^{0.2}\\
&=1-e^{-1.6}\\
&=0.7981
\end{aligned}$$

Both methods give the same answer, as they must. (This $X$ is exponential with rate $\lambda=8$ per hour, so its mean is $1/8$ hour $=7.5$ minutes.)

> [!success] Answer
> 
> $f(x)=8e^{-8x}$ for $x\ge0$.
>
> $$P(\text{wait} < 12\text{ min})=1-e^{-1.6}\approx 0.7981$$

Concept: [[P3 Random Variables PMF PDF CDF]] · [[P9 Uniform Exponential and Other Continuous Distributions]]

## Q2(b) — Joint distribution of red and blue pens (20 marks)

**Given / setup.** The bag has 3 red, 2 blue and 3 black pens, 8 in total. Two pens are selected, so the number of equally likely samples is

$$\binom{8}{2}=28$$

Let $X$ = number of red pens and $Y$ = number of blue pens.

**Step 1 — Joint pmf.** This is the multivariate hypergeometric distribution:

$$f(x,y)=\frac{\binom{3}{x}\binom{2}{y}\binom{3}{2-x-y}}{\binom{8}{2}}$$

for $x=0,1,2$, $y=0,1,2$ and $0\le x+y\le 2$.

A few sample values:

$$f(0,0)=\frac{\binom30\binom20\binom32}{28}=\frac{3}{28}$$

$$f(1,0)=\frac{\binom31\binom20\binom31}{28}=\frac{9}{28}$$

$$f(1,1)=\frac{3\cdot2\cdot1}{28}=\frac{6}{28}$$

The full table:

| $f(x,y)$ | $y=0$ | $y=1$ | $y=2$ | $g(x)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $x=0$ | 3/28 | 6/28 | 1/28 | 10/28 |
| $x=1$ | 9/28 | 6/28 | 0 | 15/28 |
| $x=2$ | 3/28 | 0 | 0 | 3/28 |
| $h(y)$ | 15/28 | 12/28 | 1/28 | 1 |

**(i) Plot of $f(x,y)$ against $(x,y)$.**

Since $X$ and $Y$ are discrete, the plot is a three-dimensional "stick" (bar) diagram. Draw the $x$- and $y$-axes on the floor, and at each point $(x,y)$ raise a vertical stick whose height equals $f(x,y)$.

The tallest stick is at $(1,0)$ with height $9/28$. Sticks of height $6/28$ stand at $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$. Sticks of height $3/28$ stand at $(0,0)$ and $(2,0)$. The shortest stick, of height $1/28$, stands at $(0,2)$.

No sticks are drawn at $(1,2)$, $(2,1)$, $(2,2)$ because those points have zero probability.

A top view, with heights in units of $1/28$:

```
 y=2 |  1
 y=1 |  6    6
 y=0 |  3    9    3
     +---------------
       x=0  x=1  x=2      (heights in 1/28)
```

**(ii) $P[(X,Y)\in A]$.** The set $A=\{(x,y): x+y\le 1\}$ contains $(0,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,0)$:

$$\begin{aligned}
P[(X,Y)\in A]&=\frac{3}{28}+\frac{6}{28}+\frac{9}{28}\\
&=\frac{18}{28}\\
&=\frac{9}{14}
\end{aligned}$$

**(iii) Marginal distributions.** Add along the rows and columns of the table.

Marginal of $X$:

$$g(0)=\tfrac{10}{28}=\tfrac{5}{14},\qquad g(1)=\tfrac{15}{28},\qquad g(2)=\tfrac{3}{28}$$

Marginal of $Y$:

$$h(0)=\tfrac{15}{28},\qquad h(1)=\tfrac{12}{28}=\tfrac{3}{7},\qquad h(2)=\tfrac{1}{28}$$

**(iv) Variance of $X$.**

$$E(X)=0\cdot\tfrac{10}{28}+1\cdot\tfrac{15}{28}+2\cdot\tfrac{3}{28}=\tfrac{21}{28}=\tfrac34$$

$$E(X^2)=0+1\cdot\tfrac{15}{28}+4\cdot\tfrac{3}{28}=\tfrac{27}{28}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(X)&=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2\\
&=\frac{27}{28}-\frac{9}{16}\\
&=\frac{108-63}{112}\\
&=\frac{45}{112}\approx 0.4018
\end{aligned}$$

**(v) Covariance.**

$$E(Y)=0\cdot\tfrac{15}{28}+1\cdot\tfrac{12}{28}+2\cdot\tfrac{1}{28}=\tfrac{14}{28}=\tfrac12$$

The only non-zero product term in $E(XY)=\sum\sum xy\,f(x,y)$ is at $(1,1)$:

$$E(XY)=1\cdot1\cdot\frac{6}{28}=\frac{3}{14}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)&=E(XY)-E(X)E(Y)\\
&=\frac{3}{14}-\frac34\cdot\frac12\\
&=\frac{3}{14}-\frac38\\
&=\frac{12-21}{56}\\
&=-\frac{9}{56}\approx-0.1607
\end{aligned}$$

The covariance is negative, which makes sense: with only two pens drawn, getting more red pens leaves less room for blue pens.

> $g(x)=5/14,\ 15/28,\ 3/28$ and $h(y)=15/28,\ 3/7,\ 1/28$

## Q3(a) — Chebyshev's theorem and the job applicants (11 marks)

**Chebyshev's theorem.** For any random variable $X$ (any distribution) with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, the probability that $X$ lies within $k$ standard deviations of the mean is at least $1-\frac{1}{k^2}$:

$$P(\mu-k\sigma<X<\mu+k\sigma)\ \ge\ 1-\frac1{k^2}$$

Equivalently, for $k>1$:

$$P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)\le\frac1{k^2}$$

**Given / setup.** $\mu=60$, $\sigma=6$, 1000 applicants, 70 jobs.

**Step 1 — How many SDs is 84 above the mean?**

$$k=\frac{84-60}{6}=4$$

**Step 2 — Apply Chebyshev.**

$$P(|X-60|\ge 24)\le\frac{1}{4^2}=\frac{1}{16}$$

**Step 3 — Use symmetry.** The event $|X-60|\ge 24$ means $X\le 36$ or $X\ge 84$. The distribution is symmetric, so the two tails have equal probability:

$$P(X\ge 84)\le\frac12\cdot\frac1{16}=\frac1{32}$$

**Step 4 — Convert to a number of people.**

$$1000\times\frac1{32}=31.25$$

So at most about 31 people score 84 or more. Since 70 jobs are available, a person scoring 84 is certainly among the top 70.

> [!success] Answer
> 
> At most $1000/32\approx31$ applicants can score $\ge 84$.
>
> Since there are 70 positions, the person scoring 84 **can count on getting a job**.

## Q3(b) — Binomial to Poisson, and calls at a switchboard (12 marks)

**Relation between binomial and Poisson.** The Poisson distribution is the limiting form of the binomial when the number of trials $n$ is very large, the success probability $p$ is very small, and the mean $np=\lambda$ stays fixed.

**Step 1 — Start from the binomial and put $p=\lambda/n$.**

$$b(x;n,p)=\binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x}$$

$$=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-x+1)}{x!}\left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^x\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n-x}$$

**Step 2 — Regroup the factors.**

$$=\frac{\lambda^x}{x!}\cdot\underbrace{1\left(1-\frac1n\right)\left(1-\frac2n\right)\cdots\left(1-\frac{x-1}{n}\right)}_{\to\,1}\cdot\underbrace{\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n}}_{\to\,e^{-\lambda}}\cdot\underbrace{\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{-x}}_{\to\,1}$$

**Step 3 — Take the limit.** As $n\to\infty$ with $\lambda=np$ fixed, using

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^n=e^{-\lambda}$$

we get

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}b(x;n,p)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!},\qquad x=0,1,2,\dots$$

which is the Poisson pmf.

Both distributions then have mean $\lambda=np$. The binomial variance $np(1-p)$ also tends to $\lambda$ because $1-p\to 1$. In practice the approximation is good when $n\ge 20$ and $p\le 0.05$ (or $n\ge100$, $np\le 10$).

**Problem.** Calls arrive at 0.5 per minute, so in a 5-minute period the mean is

$$\lambda=0.5\times5=2.5$$

With $X\sim\text{Poisson}(2.5)$:

$$\begin{aligned}
P(X=2)&=\frac{e^{-2.5}(2.5)^2}{2!}\\
&=\frac{0.082085\times6.25}{2}\\
&=0.2565
\end{aligned}$$

> [!success] Answer
> 
> Poisson is the limit of binomial as $n\to\infty$, $p\to0$, $np=\lambda$.
>
> $$P(\text{2 calls in 5 min})=\frac{e^{-2.5}\,2.5^2}{2!}\approx0.2565$$

## Q4(a) — Mode of the normal distribution, and the light bulbs (11 marks)

**Mode $=\mu$.** The normal density is

$$f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}},\qquad -\infty<x<\infty$$

The mode is the value of $x$ where $f(x)$ is maximum.

**Step 1 — First derivative.**

$$f'(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\cdot\left(-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\right)=-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\,f(x)$$

Since $f(x)>0$ for all $x$, $f'(x)=0$ only when $x=\mu$.

**Step 2 — Second derivative.**

$$f''(x)=-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}f(x)-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}f'(x)=\frac{f(x)}{\sigma^2}\left[\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2}-1\right]$$

At $x=\mu$:

$$f''(\mu)=-\frac{f(\mu)}{\sigma^2}<0$$

So $f$ has its maximum at $x=\mu$. The mode of the normal distribution is $\mu$, the same as its mean.

**Light bulbs.** $X\sim N(\mu=800,\ \sigma=40)$.

**Step 1 — Standardise.**

$$z_1=\frac{778-800}{40}=-0.55$$

$$z_2=\frac{834-800}{40}=0.85$$

**Step 2 — Read the table.**

$$\begin{aligned}
P(778<X<834)&=P(-0.55<Z<0.85)\\
&=\Phi(0.85)-\Phi(-0.55)\\
&=0.8023-0.2912\\
&=0.5111
\end{aligned}$$

> [!success] Answer
> 
> Mode $=\mu$ (shown by $f'(\mu)=0$ and $f''(\mu)<0$).
>
> $P(778<X<834)\approx0.5111$, i.e. about 51% of bulbs.

## Q4(b) — Pearson's r and rank correlation with repeated ranks (12 marks)

**Pearson's correlation coefficient** measures the strength and direction of the **linear** relationship between two quantitative variables $X$ and $Y$:

$$r=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\,\sigma_Y}$$

In computing form:

$$r=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{\sqrt{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}\ \sqrt{n\sum y^2-(\sum y)^2}},\qquad -1\le r\le 1$$

**Rank correlation with repeated observations.** Spearman's coefficient is

$$r_s=1-\frac{6\sum D^2}{n(n^2-1)}$$

where $D$ is the difference between the ranks of each pair.

When observations are repeated (tied), each tied value gets the **average** of the ranks it would have occupied. A correction $\frac{m^3-m}{12}$ is added to $\sum D^2$ for every group of $m$ tied values, in either series:

$$r_s=1-\frac{6\left[\sum D^2+\sum\frac{m^3-m}{12}\right]}{n(n^2-1)}$$

**Step 1 — Rank both series** in ascending order (smallest $=1$), averaging tied ranks.

| Store | $x$ | $R_x$ | $y$ | $R_y$ | $D=R_x-R_y$ | $D^2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50 | 1.5 | 11 | 1 | 0.5 | 0.25 |
| 2 | 50 | 1.5 | 13 | 3 | −1.5 | 2.25 |
| 3 | 55 | 3 | 14 | 5.5 | −2.5 | 6.25 |
| 4 | 60 | 5.5 | 16 | 9.5 | −4 | 16 |
| 5 | 65 | 9 | 16 | 9.5 | −0.5 | 0.25 |
| 6 | 65 | 9 | 15 | 7.5 | 1.5 | 2.25 |
| 7 | 65 | 9 | 15 | 7.5 | 1.5 | 2.25 |
| 8 | 60 | 5.5 | 14 | 5.5 | 0 | 0 |
| 9 | 60 | 5.5 | 13 | 3 | 2.5 | 6.25 |
| 10 | 60 | 5.5 | 13 | 3 | 2.5 | 6.25 |
| | | | | | Total | 42 |

**Step 2 — Tie corrections.**

Ties in $x$: 50 occurs twice ($m=2$), 60 four times ($m=4$), 65 three times ($m=3$).

Ties in $y$: 13 three times ($m=3$); 14, 15 and 16 each twice ($m=2$).

$$\sum\frac{m^3-m}{12}=\underbrace{0.5+5+2}_{x}+\underbrace{2+0.5+0.5+0.5}_{y}=7.5+3.5=11$$

**Step 3 — Compute $r_s$.**

$$\begin{aligned}
r_s&=1-\frac{6(42+11)}{10(10^2-1)}\\
&=1-\frac{318}{990}\\
&=1-0.3212\\
&=0.679
\end{aligned}$$

> $r_s\approx0.68$: a fairly high positive rank correlation — stores with higher sales tend to have higher expenses.

## Q4(c) — Objectives of correlation/regression, and a second-degree polynomial fit (12 marks)

**Objectives.**

Correlation analysis aims to find out whether two variables are related, and to measure the strength and direction of the relationship by a single number such as $r$.

Regression analysis aims to find the actual functional form of the relationship — an equation expressing a dependent variable in terms of an independent variable. This lets us estimate or predict the dependent variable for a given value of the independent variable, and measure how well the fitted equation explains the variation in the data (through the coefficient of determination).

**Fitting $y=a+bx+cx^2$.** By least squares, the normal equations are:

$$\sum y=na+b\sum x+c\sum x^2$$

$$\sum xy=a\sum x+b\sum x^2+c\sum x^3$$

$$\sum x^2y=a\sum x^2+b\sum x^3+c\sum x^4$$

**Step 1 — Calculation table.**

| $x$ | $y$ | $x^2$ | $x^3$ | $x^4$ | $xy$ | $x^2y$ | $y^2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 15 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 225 |
| 1 | 25 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 25 | 25 | 625 |
| 2 | 40 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 80 | 160 | 1600 |
| 3 | 55 | 9 | 27 | 81 | 165 | 495 | 3025 |
| 4 | 52 | 16 | 64 | 256 | 208 | 832 | 2704 |
| 5 | 43 | 25 | 125 | 625 | 215 | 1075 | 1849 |
| 15 | 230 | 55 | 225 | 979 | 693 | 2587 | 10028 |

**Step 2 — Substitute** ($n=6$):

$$230=6a+15b+55c\qquad(1)$$

$$693=15a+55b+225c\qquad(2)$$

$$2587=55a+225b+979c\qquad(3)$$

**Step 3 — Eliminate $a$.**

$(2)-2.5\times(1)$:

$$118=17.5b+87.5c\qquad(4)$$

$(3)-\frac{55}{6}\times(1)$:

$$478.667=87.5b+474.833c\qquad(5)$$

**Step 4 — Solve.**

$(5)-5\times(4)$:

$$-111.333=37.333c\ \Rightarrow\ c=-2.982$$

From (4):

$$b=\frac{118-87.5(-2.982)}{17.5}=21.654$$

From (1):

$$a=\frac{230-15(21.654)-55(-2.982)}{6}=11.536$$

So the fitted curve is

$$\hat y=11.536+21.654x-2.982x^2$$

**Step 5 — Coefficient of determination.**

Fitted values for $x=0,\dots,5$: $11.54,\ 30.21,\ 42.91,\ 49.66,\ 50.44,\ 45.25$.

Residuals $y-\hat y$: $3.46,\ -5.21,\ -2.91,\ 5.34,\ 1.56,\ -2.25$.

$$SSE=\sum(y-\hat y)^2=83.66$$

$$SST=\sum y^2-\frac{(\sum y)^2}{n}=10028-\frac{230^2}{6}=1211.33$$

$$R^2=1-\frac{SSE}{SST}=1-\frac{83.66}{1211.33}=0.931$$

So about 93.1% of the variation in rice yield is explained by the quadratic relationship with the nitrogen dose. The negative coefficient of $x^2$ shows the yield rises first and then falls at high doses.

## Q5(a) — Stem-and-leaf plots (10 marks)

A **stem-and-leaf plot** organises quantitative data so that it shows the shape of the distribution like a histogram, while still keeping every original value visible.

Each number is split into two parts: the **stem** (the leading digit or digits) and the **leaf** (the last digit). All values sharing the same stem are written on one row.

**How to create one.**

**Step 1 —** Decide how to split the numbers. For two-digit data, the tens digit is the stem and the units digit is the leaf.

**Step 2 —** Write the stems in a vertical column in increasing order, with a vertical line to their right.

**Step 3 —** Write the leaf of each data value on the row of its stem.

**Step 4 —** Arrange the leaves in each row in increasing order, and add a key such as "3 | 2 means 32".

**Example.** Data: 12, 15, 21, 24, 24, 27, 30, 33, 38, 41.

```
 1 | 2 5
 2 | 1 4 4 7
 3 | 0 3 8
 4 | 1          Key: 2 | 4 means 24
```

From this plot we see directly that most values lie in the twenties. We can read the minimum (12), maximum (41) and mode (24). The median is the average of the 5th and 6th values, $\frac{24+27}{2}=25.5$. Turning the plot sideways shows the shape of the distribution.

> [!success] Answer
> 
> Split each value into stem (leading digits) and leaf (last digit), list stems vertically, write ordered leaves beside them, and add a key.
>
> It shows the distribution shape while keeping the raw data.

## Q5(c) — Correcting mean and standard deviation (12 marks)

**Given / setup.** $n=200$, wrong mean $\bar x=60$, wrong SD $\sigma=20$. Wrongly taken: 3 and 67. Correct values: 13 and 17.

**Step 1 — Corrected sum.**

$$\sum x_{\text{wrong}}=n\bar x=200\times60=12000$$

$$\sum x_{\text{correct}}=12000-(3+67)+(13+17)=11960$$

**Step 2 — Corrected mean.**

$$\bar x_{\text{correct}}=\frac{11960}{200}=59.8$$

**Step 3 — Corrected sum of squares.** From $\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar x^2$ we have

$$\sum x^2=n(\sigma^2+\bar x^2)$$

So

$$\sum x^2_{\text{wrong}}=200(20^2+60^2)=200(400+3600)=800000$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\sum x^2_{\text{correct}}&=800000-(3^2+67^2)+(13^2+17^2)\\
&=800000-4498+458\\
&=795960
\end{aligned}$$

**Step 4 — Corrected SD.**

$$\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2_{\text{correct}}&=\frac{795960}{200}-(59.8)^2\\
&=3979.8-3576.04\\
&=403.76
\end{aligned}$$

$$\sigma_{\text{correct}}=\sqrt{403.76}=20.09$$

**Step 5 — Corrected coefficient of variation.**

$$CV=\frac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100\%=\frac{20.09}{59.8}\times100\%=33.60\%$$

> [!success] Answer
> 
> Correct mean $=59.8$
>
> Correct SD $=20.09$
>
> Correct CV $=33.60\%$

## Q6(b) — Central Limit Theorem, algorithm and applications (10 marks)

**Statement.** If $\bar X$ is the mean of a random sample of size $n$ from a population (of any shape) with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$, then as $n$ becomes large the sampling distribution of $\bar X$ approaches a normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2/n$:

$$Z=\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\ \longrightarrow\ N(0,1)\quad\text{as } n\to\infty$$

The approximation is generally good when $n\ge30$, whatever the shape of the population. If the population itself is normal, $\bar X$ is exactly normal for every $n$.

The theorem matters because it lets us use the normal table for problems about averages (and sums) even when the original population is not normal.

**Algorithm for solving CLT problems.**

**Step 1 —** Identify the population mean $\mu$, population SD $\sigma$ and sample size $n$. Check that $n$ is large (at least about 30) or that the population is normal.

**Step 2 —** Write the mean and standard error of the sample mean:

$$\mu_{\bar X}=\mu,\qquad \sigma_{\bar X}=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$$

(For a sum $T=n\bar X$, use mean $n\mu$ and SD $\sigma\sqrt n$.)

**Step 3 —** Convert the required value(s) of $\bar x$ into $z$:

$$z=\frac{\bar x-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$$

**Step 4 —** Read the probability from the standard normal table, using $P(Z<z)=\Phi(z)$, $P(Z>z)=1-\Phi(z)$ and $P(a<Z<b)=\Phi(b)-\Phi(a)$.

**Step 5 —** State the answer in the words of the problem.

**Applications in Computer Science.**

**Performance analysis.** The average response time of a server over many requests is approximately normal, so confidence intervals and service-level guarantees can be computed even though individual response times are highly skewed.

**A/B testing.** For websites and apps, the CLT justifies the z-test on average click rates or conversion rates.

**Networking.** The total number of packets or bytes arriving in a time window (a sum of many independent contributions) is modelled as normal for buffer sizing.

**Machine learning.** The error of an average over mini-batches (stochastic gradient) and the accuracy measured on a large test set are approximately normal, which allows error bars and significance tests.

**Simulation and randomized algorithms.** In Monte Carlo methods, the average of many random runs is approximately normal, which gives the error of the estimate as $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

## Q6(c) — Stratified sampling, and testing the delivery-time claim (12 marks)

**Stratified random sampling.** The population is first divided into non-overlapping groups called **strata**, such that units inside each stratum are similar (homogeneous) while the strata differ from each other.

A simple random sample is then drawn independently from every stratum, usually with sample size proportional to the stratum size, and these samples are combined. This gives more precise estimates than simple random sampling and guarantees that every important subgroup is represented.

**Example.** To estimate the average CGPA of a university of 10,000 students — 4,000 in engineering, 3,500 in science and 2,500 in arts — a stratified sample of 200 would take 80 engineering, 70 science and 50 arts students, each chosen at random within their faculty.

**Test.** Claim: mean delivery time is less than 120 minutes. Given $\sigma=30$, $n=49$, $\bar x=100$.

**Hypothesis.**

$$H_0:\mu=120\quad\text{against}\quad H_1:\mu<120\ \ (\text{left-tailed})$$

**Level of significance.** $\alpha=0.05$.

**Test statistic** ($\sigma$ known, large sample):

$$z=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$$

**Critical region.** $z<-1.645$.

**Calculated value.**

$$\begin{aligned}
z&=\frac{100-120}{30/\sqrt{49}}\\
&=\frac{-20}{30/7}\\
&=\frac{-20}{4.286}\\
&=-4.67
\end{aligned}$$

**Decision.** $z=-4.67<-1.645$, so it falls in the critical region; we reject $H_0$.

**Comment.** There is enough evidence at the 5% level to support the shop's claim that the mean delivery time is less than 120 minutes.

> [!success] Answer
> 
> $z=-4.67<-1.645$ ⇒ reject $H_0$.
>
> The claim that mean delivery time is below 120 minutes is supported.

Concept: [[S1 Introduction to Statistics Data and Sampling]] · [[S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests]]
